Once you start wanting other things, you won't be able to focus completely on what is truly your own good.

meditations_book-03.originalText: For it is not lawful, that anything that is of another and inferior kind and nature, be it what it will, as either popular applause, or honour, or riches, or pleasures; should be suffered to confront and contest as it were, with that which is rational, and operatively good. For all these things, if once though but for a while, they begin to please, they presently prevail, and pervert a man's mind, or turn a man from the right way. Do thou therefore I say absolutely and freely make choice of that which is best, and stick unto it. Now, that they say is best, which is most profitable. If they mean profitable to man as he is a rational man, stand thou to it, and maintain it; but if they mean profitable, as he is a creature, only reject it; and from this thy tenet and conclusion keep off carefully all plausible shows and colours of external appearance, that thou mayest be able to discern things rightly.
meditations_book-03.plainEnglish: Don't let anything lesser compete with what is rational and good. Things like popularity, honor, wealth, or pleasure should not be allowed to challenge your reason. These things are tempting. If you give them even a little space, they quickly take over. They twist your mind and pull you off course. So make your choice clearly and stick with it. Choose what is truly best. People say the most profitable thing is best. If they mean profitable for humans as rational beings, then hold to that. But if they just mean profitable as mere creatures, reject it. Guard yourself carefully against anything that looks appealing on the surface. This way you can see things clearly.

meditations_book-03.originalText:
Never esteem of anything as profitable, which shall ever constrain
thee either to break thy faith, or to lose thy modesty; to hate any man,
to suspect, to curse, to dissemble, to lust after anything, that
requireth the secret of walls or veils. But he that preferreth before
all things his rational part and spirit, and the sacred mysteries of
virtue which issueth from it, he shall never lament and exclaim, never
sigh; he shall never want either solitude or company: and which is
chiefest of all, he shall live without either desire or fear. And as for
life, whether for a long or short time he shall enjoy his soul thus
compassed about with a body, he is altogether indifferent. For if even
now he were to depart, he is as ready for it, as for any other action,
which may be performed with modesty and decency. For all his life long,
this is his only care, that his mind may always be occupied in such
intentions and objects, as are proper to a rational sociable creature.
meditations_book-03.plainEnglish: Never think something is good for you if it forces you to break promises, lose your dignity, hate anyone, be suspicious, curse, lie, or crave things you must hide. But the person who puts their reason and spirit first — and the sacred truths that come from virtue — will never complain or cry out. They will never sigh. They will never need to be alone or with others. Most important of all, they will live without desire or fear. Whether they live a long life or short life in this body, it makes no difference to them. If they had to die right now, they would be as ready for that as for any other decent action. All their life, they care about only one thing: keeping their mind focused on thoughts and goals that fit a reasonable, social person.

meditations_book-03.originalText:
In the mind that is once truly disciplined and purged, thou canst
not find anything, either foul or impure, or as it were festered:
nothing that is either servile, or affected: no partial tie; no
malicious averseness; nothing obnoxious; nothing concealed. The life of
such an one, death can never surprise as imperfect; as of an actor, that
should die before he had ended, or the play itself were at an end, a man
might speak.
meditations_book-03.plainEnglish: In a mind that is truly disciplined and cleaned out, you won't find anything foul or impure, or anything rotting. Nothing servile or fake. No favoritism. No bitter hatred. Nothing harmful. Nothing hidden. Death can never catch such a person off guard, as if their life were incomplete. You couldn't say of them what you might say of an actor who dies before finishing their part or before the play ends.

meditations_book-03.originalText: Use thine opinative faculty with all honour and respect, for in her indeed is all: that thy opinion do not beget in thy understanding anything contrary to either nature, or the proper constitution of a rational creature. The end and object of a rational constitution is, to do nothing rashly, to be kindly affected towards men, and in all things willingly to submit unto the gods.
meditations_book-03.plainEnglish: Use your power to form opinions with care and respect. Everything depends on this. Don't let your opinions create thoughts that go against nature or against what it means to be a rational person. The goal of being rational is simple: don't act rashly, treat people with kindness, and accept what the gods send your way.

meditations_book-03.originalText: Casting therefore all other things aside, keep thyself to these few, and remember withal that no man properly can be said to live more than that which is now present, which is but a moment of time. Whatsoever is besides either is already past, or uncertain. The time therefore that any man doth live, is but a little, and the place where he liveth, is but a very little corner of the earth, and the greatest fame that can remain of a man after his death, even that is but little, and that too, such as it is whilst it is, is by the succession of silly mortal men preserved, who likewise shall shortly die, and even whiles they live know not what in very deed they themselves are: and much less can know one, who long before is dead and gone.
meditations_book-03.plainEnglish: So put aside all other things and focus on these few truths. Remember that no one really lives more than this present moment — just a brief instant. Everything else is either past or uncertain. The time any person lives is short. The place where they live is just a tiny corner of the earth. Even the greatest fame someone can have after death is small. And that fame depends on foolish mortals to keep it alive — people who will soon die themselves. Even while they're alive, they don't know what they really are, much less understand someone who died long ago.

meditations_book-03.originalText:
To these ever-present helps and mementoes, let one more be added,
ever to make a particular description and delineation as it were of
every object that presents itself to thy mind, that thou mayest wholly
and throughly contemplate it, in its own proper nature, bare and naked;
wholly, and severally; divided into its several parts and quarters: and
then by thyself in thy mind, to call both it, and those things of which
it doth consist, and in which it shall be resolved, by their own proper
true names, and appellations. For there is nothing so effectual to beget
true magnanimity, as to be able truly and methodically to examine and
consider all things that happen in this life, and so to penetrate
into their natures, that at the same time, this also may concur in our
apprehensions: what is the true use of it? and what is the true nature
of this universe, to which it is useful? how much in regard of the
universe may it be esteemed? how much in regard of man, a citizen of the
supreme city, of which all other cities in the world are as it were but
houses and families?
meditations_book-03.plainEnglish:
To these constant helps and reminders, add one more. Always make a clear picture of every object that comes to your mind. Study it completely and thoroughly in its bare, true nature. Look at it whole, then separately. Break it down into its parts. Then call both the thing itself and its components by their real names.

Nothing builds true greatness of spirit like being able to examine and consider all things that happen in life truly and systematically. Pierce through to their real natures. At the same time, ask yourself: what is its real purpose? What is the nature of this universe that it serves? How much does it matter to the universe? How much does it matter to a human being — a citizen of the greatest city, of which all other cities are just houses and families?

meditations_book-03.originalText:
What is this, that now my fancy is set upon? of what things doth
it consist? how long can it last? which of all the virtues is the proper
virtue for this present use? as whether meekness, fortitude, truth,
faith, sincerity, contentation, or any of the rest? Of everything
therefore thou must use thyself to say, This immediately comes from God,
this by that fatal connection, and concatenation of things, or (which
almost comes to one) by some coincidental casualty. And as for this, it
proceeds from my neighbour, my kinsman, my fellow: through his ignorance
indeed, because he knows not what is truly natural unto him: but I know
it, and therefore carry myself towards him according to the natural law
of fellowship; that is kindly, and justly. As for those things that of
themselves are altogether indifferent, as in my best judgment I conceive
everything to deserve more or less, so I carry myself towards it.
meditations_book-03.plainEnglish: What is this thing I'm focused on right now? What parts make it up? How long will it last? Which virtue should I use here? Should I be gentle, brave, honest, faithful, sincere, content, or something else? For everything that happens, you must tell yourself: This comes straight from God. This comes from the chain of cause and effect. Or this just happened by chance. As for this situation, it comes from my neighbor, my relative, my fellow human. Yes, they act from ignorance because they don't know what's truly natural for them. But I do know. So I treat them according to the natural law of fellowship — with kindness and justice. For those things that don't really matter either way, I respond based on how much I think each one deserves.

meditations_book-03.originalText:
If thou shalt intend that which is present, following the rule of
right and reason carefully, solidly, meekly, and shalt not intermix
any other businesses, but shall study this only to preserve thy spirit
unpolluted, and pure, and shall cleave unto him without either hope
or fear of anything, in all things that thou shalt either do or speak,
contenting thyself with heroical truth, thou shalt live happily; and
from this, there is no man that can hinder thee.
meditations_book-03.plainEnglish: If you focus on what is happening right now, following what is right and reasonable with care and strength and gentleness, and if you don't get distracted by other things, but work only to keep your spirit clean and pure, and if you hold onto God without hoping for anything or fearing anything, and if in everything you do or say you are content with simple truth, then you will live happily. And no one can stop you from this.

meditations_book-03.originalText:
As physicians and chirurgeons have always their instruments ready
at hand for all sudden cures; so have thou always thy dogmata in a
readiness for the knowledge of things, both divine and human: and
whatsoever thou dost, even in the smallest things that thou dost, thou
must ever remember that mutual relation, and connection that is between
these two things divine, and things human. For without relation unto
God, thou shalt never speed in any worldly actions; nor on the other
side in any divine, without some respect had to things human.
meditations_book-03.plainEnglish: Just as doctors and surgeons keep their tools ready for emergencies, you should keep your principles ready for understanding both divine and human matters. Whatever you do, even the smallest actions, remember that divine things and human things are connected. You cannot succeed in worldly matters without considering God. And you cannot handle divine matters without understanding human concerns.

meditations_book-03.originalText:
Be not deceived; for thou shalt never live to read thy moral
commentaries, nor the acts of the famous Romans and Grecians; nor those
excerpta from several books; all which thou hadst provided and laid
up for thyself against thine old age. Hasten therefore to an end, and
giving over all vain hopes, help thyself in time if thou carest for
thyself, as thou oughtest to do.
meditations_book-03.plainEnglish: Don't fool yourself. You will never live to read your moral commentaries, or the acts of famous Romans and Greeks, or those excerpts from books — all the things you have been saving for your old age. So hurry to finish what matters. Give up these empty hopes. Help yourself now, while you still can, if you care about yourself at all.

meditations_book-03.originalText:
To steal, to sow, to buy, to be at rest, to see what is to be done
(which is not seen by the eyes, but by another kind of sight:) what
these words mean, and how many ways to be understood, they do not
understand. The body, the soul, the understanding. As the senses
naturally belong to the body, and the desires and affections to the
soul, so do the dogmata to the understanding.
meditations_book-03.plainEnglish: To steal, to plant, to buy, to rest, to see what needs to be done — this kind of seeing isn't with the eyes, but with a different kind of sight. People don't understand what these words really mean or how many ways they can be taken. The body, the soul, the mind. Just as the senses belong naturally to the body, and desires and feelings belong to the soul, so do beliefs and principles belong to the mind.

meditations_book-03.originalText: To be capable of fancies and imaginations, is common to man and beast. To be violently drawn and moved by the lusts and desires of the soul, is proper to wild beasts and monsters, such as Phalaris and Nero were. To follow reason for ordinary duties and actions is common to them also, who believe not that there be any gods, and for their advantage would make no conscience to betray their own country; and who when once the doors be shut upon them, dare do anything.
meditations_book-03.plainEnglish: Animals and humans both can imagine things. Wild beasts and monsters like Phalaris and Nero are driven by violent desires. Following reason for everyday tasks is also common to people who don't believe in gods, who would betray their country for gain, and who do shameful things behind closed doors.

meditations_book-03.originalText: If therefore all things else be common to these likewise, it follows, that for a man to like and embrace all things that happen and are destinated unto him, and not to trouble and molest that spirit which is seated in the temple of his own breast, with a multitude of vain fancies and imaginations, but to keep him propitious and to obey him as a god, never either speaking anything contrary to truth, or doing anything contrary to justice, is the only true property of a good man. And such a one, though no man should believe that he liveth as he doth, either sincerely and conscionably, or cheerful and contentedly; yet is he neither with any man at all angry for it, nor diverted by it from the way that leadeth to the end of his life, through which a man must pass pure, ever ready to depart, and willing of himself without any compulsion to fit and accommodate himself to his proper lot and portion.
meditations_book-03.plainEnglish: If this is true, then a good person should accept everything that happens to them without complaint. They should not trouble the spirit within them with useless thoughts and fantasies. Instead, they should keep that inner spirit calm and obey it like a god. They should never speak against truth or act against justice. This is what truly makes someone good. Even if no one believes they live honestly, consciously, or happily, they should not get angry about it. They should not let it pull them off the path that leads to the end of life. A person must walk that path purely, always ready to leave, and willing to accept their fate without being forced to.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
That inward mistress part of man if it be in its own true natural
temper, is towards all worldly chances and events ever so disposed and
affected, that it will easily turn and apply itself to that which may
be, and is within its own power to compass, when that cannot be which at
first it intended. For it never doth absolutely addict and apply itself
to any one object, but whatsoever it is that it doth now intend and
prosecute, it doth prosecute it with exception and reservation; so that
whatsoever it is that falls out contrary to its first intentions, even
that afterwards it makes its proper object. Even as the fire when it
prevails upon those things that are in his way; by which things indeed a
little fire would have been quenched, but a great fire doth soon turn to
its own nature, and so consume whatsoever comes in his way: yea by those
very things it is made greater and greater.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: The ruling part of your mind, when it's working right, stays flexible toward whatever happens in the world. It can easily shift to what's actually possible when its first plan doesn't work out. It never locks itself completely onto one goal. Whatever it's working toward, it holds lightly — ready to change course. When things go against what it first wanted, it makes that setback into its new material to work with. It's like fire meeting obstacles in its path. A small fire gets put out by what blocks it. But a big fire turns everything into fuel. It consumes whatever gets in its way and grows stronger from it.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Let nothing be done rashly, and at random, but all things according
to the most exact and perfect rules of art.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Don't do anything hastily or carelessly. Do everything according to the most precise and perfect principles.

meditations_book-04.originalText: They seek for themselves private retiring places, as country villages, the sea-shore, mountains; yea thou thyself art wont to long much after such places. But all this thou must know proceeds from simplicity in the highest degree. At what time soever thou wilt, it is in thy power to retire into thyself, and to be at rest, and free from all businesses. A man cannot any whither retire better than to his own soul; he especially who is beforehand provided of such things within, which whensoever he doth withdraw himself to look in, may presently afford unto him perfect ease and tranquillity. By tranquillity I understand a decent orderly disposition and carriage, free from all confusion and tumultuousness. Afford then thyself this retiring continually, and thereby refresh and renew thyself. Let these precepts be brief and fundamental, which as soon as thou dost call them to mind, may suffice thee to purge thy soul throughly, and to send thee away well pleased with those things whatsoever they be, which now again after this short withdrawing of thy soul into herself thou dost return unto.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: People look for private places to escape to — country villages, the seashore, mountains. You yourself often crave such places. But you should know this comes from the simplest kind of thinking. You can retire into yourself whenever you want, and find rest there, free from all troubles. No one can retreat to a better place than his own soul. This is especially true if he has already prepared good things within himself. When he turns inward to look, he can immediately find perfect peace and calm. By calm I mean a proper, orderly state of mind, free from all confusion and chaos. Give yourself this retreat constantly, and refresh yourself through it. Keep these ideas brief and basic. As soon as you remember them, they should be enough to cleanse your soul completely. Then you can return to whatever you were doing, pleased with those things, after this short withdrawal into yourself.

meditations_book-04.originalText: For what is it that thou art offended at? Can it be at the wickedness of men, when thou dost call to mind this conclusion, that all reasonable creatures are made one for another? and that it is part of justice to bear with them? and that it is against their wills that they offend? and how many already, who once likewise prosecuted their enmities, suspected, hated, and fiercely contended, are now long ago stretched out, and reduced unto ashes? It is time for thee to make an end.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: What are you upset about? Are you offended by people's bad behavior? Remember that all thinking beings were made to help each other. It's part of justice to put up with them. They don't mean to do wrong. And think about this — how many people who once fought bitterly, who hated and suspected each other, are now long dead and turned to ash? It's time to let it go.

meditations_book-04.originalText: As for those things which among the common chances of the world happen unto thee as thy particular lot and portion, canst thou be displeased with any of them, when thou dost call that our ordinary dilemma to mind, either a providence, or Democritus his atoms; and with it, whatsoever we brought to prove that the whole world is as it were one city? And as for thy body, what canst thou fear, if thou dost consider that thy mind and understanding, when once it hath recollected itself, and knows its own power, hath in this life and breath (whether it run smoothly and gently, or whether harshly and rudely), no interest at all, but is altogether indifferent: and whatsoever else thou hast heard and assented unto concerning either pain or pleasure? But the care of thine honour and reputation will perchance distract thee?
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: When things happen to you in life, can you really be upset about them? Remember our choice: either the universe has a plan, or it's just random atoms colliding. Either way, we proved that the whole world is like one city. As for your body, what is there to fear? Your mind, once it remembers its own strength, doesn't care whether life goes smoothly or roughly. It stays detached. You've heard this before about pain and pleasure. But maybe worry about your reputation still distracts you?

meditations_book-04.originalText: How can that be, if thou dost look back, and consider both how quickly all things that are, are forgotten, and what an immense chaos of eternity was before, and will follow after all things: and the vanity of praise, and the inconstancy and variableness of human judgments and opinions, and the narrowness of the place, wherein it is limited and circumscribed? For the whole earth is but as one point; and of it, this inhabited part of it, is but a very little part; and of this part, how many in number, and what manner of men are they, that will commend thee? What remains then, but that thou often put in practice this kind of retiring of thyself, to this little part of thyself; and above all things, keep thyself from distraction, and intend not anything vehemently, but be free and consider all things, as a man whose proper object is Virtue, as a man whose true nature is to be kind and sociable, as a citizen, as a mortal creature.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: How can any of this matter when you look back and see how quickly everything gets forgotten? Think about the endless chaos of time before us and after us. Think about how empty praise really is. Think about how people's opinions shift and change. Think about how small the place is where this all happens. The whole earth is just a dot. The part we live on is tiny. And of that tiny part, how many people are there who might praise you? What kind of people are they anyway? What's left then is to practice pulling back into yourself often. Most important of all, don't let yourself get scattered. Don't chase after anything too hard. Stay free and look at everything simply. Remember you're someone whose goal is virtue. Remember you're someone whose nature is to be kind and connected to others. You're a citizen. You're going to die.

meditations_book-04.originalText: Among other things, which to consider, and look into thou must use to withdraw thyself, let those two be among the most obvious and at hand. One, that the things or objects themselves reach not unto the soul, but stand without still and quiet, and that it is from the opinion only which is within, that all the tumult and all the trouble doth proceed. The next, that all these things, which now thou seest, shall within a very little while be changed, and be no more: and ever call to mind, how many changes and alterations in the world thou thyself hast already been an eyewitness of in thy time. This world is mere change, and this life, opinion.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Among other things you can use to pull yourself back, keep these two close at hand. First, that things themselves don't reach your soul. They stay outside, quiet and still. All the noise and trouble comes from your opinions about them. Second, that everything you see now will change very soon and be gone. Remember how many changes you have already witnessed in your lifetime. This world is nothing but change, and this life is just opinion.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
If to understand and to be reasonable be common unto all men, then
is that reason, for which we are termed reasonable, common unto all. If
reason is general, then is that reason also, which prescribeth what is
to be done and what not, common unto all. If that, then law. If law,
then are we fellow-citizens. If so, then are we partners in some one
commonweal. If so, then the world is as it were a city. For which other
commonweal is it, that all men can be said to be members of? From this
common city it is, that understanding, reason, and law is derived unto
us, for from whence else? For as that which in me is earthly I have from
some common earth; and that which is moist from some other element is
imparted; as my breath and life hath its proper fountain; and that
likewise which is dry and fiery in me: (for there is nothing which doth
not proceed from something; as also there is nothing that can be reduced
unto mere nothing:) so also is there some common beginning from whence
my understanding hath proceeded.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: If all people can understand and think clearly, then the ability to reason is shared by everyone. If reasoning is universal, then the part of reason that tells us what to do and what not to do is also shared. If that's true, then law is shared. If law is shared, then we are all fellow citizens. If we are fellow citizens, then we belong to one common state. If that's so, then the world is like a single city. What other state could include all people as members? From this shared city we get our understanding, our reason, and our laws. Where else could they come from? Just as the earthy part of me comes from common earth, and the wet part comes from water, and my breath and life have their source, and the dry and fiery parts in me have their origin — nothing comes from nowhere, and nothing becomes nothing — so my understanding must also come from some shared source.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
As generation is, so also death, a secret of nature's wisdom: a
mixture of elements, resolved into the same elements again, a thing
surely which no man ought to be ashamed of: in a series of other fatal
events and consequences, which a rational creature is subject unto,
not improper or incongruous, nor contrary to the natural and proper
constitution of man himself.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Birth is natural, and so is death — both are part of nature's wisdom. We are made of elements that return to the same elements when we die. No one should be ashamed of this. It's just one event in a series of things that happen to thinking creatures like us. It's not wrong or out of place. It fits with how humans are naturally made.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Such and such things, from such and such causes, must of necessity
proceed. He that would not have such things to happen, is as he that
would have the fig-tree grow without any sap or moisture. In sum,
remember this, that within a very little while, both thou and he shall
both be dead, and after a little while more, not so much as your names
and memories shall be remaining.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: These things happen for these reasons. They have to happen. Someone who doesn't want these things to happen is like someone who wants a fig tree to grow without sap. Remember this: very soon, both you and he will be dead. And soon after that, even your names will be forgotten.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Let opinion be taken away, and no man will think himself wronged.
If no man shall think himself wronged, then is there no more any such
thing as wrong. That which makes not man himself the worse, cannot
make his life the worse, neither can it hurt him either inwardly
or outwardly. It was expedient in nature that it should be so, and
therefore necessary.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Take away opinion, and no one will think they've been wronged. If no one thinks they've been wronged, then there is no such thing as wrong. What doesn't make a person worse cannot make his life worse. It cannot hurt him inside or out. Nature made it this way because it had to be so.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Whatsoever doth happen in the world, doth happen justly, and so if
thou dost well take heed, thou shalt find it. I say not only in right
order by a series of inevitable consequences, but according to justice
and as it were by way of equal distribution, according to the true worth
of everything. Continue then to take notice of it, as thou hast begun,
and whatsoever thou dost, do it not without this proviso, that it be a
thing of that nature that a good man (as the word good is properly
taken) may do it. This observe carefully in every action.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Whatever happens in the world happens justly. If you pay close attention, you will see this. I don't just mean things follow in logical order. I mean they happen according to true justice, like fair distribution based on what everything truly deserves. Keep noticing this, as you have started to do. Whatever you do, make sure it's something a truly good person would do. Watch for this in every action.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Conceit no such things, as he that wrongeth thee conceiveth,
or would have thee to conceive, but look into the matter itself, and see
what it is in very truth.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Don't accept the twisted ideas of someone who wrongs you, or let them shape how you see things. Look at the situation itself and see what it really is.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
These two rules, thou must have always in a readiness. First, do
nothing at all, but what reason proceeding from that regal and supreme
part, shall for the good and benefit of men, suggest unto thee. And
secondly, if any man that is present shall be able to rectify thee or to
turn thee from some erroneous persuasion, that thou be always ready to
change thy mind, and this change to proceed, not from any respect of any
pleasure or credit thereon depending, but always from some probable
apparent ground of justice, or of some public good thereby to be
furthered; or from some other such inducement.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Keep these two rules ready at all times. First, do nothing unless your reason — that royal part of your mind — tells you it will help other people. Second, if someone can correct you or show you where you're wrong, be ready to change your mind. Don't change because it feels good or makes you look better. Change only when you see real evidence of what's right, or what serves the common good, or some other worthy reason.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Hast thou reason? I have. Why then makest thou not use of it? For if
thy reason do her part, what more canst thou require?
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Do you have reason? I do. Then why don't you use it? If your reason does its job, what more could you need?

meditations_book-04.originalText:
As a part hitherto thou hast had a particular subsistence: and now
shalt thou vanish away into the common substance of Him, who first begot
thee, or rather thou shalt be resumed again into that original rational
substance, out of which all others have issued, and are propagated.
Many small pieces of frankincense are set upon the same altar, one drops
first and is consumed, another after; and it comes all to one.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Until now you have existed as a separate part. Soon you will dissolve back into the common substance of the one who first created you. Or rather, you will return to that original rational substance from which everything else came. Many small pieces of incense are placed on the same altar. One burns up first, then another. In the end, it all comes to the same thing.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Within ten days, if so happen, thou shalt be esteemed a god of
them, who now if thou shalt return to the dogmata and to the honouring
of reason, will esteem of thee no better than of a mere brute, and of an
ape.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: In ten days, if it happens, you'll be seen as a god by the same people who right now would think of you as nothing more than a dumb animal or an ape—if you went back to old beliefs and stopped honoring reason.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Not as though thou hadst thousands of years to live. Death hangs
over thee: whilst yet thou livest, whilst thou mayest, be good.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Not as if you had thousands of years to live. Death hangs over you. While you are still alive, while you can, be good.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Now much time and leisure doth he gain, who is not curious to know
what his neighbour hath said, or hath done, or hath attempted, but only
what he doth himself, that it may be just and holy? or to express it in
Agathos' words, Not to look about upon the evil conditions of others,
but to run on straight in the line, without any loose and extravagant
agitation.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: How much time and peace you gain when you don't worry about what your neighbor said, did, or tried to do. Focus only on your own actions — that they may be just and good. As Agathos said: Don't look around at the faults of others, but run straight ahead without getting distracted or agitated.

meditations_book-04.originalText: He who is greedy of credit and reputation after his death, doth not consider, that they themselves by whom he is remembered, shall soon after every one of them be dead; and they likewise that succeed those; until at last all memory, which hitherto by the succession of men admiring and soon after dying hath had its course, be quite extinct. But suppose that both they that shall remember thee, and thy memory with them should be immortal, what is that to thee? I will not say to thee after thou art dead; but even to thee living, what is thy praise? But only for a secret and politic consideration, which we call οἰκονομίαν, or dispensation.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish:
Someone who craves fame and wants to be remembered after death doesn't think this through. The people who remember him will soon die too. And the people who come after them will also die. Eventually all memory of him will disappear completely. This chain of people admiring him and then dying will finally end.

But let's say the people who remember you and your memory itself could last forever. What good would that do you? I won't even ask what good it does after you're dead. What good does praise do you even while you're alive? It only helps for practical reasons — what we might call good management.

meditations_book-04.originalText: For as for that, that it is the gift of nature, whatsoever is commended in thee, what might be objected from thence, let that now that we are upon another consideration be omitted as unseasonable. That which is fair and goodly, whatsoever it be, and in what respect soever it be, that it is fair and goodly, it is so of itself, and terminates in itself, not admitting praise as a part or member: that therefore which is praised, is not thereby made either better or worse. This I understand even of those things, that are commonly called fair and good, as those which are commended either for the matter itself, or for curious workmanship. As for that which is truly good, what can it stand in need of more than either justice or truth; or more than either kindness and modesty? Which of all those, either becomes good or fair, because commended; or dispraised suffers any damage? Doth the emerald become worse in itself, or more vile if it be not commended? Doth gold, or ivory, or purple? Is there anything that doth though never so common, as a knife, a flower, or a tree?
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Whatever good qualities you have that come naturally to you — let's set that aside for now, since we're talking about something else. Anything that is truly beautiful or good is beautiful and good in itself. It doesn't need praise to complete it. So the thing that gets praised isn't made better or worse by the praise. I mean this even for things we usually call beautiful and good — things praised for their materials or skilled craftsmanship. As for what is truly good, what more does it need beyond justice or truth? What more than kindness and humility? Which of these becomes good or beautiful because someone praises it? Or gets damaged when criticized? Does an emerald become worse if no one praises it? Do gold, ivory, or purple fabric? Is there anything — even common things like a knife, a flower, or a tree — that changes based on praise?

meditations_book-04.originalText:
If so be that the souls remain after death (say they that will not
believe it); how is the air from all eternity able to contain them? How
is the earth (say I) ever from that time able to Contain the bodies
of them that are buried? For as here the change and resolution of dead
bodies into another kind of subsistence (whatsoever it be;) makes place
for other dead bodies: so the souls after death transferred into the
air, after they have conversed there a while, are either by way of
transmutation, or transfusion, or conflagration, received again into
that original rational substance, from which all others do proceed:
and so give way to those souls, who before coupled and associated unto
bodies, now begin to subsist single.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: If souls do survive death (as some people claim), how could the air hold them all forever? How could the earth hold all the buried bodies? Here on earth, dead bodies decay and change into something else. This makes room for new bodies. The same thing must happen with souls. After death, they move into the air for a while. Then they change or merge back into the original source that all souls come from. This makes room for new souls that were once joined to bodies and now exist alone.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
This, upon a supposition that the
souls after death do for a while subsist single, may be answered. And
here, (besides the number of bodies, so buried and contained by the
earth), we may further consider the number of several beasts, eaten
by us men, and by other creatures. For notwithstanding that such a
multitude of them is daily consumed, and as it were buried in the bodies
of the eaters, yet is the same place and body able to contain them, by
reason of their conversion, partly into blood, partly into air and fire.
What in these things is the speculation of truth? to divide things into
that which is passive and material; and that which is active and formal.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: This can be explained if we assume souls exist alone for a while after death. Think about this: beyond all the bodies buried in the earth, consider how many animals we and other creatures eat every day. Despite this huge number being consumed and buried in the bodies that eat them, the same space can hold them all. This happens because they transform — some into blood, some into air and fire. What's the real insight here? We must separate things into what receives action (matter) and what gives action (form).

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Not to wander out of the way, but upon every motion and desire,
to perform that which is just: and ever to be careful to attain to the
true natural apprehension of every fancy, that presents itself.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Don't get off track. With every impulse and desire, do what is right. And always be careful to see clearly what every thought or impression really is.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Whatsoever is expedient unto thee, O World, is expedient unto me;
nothing can either be 'unseasonable unto me, or out of date, which unto
thee is seasonable. Whatsoever thy seasons bear, shall ever by me be
esteemed as happy fruit, and increase. O Nature! from thee are all
things, in thee all things subsist, and to thee all tend. Could he say
of Athens, Thou lovely city of Cecrops; and shalt not thou say of the
world, Thou lovely city of God?
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Whatever works for you, O World, works for me. Nothing can be out of time for me if it's the right time for you. Whatever your seasons bring, I will always welcome as good fruit. O Nature! All things come from you, exist in you, and return to you. If someone could say of Athens, 'You lovely city of Cecrops,' shouldn't I say of the world, 'You lovely city of God?'

meditations_book-04.originalText:
They will say commonly, Meddle not with many things, if thou wilt
live cheerfully. Certainly there is nothing better, than for a man
to confine himself to necessary actions; to such and so many only, as
reason in a creature that knows itself born for society, will command
and enjoin. This will not only procure that cheerfulness, which from the
goodness, but that also, which from the paucity of actions doth usually
proceed. For since it is so, that most of those things, which we either
speak or do, are unnecessary; if a man shall cut them off, it must needs
follow that he shall thereby gain much leisure, and save much trouble,
and therefore at every action a man must privately by way of admonition
suggest unto himself, What? may not this that now I go about, be of the
number of unnecessary actions? Neither must he use himself to cut off
actions only, but thoughts and imaginations also, that are unnecessary
for so will unnecessary consequent actions the better be prevented and
cut off.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: People often say, "Don't get involved in too many things if you want to be happy." There's truth in this. The best thing you can do is stick to necessary actions only — the ones that reason commands in someone who knows they were born to live with others. This brings two kinds of happiness: the joy that comes from doing good, and the peace that comes from doing less. Most of what we say and do is unnecessary. Cut these things out and you'll have more time and less trouble. So before each action, ask yourself: "Is this something I actually need to do?" Don't just cut out unnecessary actions — cut out unnecessary thoughts too. When you stop the pointless thinking, you prevent the pointless actions that follow.

meditations_book-04.originalText: Try also how a good man's life; (of one, who is well pleased with those things whatsoever, which among the common changes and chances of this world fall to his own lot and share; and can live well contented and fully satisfied in the justice of his own proper present action, and in the goodness of his disposition for the future:) will agree with thee. Thou hast had experience of that other kind of life: make now trial of this also. Trouble not thyself any more henceforth, reduce thyself unto perfect simplicity.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Try living like a good person. Someone who accepts whatever happens to him in this world. Someone who is content with doing what's right now and keeping a good heart for the future. See how that feels to you. You have tried the other way of living. Now try this way. Stop troubling yourself from now on. Make your life simple.

meditations_book-04.originalText: Doth any man offend? It is against himself that he doth offend: why should it trouble thee? Hath anything happened unto thee? It is well, whatsoever it be, it is that which of all the common chances of the world from the very beginning in the series of all other things that have, or shall happen, was destinated and appointed unto thee. To comprehend all in a few words, our life is short; we must endeavour to gain the present time with best discretion and justice. Use recreation with sobriety.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Does someone offend you? They harm themselves, not you. Why let it bother you? Has something happened to you? Good. Whatever it is, it was meant for you from the beginning of time. It's part of the pattern of everything that has happened or will happen. To sum it all up: life is short. We must make the most of the present moment with wisdom and fairness. Enjoy yourself, but stay balanced.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Either this world is a κόσμος or comely piece, because all
disposed and governed by certain order: or if it be a mixture, though
confused, yet still it is a comely piece. For is it possible that in
thee there should be any beauty at all, and that in the whole world
there should be nothing but disorder and confusion? and all things in it
too, by natural different properties one from another differenced and
distinguished; and yet all through diffused, and by natural sympathy,
one to another united, as they are?
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Either this world is a beautiful, ordered whole — everything arranged and ruled by design. Or even if it's a confused mixture, it's still beautiful. How could there be any beauty in you while the whole world contains nothing but chaos? All things are different from each other by their natural properties. Yet they are spread throughout everything and united by natural connection.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
A black or malign disposition, an effeminate disposition; an
hard inexorable disposition, a wild inhuman disposition, a sheepish
disposition, a childish disposition; a blockish, a false, a scurril, a
fraudulent, a tyrannical: what then? If he be a stranger in the world,
that knows not the things that are in it; why not be a stranger as well,
that wonders at the things that are done in it?
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Some people are cruel or spiteful. Others are weak. Some are harsh and unforgiving. Others are wild and inhuman. Some act like sheep. Others act like children. Some are stupid, dishonest, vulgar, deceptive, or tyrannical. So what? If someone can be a stranger to the world who doesn't understand what's in it, why can't you be a stranger who simply wonders at what happens in it?

meditations_book-04.originalText:
He is a true fugitive, that flies from reason, by which men are
sociable. He blind, who cannot see with the eyes of his understanding.
He poor, that stands in need of another, and hath not in himself all
things needful for this life. He an aposteme of the world, who by being
discontented with those things that happen unto him in the world,
doth as it were apostatise, and separate himself from common nature's
rational administration. For the same nature it is that brings this
unto thee, whatsoever it be, that first brought thee into the world. He
raises sedition in the city, who by irrational actions withdraws his own
soul from that one and common soul of all rational creatures.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: The real runaway is the one who flees from reason — the thing that makes us social beings. The truly blind person cannot see with their mind's eye. The truly poor person needs others and lacks everything necessary for life within themselves. Someone who complains about what happens to them becomes like a disease on the world. They separate themselves from the rational order that governs all of us. The same nature that brings you whatever you face now is the same nature that brought you into existence. The person who stirs up trouble in the city is the one whose irrational actions pull their soul away from the one soul we all share as thinking beings.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
There is, who without so much as a coat; and there is, who without
so much as a book, doth put philosophy in practice. I am half naked,
neither have I bread to eat, and yet I depart not from reason, saith
one. But I say; I want the food of good teaching, and instructions, and
yet I depart not from reason.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: One person says: 'I don't even have a coat, I don't even have a book, but I still practice philosophy. I'm half naked and have no bread to eat, yet I don't abandon reason.' But I say: I lack good teaching and instruction, yet I don't abandon reason either.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
What art and profession soever thou hast learned, endeavour to
affect it, and comfort thyself in it; and pass the remainder of thy life
as one who from his whole heart commits himself and whatsoever belongs
unto him, unto the gods: and as for men, carry not thyself either
tyrannically or servilely towards any.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Whatever skills and work you have learned, try to love them and find comfort in them. Live the rest of your life as someone who trusts the gods completely with himself and everything he has. As for other people, don't be a tyrant or a servant to anyone.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Consider in my mind, for example's sake, the times of Vespasian:
thou shalt see but the same things: some marrying, some bringing up
children, some sick, some dying, some fighting, some feasting, some
merchandising, some tilling, some flattering, some boasting, some
suspecting, some undermining, some wishing to die, some fretting and
murmuring at their present estate, some wooing, some hoarding, some
seeking after magistracies, and some after kingdoms. And is not that
their age quite over, and ended? Again, consider now the times of
Trajan. There likewise thou seest the very self-same things, and that
age also is now over and ended.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Think about the times of Vespasian, for example. You'll see the same things: people marrying, raising children, getting sick, dying, fighting, celebrating, doing business, farming, flattering others, bragging, being suspicious, scheming, wishing they were dead, complaining about their lives, courting lovers, hoarding money, chasing political office, seeking power. And isn't that whole era completely over and done? Now think about the times of Trajan. You see exactly the same things there too. And that age is also over and finished.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
In the like manner consider other
periods, both of times and of whole nations, and see how many men, after
they had with all their might and main intended and prosecuted some one
worldly thing or other did soon after drop away, and were resolved into
the elements. But especially thou must call to mind them, whom thou
thyself in thy lifetime hast known much distracted about vain things,
and in the meantime neglecting to do that, and closely and unseparably
(as fully satisfied with it) to adhere unto it, which their own proper
constitution did require. And here thou must remember, that thy carriage
in every business must be according to the worth and due proportion of
it, for so shalt thou not easily be tired out and vexed, if thou shalt
not dwell upon small matters longer than is fitting.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Think about other times and whole nations in the same way. See how many people chased some worldly goal with everything they had, only to die soon after and return to dust. But especially remember the people you knew in your own lifetime. You watched them get completely caught up in pointless things. Meanwhile, they ignored what they should have been doing — the work their own nature demanded of them. Remember this: how much effort you put into something should match how important it really is. If you do this, you won't wear yourself out or get frustrated by spending too much time on small things.

meditations_book-04.originalText: Those words which once were common and ordinary, are now become obscure and obsolete; and so the names of men once commonly known and famous, are now become in a manner obscure and obsolete names. Camillus, Cæso, Volesius, Leonnatus; not long after, Scipio, Cato, then Augustus, then Adrianus, then Antoninus Pius: all these in a short time will be out of date, and, as things of another world as it were, become fabulous. And this I say of them, who once shined as the wonders of their ages, for as for the rest, no sooner are they expired, than with them all their fame and memory. And what is it then that shall always be remembered? all is vanity.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Words that were once common and ordinary are now hard to understand and forgotten. The same thing happens to the names of people who were once famous. Camillus, Cæso, Volesius, Leonnatus — not long after, Scipio, Cato, then Augustus, then Hadrian, then Antoninus Pius. All these names will soon be outdated. They will seem like stories from another world. And I'm talking about men who once amazed their generations. As for everyone else, they die and their fame dies with them. So what will always be remembered? Nothing. It's all meaningless.

meditations_book-04.originalText: What is it that we must bestow our care and diligence upon? even upon this only: that our minds and wills be just; that our actions be charitable; that our speech be never deceitful, or that our understanding be not subject to error; that our inclination be always set to embrace whatsoever shall happen unto us, as necessary, as usual, as ordinary, as flowing from such a beginning, and such a fountain, from which both thou thyself and all things are. Willingly therefore, and wholly surrender up thyself unto that fatal concatenation, yielding up thyself unto the fates, to be disposed of at their pleasure.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: What should we focus our care and effort on? Just this: that our thoughts and intentions are fair. That our actions help others. That we never lie. That we don't fool ourselves. That we're always ready to accept whatever happens to us as necessary, normal, ordinary — flowing from the same source that made both you and everything else. So give yourself over willingly to this chain of fate. Let the fates do with you what they will.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Whatsoever is now present, and from day to day hath its existence;
all objects of memories, and the minds and memories themselves,
incessantly consider, all things that are, have their being by change
and alteration. Use thyself therefore often to meditate upon this, that
the nature of the universe delights in nothing more, than in altering
those things that are, and in making others like unto them. So that we
may say, that whatsoever is, is but as it were the seed of that which
shall be. For if thou think that that only is seed, which either the
earth or the womb receiveth, thou art very simple.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Everything that exists right now, everything that has existed day by day — all the things we remember, and our minds and memories themselves — constantly think about this: all things exist through change and transformation. Get used to thinking about this often. The universe loves nothing more than changing the things that exist and making new things like them. So we can say that whatever exists is just the seed of what will come next. If you think that only what the earth or a womb receives is a seed, you're being too narrow in your thinking.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Thou art now ready to die, and yet hast thou not attained to
that perfect simplicity: thou art yet subject to many troubles and
perturbations; not yet free from all fear and suspicion of external
accidents; nor yet either so meekly disposed towards all men, as thou
shouldest; or so affected as one, whose only study and only wisdom is,
to be just in all his actions.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: You are ready to die, but you still haven't reached that perfect simplicity. You are still troubled by many things. You still worry about what might happen. You are not yet gentle enough with everyone. You have not yet become someone whose only focus is being just in everything you do.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Behold and observe, what is the state of their rational part; and
those that the world doth account wise, see what things they fly and are
afraid of; and what things they hunt after.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Look and see what state their minds are in. Those the world calls wise — see what they run from and fear, and what they chase after.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
In another man's mind and understanding thy evil Cannot subsist,
nor in any proper temper or distemper of the natural constitution of thy
body, which is but as it were the coat or cottage of thy soul. Wherein
then, but in that part of thee, wherein the conceit, and apprehension
of any misery can subsist? Let not that part therefore admit any such
conceit, and then all is well. Though thy body which is so near it
should either be cut or burnt, or suffer any corruption or putrefaction,
yet let that part to which it belongs to judge of these, be still at
rest; that is, let her judge this, that whatsoever it is, that equally
may happen to a wicked man, and to a good man, is neither good nor evil.
For that which happens equally to him that lives according to nature,
and to him that doth not, is neither according to nature, nor against
it; and by consequent, neither good nor bad.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Your suffering cannot exist in another person's mind or body. It cannot exist in your own body either, which is just the house where your soul lives. So where can it exist? Only in the part of you that forms ideas about misery. Don't let that part form such ideas, and you'll be fine. Even if your body gets cut, burned, corrupted, or rotten, let the part of you that judges these things stay calm. Let it judge this way: whatever happens equally to both good and bad people is neither good nor bad itself. What affects people who live well and people who live badly in the same way is neither natural nor unnatural. So it's neither good nor bad.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Ever consider and think upon the world as being but one living
substance, and having but one soul, and how all things in the world, are
terminated into one sensitive power; and are done by one general motion
as it were, and deliberation of that one soul; and how all things that
are, concur in the cause of one another's being, and by what manner of
connection and concatenation all things happen.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Think of the world as one living thing with one soul. All things flow into one shared awareness. Everything moves together as if guided by one mind making decisions. All things work together to cause each other's existence. Everything is connected in an endless chain.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
What art thou, that better and divine part excepted, but as
Epictetus said well, a wretched soul, appointed to carry a carcass up
and down?
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: What are you, except for that better and divine part, but as Epictetus said well, a wretched soul appointed to carry a corpse up and down?

meditations_book-04.originalText:
To suffer change can be no hurt; as no benefit it is, by change to
attain to being. The age and time of the world is as it were a flood and
swift current, consisting of the things that are brought to pass in
the world. For as soon as anything hath appeared, and is passed away,
another succeeds, and that also will presently out of sight.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Change itself cannot hurt you. And change cannot benefit you either. The age and time of the world is like a flood or fast river made up of all the things that happen. As soon as something appears and passes away, another thing takes its place. And that too will soon be gone.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Whatsoever doth happen in the world, is, in the course of nature,
as usual and ordinary as a rose in the spring, and fruit in summer. Of
the same nature is sickness and death; slander, and lying in wait, and
whatsoever else ordinarily doth unto fools use to be occasion either
of joy or sorrow. That, whatsoever it is, that comes after, doth always
very naturally, and as it were familiarly, follow upon that which was
before. For thou must consider the things of the world, not as a loose
independent number, consisting merely of necessary events; but as a
discreet connection of things orderly and harmoniously disposed. There
is then to be seen in the things of the world, not a bare succession,
but an admirable correspondence and affinity.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Whatever happens in the world is as natural and ordinary as roses blooming in spring or fruit ripening in summer. Sickness and death are the same. So are slander and betrayal. All these things that make fools happy or sad are just natural events. Whatever comes next always follows naturally from what came before. You must see the world's events not as random accidents or isolated necessities. See them as connected pieces that fit together in order and harmony. In the world's events, there is not just one thing after another. There is a beautiful pattern and connection.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Let that of Heraclitus never be out of thy mind, that the death
of earth, is water, and the death of water, is air; and the death of
air, is fire; and so on the contrary. Remember him also who was
ignorant whither the way did lead, and how that reason being the thing
by which all things in the world are administered, and which men are
continually and most inwardly conversant with: yet is the thing, which
ordinarily they are most in opposition with, and how those things which
daily happen among them, cease not daily to be strange unto them, and
that we should not either speak, or do anything as men in their sleep,
by opinion and bare imagination: for then we think we speak and do, and
that we must not be as children, who follow their father's example; for
best reason alleging their bare καθότι παρειλήφαμεν; or, as by
successive tradition from our forefathers we have received it.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Keep Heraclitus in mind — that earth dies to become water, water dies to become air, air dies to become fire, and so on in reverse. Remember also the man who didn't know where his path led. Think about how reason governs everything in the world. We deal with reason constantly and intimately. Yet it's the very thing we fight against most. The things that happen to us every day still surprise us daily. We shouldn't speak or act like sleepwalkers, guided by opinions and fantasies. When we do that, we only think we're speaking and acting. And we shouldn't be like children who copy their fathers simply because "that's how we received it" — just following tradition without thinking.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Even as if any of the gods should tell thee, Thou shalt
certainly die to-morrow, or next day, thou wouldst not, except thou wert
extremely base and pusillanimous, take it for a great benefit, rather
to die the next day after, than to-morrow; (for alas, what is the
difference!) so, for the same reason, think it no great matter to die
rather many years after, than the very next day.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Imagine one of the gods told you: You will die tomorrow, or the day after. Unless you were completely cowardly, you wouldn't think it was some great advantage to die the day after instead of tomorrow. What's the difference, really? For the same reason, it shouldn't matter much whether you die many years from now or the very next day.

meditations_book-04.originalText: Let it be thy perpetual meditation, how many physicians who once looked so grim, and so theatrically shrunk their brows upon their patients, are dead and gone themselves. How many astrologers, after that in great ostentation they had foretold the death of some others, how many philosophers after so many elaborate tracts and volumes concerning either mortality or immortality; how many brave captains and commanders, after the death and slaughter of so many; how many kings and tyrants, after they had with such horror and insolency abused their power upon men's lives, as though themselves had been immortal; how many, that I may so speak, whole cities both men and towns: Helice, Pompeii, Herculaneum, and others innumerable are dead and gone.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Keep thinking about this: how many doctors who once looked so serious and frowned dramatically at their patients are now dead themselves. How many fortune-tellers who proudly predicted other people's deaths are gone. How many philosophers who wrote endless books about death and immortality have died. How many brave generals who killed so many others in battle are dead. How many kings and tyrants who cruelly abused their power over people's lives — as if they would live forever — are gone. And how many entire cities have vanished: Helice, Pompeii, Herculaneum, and countless others.

meditations_book-04.originalText: Run them over also, whom thou thyself, one after another, hast known in thy time to drop away. Such and such a one took care of such and such a one's burial, and soon after was buried himself. So one, so another: and all things in a short time. For herein lieth all indeed, ever to look upon all worldly things, as things for their continuance, that are but for a day: and for their worth, most vile, and contemptible, as for example, What is man? That which but the other day when he was conceived was vile snivel; and within few days shall be either an embalmed carcass, or mere ashes. Thus must thou according to truth and nature, throughly consider how man's life is but for a very moment of time, and so depart meek and contented: even as if a ripe olive falling should praise the ground that bare her, and give thanks to the tree that begat her.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Think about the people you have known who have died, one after another. This person buried that person, and soon after was buried himself. One after another, all in a short time. This is the truth: look at all worldly things as lasting only a day, and as worthless and contemptible. What is man? Just the other day he was conceived from something vile. In a few days he will be either an embalmed corpse or ashes. You must think about this according to truth and nature. Human life lasts only a moment. Accept this and depart peacefully and content, like a ripe olive that falls and praises the ground that held it and gives thanks to the tree that made it.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Thou must be like a promontory of the sea, against which though
the waves beat continually, yet it both itself stands, and about it are
those swelling waves stilled and quieted.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: You must be like a rocky cliff by the sea. The waves beat against it constantly, but the cliff stands firm. And around it, those angry waves grow still and quiet.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Oh, wretched I, to whom this mischance is happened! nay, happy I,
to whom this thing being happened, I can continue without grief; neither
wounded by that which is present, nor in fear of that which is to come.
For as for this, it might have happened unto any man, but any man having
such a thing befallen him, could not have continued without grief. Why
then should that rather be an unhappiness, than this a happiness? But
however, canst thou, O man! term that unhappiness, which is no mischance
to the nature of man I Canst thou think that a mischance to the nature
of man, which is not contrary to the end and will of his nature?
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Poor me, this bad thing happened to me! No — lucky me. This thing happened, and I can handle it without falling apart. I'm not crushed by what's happening now. I'm not scared of what might come next. This could have happened to anyone. But not everyone could get through it without breaking down. So why call this bad luck instead of good luck? Can you really call something unlucky if it doesn't go against human nature? Can you call it a disaster if it doesn't work against what we're meant to do?

meditations_book-04.originalText:
What
then hast thou learned is the will of man's nature? Doth that then which
hath happened unto thee, hinder thee from being just? or magnanimous? or
temperate? or wise? or circumspect? or true? or modest? or free? or from
anything else of all those things in the present enjoying and possession
whereof the nature of man, (as then enjoying all that is proper unto
her,) is fully satisfied? Now to conclude; upon all occasion of sorrow
remember henceforth to make use of this dogma, that whatsoever it is
that hath happened unto thee, is in very deed no such thing of itself,
as a misfortune; but that to bear it generously, is certainly great
happiness.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: What have you learned about human nature's purpose? Does what happened to you stop you from being just? Or brave? Or self-controlled? Or wise? Or careful? Or honest? Or humble? Or free? Or from having any of the other qualities that make human nature complete and satisfied? So remember this rule whenever you feel sorrow: whatever happened to you is not really a misfortune. To bear it with courage is true happiness.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
It is but an ordinary coarse one, yet it is a good effectual
remedy against the fear of death, for a man to consider in his mind the
examples of such, who greedily and covetously (as it were) did for a
long time enjoy their lives. What have they got more, than they whose
deaths have been untimely? Are not they themselves dead at the last?
as Cadiciant's, Fabius, Julianus Lepidus, or any other who in their
lifetime having buried many, were at the last buried themselves. The
whole space of any man's life, is but little; and as little as it is,
with what troubles, with what manner of dispositions, and in the society
of how wretched a body must it be passed! Let it be therefore unto thee
altogether as a matter of indifferency. For if thou shalt look backward;
behold, what an infinite chaos of time doth present itself unto thee;
and as infinite a chaos, if thou shalt look forward. In that which is
so infinite, what difference can there be between that which liveth but
three days, and that which liveth three ages?
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: This is a simple but powerful remedy against the fear of death. Think about those who greedily held onto life for a long time. What did they gain over those who died young? In the end, they all died too — Cadiciant, Fabius, Julianus Lepidus, and others who outlived many people, only to be buried themselves. The whole span of any life is short. And even that short time must be lived with troubles, difficult moods, and in a wretched body. So treat life as something that doesn't matter much either way. Look backward — you see an endless stretch of time before you were born. Look forward — you see endless time after you die. In all that infinity, what difference is there between living three days or three lifetimes?

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Let thy course ever be the most compendious way. The most
compendious, is that which is according to nature: that is, in all both
words and deeds, ever to follow that which is most sound and perfect.
For such a resolution will free a man from all trouble, strife,
dissembling, and ostentation.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Always take the shortest path. The shortest path is the natural one: in everything you say and do, follow what is most sound and right. This approach will free you from all trouble, conflict, pretending, and showing off.

meditations_book-05.originalText: In the morning when thou findest thyself unwilling to rise, consider with thyself presently, it is to go about a man's work that I am stirred up. Am I then yet unwilling to go about that, for which I myself was born and brought forth into this world? Or was I made for this, to lay me down, and make much of myself in a warm bed? 'O but this is pleasing.' And was it then for this that thou wert born, that thou mightest enjoy pleasure? Was it not in very truth for this, that thou mightest always be busy and in action? Seest thou not how all things in the world besides, how every tree md plant, how sparrows and ants, spiders and bees: how all in their kind are intent as it were orderly to perform whatsoever (towards the preservation of this orderly universe) naturally doth become and belong unto thin? And wilt not thou do that, which belongs unto a man to do? Wilt not thou run to do that, which thy nature doth require?
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: In the morning when you don't want to get up, think about this right away: I'm being called to do human work. Am I really unwilling to do what I was born for? What I was brought into this world to do? Was I made to lie around and pamper myself in a warm bed? 'But this feels good.' Is that what you were born for — to enjoy pleasure? Weren't you made to always be busy and working? Look at everything else in the world. Every tree and plant. Sparrows and ants. Spiders and bees. All of them focus on doing their part to keep this orderly universe going. Won't you do what belongs to humans? Won't you rush to do what your nature requires?

meditations_book-05.originalText: 'But thou must have some rest.' Yes, thou must. Nature hath of that also, as well as of eating and drinking, allowed thee a certain stint. But thou guest beyond thy stint, and beyond that which would suffice, and in matter of action, there thou comest short of that which thou mayest. It must needs be therefore, that thou dost not love thyself, for if thou didst, thou wouldst also love thy nature, and that which thy nature doth propose unto herself as her end. Others, as many as take pleasure in their trade and profession, can even pine themselves at their works, and neglect their bodies and their food for it; and doest thou less honour thy nature, than an ordinary mechanic his trade; or a good dancer his art? than a covetous man his silver, and vainglorious man applause? These to whatsoever they take an affection, can be content to want their meat and sleep, to further that every one which he affects: and shall actions tending to the common good of human society, seem more vile unto thee, or worthy of less respect and intention?
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: 'But you need rest.' Yes, you do. Nature allows you a certain amount of rest, just like eating and drinking. But you go beyond what you need. You exceed what would be enough. Yet when it comes to action, you fall short of what you could do. This means you don't love yourself. If you did, you would also love your nature and what your nature aims for. Look at others who enjoy their work. They can wear themselves out at their jobs. They neglect their bodies and food for it. Do you honor your nature less than a common worker honors his trade? Less than a good dancer honors his art? Less than a greedy man loves his money, or a vain man loves applause? When these people care about something, they're willing to go without food and sleep to pursue it. So why do actions that serve the common good of humanity seem worse to you? Why do they deserve less respect and effort?

meditations_book-05.originalText:
How easy a thing is it for a man to put off from him all turbulent
adventitious imaginations, and presently to be in perfect rest and
tranquillity!
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: How easy it is to push away all those chaotic, outside thoughts and be at perfect peace right away!

meditations_book-05.originalText:
Think thyself fit and worthy to speak, or to do anything that is
according to nature, and let not the reproach, or report of some that
may ensue upon it, ever deter thee. If it be right and honest to be
spoken or done, undervalue not thyself so much, as to be discouraged
from it. As for them, they have their own rational over-ruling part, and
their own proper inclination: which thou must not stand and look
about to take notice of, but go on straight, whither both thine own
particular, and the common nature do lead thee; and the way of both
these, is but one.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Think of yourself as capable of speaking or doing what feels natural and right. Don't let criticism or gossip stop you. If something is right and honest to say or do, don't sell yourself short by backing down. Other people have their own minds and their own ways of thinking. Don't waste time watching what they do. Just keep moving forward where your own nature and the common good both point you. The path is the same for both.

meditations_book-05.originalText:
I continue my course by actions according to nature, until I
fall and cease, breathing out my last breath into that air, by which
continually breathed in I did live; and falling upon that earth, out of
whose gifts and fruits my father gathered his seed, my mother her
blood, and my nurse her milk, out of which for so many years I have
been provided, both of meat and drink. And lastly, which beareth me that
tread upon it, and beareth with me that so many ways do abuse it, or
so freely make use of it, so many ways to so many ends.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: I keep living according to nature until I fall and stop, breathing my last breath into the same air I breathed all my life. I will fall on the same earth that gave the materials for my father's seed, my mother's blood, and my nurse's milk. This earth fed and watered me for years. It carries me as I walk on it. It puts up with me even though I abuse it and use it freely in so many ways for so many purposes.

meditations_book-05.originalText:
No man can admire thee for thy sharp acute language, such is thy
natural disability that way. Be it so: yet there be many other good
things, for the want of which thou canst not plead the want or natural
ability. Let them be seen in thee, which depend wholly from thee;
sincerity, gravity, laboriousness, contempt of pleasures; be not
querulous, be Content with little, be kind, be free; avoid all
superfluity, all vain prattling; be magnanimous. Doest not thou
perceive, how many things there be, which notwithstanding any pretence
of natural indisposition and unfitness, thou mightest have performed and
exhibited, and yet still thou doest voluntarily continue drooping
downwards?
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: No one can admire you for sharp, clever speech — you just don't have that gift. Fine.
