But there are many other good things you can't blame on lack of natural ability. Show the qualities that depend entirely on you: honesty, seriousness, hard work, contempt for pleasures. Don't complain. Be content with little. Be kind. Be generous. Avoid excess and empty chatter. Be noble in spirit. Don't you see how many things you could do and show, despite any excuse about natural weakness? Yet you still choose to stay down in the dumps.

meditations_book-05.originalText:
Or wilt thou say that it is through defect of thy natural
constitution, that thou art constrained to murmur, to be base and
wretched to flatter; now to accuse, and now to please, and pacify thy
body: to be vainglorious, to be so giddy-headed., and unsettled in thy
thoughts? nay (witnesses be the Gods) of all these thou mightest have
been rid long ago: only, this thou must have been contented with, to
have borne the blame of one that is somewhat slow and dull, wherein thou
must so exercise thyself, as one who neither doth much take to heart
this his natural defect, nor yet pleaseth himself in it.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Or will you say it's your natural makeup that forces you to complain, to be low and miserable, to flatter people? That makes you blame others one moment and try to please them the next? That drives you to chase praise, to be scattered and restless in your thoughts? No — the gods know better. You could have been free of all this long ago. The only thing you'd have to accept is being called a bit slow or dull. And even with that, you could train yourself not to worry about this weakness or take pride in it.

meditations_book-05.originalText: Such there be, who when they have done a good turn to any, are ready to set them on the score for it, and to require retaliation. Others there be, who though they stand not upon retaliation, to require any, yet they think with themselves nevertheless, that such a one is their debtor, and they know as their word is what they have done. Others again there be, who when they have done any such thing, do not so much as know what they have done; but are like unto the vine, which beareth her grapes, and when once she hath borne her own proper fruit, is contented and seeks for no further recompense. As a horse after a race, and a hunting dog when he hath hunted, and a bee when she hath made her honey, look not for applause and commendation; so neither doth that man that rightly doth understand his own nature when he hath done a good turn: but from one doth proceed to do another, even as the vine after she hath once borne fruit in her own proper season, is ready for another time.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Some people do a good deed and then expect payment for it. They want something back. Others don't demand payment, but they still think the person owes them something. They keep track of what they've done. But there are others who do good things and don't even think about it afterward. They're like a vine that grows grapes. Once it has produced its fruit, it's satisfied and doesn't look for any reward. After a horse runs a race, or a hunting dog finishes the hunt, or a bee makes honey, they don't wait around for praise. The same goes for someone who truly understands their nature. When they do something good, they just move on to the next good thing. Like the vine that bears fruit in season and then gets ready to bear fruit again.

meditations_book-05.originalText: Thou therefore must be one of them, who what they do, barely do it without any further thought, and are in a manner insensible of what they do. 'Nay but,' will some reply perchance, 'this very thing a rational man is bound unto, to understand what it is, that he doeth.' For it is the property, say they, of one that is naturally sociable, to be sensible, that he doth operate sociably: nay, and to desire, that the party him self that is sociably dealt with, should be sensible of it too. I answer, That which thou sayest is true indeed, but the true meaning of that which is said, thou dost not understand. And therefore art thou one of those first, whom I mentioned. For they also are led by a probable appearance of reason. But if thou dost desire to understand truly what it is that is said, fear not that thou shalt therefore give over any sociable action.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: So you must be one of those people who just do things without thinking much about it. They hardly notice what they're doing. 'But wait,' someone might say, 'a thinking person should understand what he's doing. That's what makes us naturally social — we're aware that we're helping others, and we want them to notice it too.' What you're saying sounds right, but you don't really understand what it means. So you're actually one of those first people I mentioned. They also think they have good reasons. But if you want to truly understand what this means, don't worry — you won't stop doing good things for others.

meditations_book-05.originalText:
The form of the Athenians' prayer did run thus: 'O rain, rain, good
Jupiter, upon all the grounds and fields that belong to the Athenians.'
Either we should not pray at all, or thus absolutely and freely; and not
every one for himself in particular alone.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: The Athenians used to pray like this: 'O rain, rain, good Jupiter, on all the lands and fields that belong to the Athenians.' Either we should not pray at all, or we should pray this way — completely and freely, not just for ourselves alone.

meditations_book-05.originalText: As we say commonly, The physician hath prescribed unto this man, riding; unto another, cold baths; unto a third, to go barefoot: so it is alike to say, The nature of the universe hath prescribed unto this man sickness, or blindness, or some loss, or damage or some such thing. For as there, when we say of a physician, that he hath prescribed anything, our meaning is, that he hath appointed this for that, as subordinate and conducing to health: so here, whatsoever doth happen unto any, is ordained unto him as a thing subordinate unto the fates, and therefore do we say of such things, that they do συμβαίνειν, that is, happen, or fall together; as of square stones, when either in walls, or pyramids in a certain position they fit one another, and agree as it were in an harmony, the masons say, that they do συμβαίνειν; as if thou shouldest say, fall together: so that in the general, though the things be divers that make it, yet the consent or harmony itself is but one.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: We say the doctor has prescribed one man riding, another cold baths, and a third walking barefoot. In the same way, the nature of the universe has prescribed sickness, blindness, loss, or damage to different people. When we say a doctor prescribed something, we mean he assigned it to help with healing. So whatever happens to anyone was meant for them by fate. This is why we say things "fall together." When square stones fit perfectly in walls or pyramids, masons say they "fall together" in harmony. Even though the individual things are different, they create one unified pattern.

meditations_book-05.originalText: And as the whole world is made up of all the particular bodies of the world, one perfect and complete body, of the same nature that particular bodies; so is the destiny of particular causes and events one general one, of the same nature that particular causes are. What I now say, even they that are mere idiots are not ignorant of: for they say commonly τοῦτο ἔφερεν ἀυτῷ, that is, This his destiny hath brought upon him. This therefore is by the fates properly and particularly brought upon this, as that unto this in particular is by the physician prescribed. These therefore let us accept of in like manner, as we do those that are prescribed unto us our physicians. For them also in themselves shall We find to contain many harsh things, but we nevertheless, in hope of health, and recovery, accept of them.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: The whole world is made up of all the individual bodies in it — one complete body that works the same way as individual bodies do. In the same way, the destiny of individual causes and events is part of one general destiny that works like individual causes do. Even simple people understand this. They say 'This is what fate brought him' — meaning his destiny brought this to him specifically. So fate brings each thing to each person in particular, just like a doctor prescribes specific treatments for specific patients. We should accept what fate brings us the same way we accept what doctors prescribe. Medicine often tastes bitter and harsh, but we take it anyway because we hope it will make us healthy.

meditations_book-05.originalText: Let the fulfilling and accomplishment of those things which the common nature hath determined, be unto thee as thy health. Accept then, and be pleased with whatsoever doth happen, though otherwise harsh and un-pleasing, as tending to that end, to the health and welfare of the universe, and to Jove's happiness and prosperity. For this whatsoever it be, should not have been produced, had it not conduced to the good of the universe. For neither doth any ordinary particular nature bring anything to pass, that is not to whatsoever is within the sphere of its own proper administration and government agreeable and subordinate. For these two considerations then thou must be well pleased with anything that doth happen unto thee.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Let the things that nature has set in motion be like your own health to you. Accept whatever happens, even when it feels harsh and unpleasant. See it as serving a purpose—the health of the universe and the good of all things. Whatever happens to you would not have occurred unless it helped the whole universe. No force in nature creates anything that doesn't serve its proper role. For these two reasons, you should be content with whatever happens to you.

meditations_book-05.originalText: First, because that for thee properly it was brought to pass, and unto thee it was prescribed; and that from the very beginning by the series and connection of the first causes, it hath ever had a reference unto thee. And secondly, because the good success and perfect welfare, and indeed the very continuance of Him, that is the Administrator of the whole, doth in a manner depend on it. For the whole (because whole, therefore entire and perfect) is maimed, and mutilated, if thou shalt cut off anything at all, whereby the coherence, and contiguity as of parts, so of causes, is maintained and preserved. Of which certain it is, that thou doest (as much as lieth in thee) cut off, and in some sort violently take somewhat away, as often as thou art displeased with anything that happeneth.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: First, what happened to you was meant for you specifically. It was assigned to you from the very beginning through the chain of causes that led to this moment. Second, the success and health of the whole universe—and even its continued existence—depends on each part playing its role. The whole is complete and perfect only when all its parts stay connected. If you cut away any piece, you damage the links between parts and causes. And you do cut something away—as much as you can—whenever you resist what happens to you.

meditations_book-05.originalText: Be not discontented, be not disheartened, be not out of hope, if often it succeed not so well with thee punctually and precisely to do all things according to the right dogmata, but being once cast off, return unto them again: and as for those many and more frequent occurrences, either of worldly distractions, or human infirmities, which as a man thou canst not but in some measure be subject unto, be not thou discontented with them; but however, love and affect that only which thou dust return unto: a philosopher's life, and proper occupation after the most exact manner. And when thou dust return to thy philosophy, return not unto it as the manner of some is, after play and liberty as it were, to their schoolmasters and pedagogues; but as they that have sore eyes to their sponge and egg: or as another to his cataplasm; or as others to their fomentations: so shalt not thou make it a matter of ostentation at all to obey reason but of ease and comfort.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Don't get frustrated. Don't get discouraged. Don't lose hope. Often you won't do everything perfectly according to what is right. When you fall short, just come back to it again. You will face many distractions from the world and human weaknesses. As a person, you can't avoid these completely. Don't be upset about them. But love and care for the one thing you can return to: living like a philosopher and doing your work in the most careful way. When you come back to philosophy, don't approach it like some students do — returning to their teachers after time off, as if it were a chore. Instead, be like someone with sore eyes reaching for a sponge and egg white. Or like someone reaching for a healing bandage. Or like others reaching for warm compresses. Don't make following reason into a show. Make it your comfort and relief.

meditations_book-05.originalText: And remember that philosophy requireth nothing of thee, but what thy nature requireth, and wouldest thou thyself desire anything that is not according to nature? for which of these sayest thou; that which is according to nature or against it, is of itself more kind and pleasing? Is it not for that respect especially, that pleasure itself is to so many men's hurt and overthrow, most prevalent, because esteemed commonly most kind, and natural? But consider well whether magnanimity rather, and true liberty, and true simplicity, and equanimity, and holiness; whether these be not most kind and natural? And prudency itself, what more kind and amiable than it, when thou shalt truly consider with thyself, what it is through all the proper objects of thy rational intellectual faculty currently to go on without any fall or stumble?
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Remember that philosophy asks nothing of you except what your nature already asks. Would you really want anything that goes against nature? Which do you think is more pleasant and agreeable — what follows nature or what fights against it? Isn't this why pleasure itself brings so many people to ruin? Because it seems natural and pleasant? But think about this: aren't true greatness, real freedom, honesty, balance, and goodness more natural and pleasant? And wisdom itself — what could be more agreeable when you consider what it means to move through life using your mind properly, without stumbling?

meditations_book-05.originalText: As for the things of the world, their true nature is in a manner so involved with obscurity, that unto many philosophers, and those no mean ones, they seemed altogether incomprehensible, and the Stoics themselves, though they judge them not altogether incomprehensible, yet scarce and not without much difficulty, comprehensible, so that all assent of ours is fallible, for who is he that is infallible in his conclusions? From the nature of things, pass now unto their subjects and matter: how temporary, how vile are they I such as may be in the power and possession of some abominable loose liver, of some common strumpet, of some notorious oppressor and extortioner.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: The true nature of worldly things is so wrapped in mystery that many great philosophers found them completely beyond understanding. Even the Stoics, who think we can grasp them, say it's barely possible and very difficult. So all our judgments are shaky — who among us never makes mistakes? Now move from thinking about the nature of things to their actual substance. How temporary and worthless they are! They might belong to some disgusting person, some prostitute, or some well-known tyrant who steals from others.

meditations_book-05.originalText: Pass from thence to the dispositions of them that thou doest ordinarily converse with, how hardly do we bear, even with the most loving and amiable! that I may not say, how hard it is for us to bear even with our own selves, in such obscurity, and impurity of things: in such and so continual a flux both of the substances and time; both of the motions themselves, and things moved; what it is that we can fasten upon; either to honour, and respect especially; or seriously, and studiously to seek after; I cannot so much as conceive For indeed they are things contrary.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Think about the people you spend time with every day. How hard it is to put up with them, even the ones we love most! I won't even mention how hard it is to put up with ourselves. Everything is so unclear and messy. Everything keeps changing — the world itself, time, movement, the things that move. What can we hold onto? What deserves our respect or our serious effort? I can't even imagine. These things seem to work against each other.

meditations_book-05.originalText:
Thou must comfort thyself in the expectation of thy natural
dissolution, and in the meantime not grieve at the delay; but rest
contented in those two things. First, that nothing shall happen unto
thee, which is not according to the nature of the universe. Secondly,
that it is in thy power, to do nothing against thine own proper God, and
inward spirit. For it is not in any man's power to constrain thee to
transgress against him.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: You must find comfort in knowing that your natural death will come, and meanwhile not worry about the delay. Rest easy in two truths. First, nothing will happen to you that goes against the nature of the universe. Second, you have the power to do nothing against your own inner god and spirit. No one can force you to betray what is sacred within you.

meditations_book-05.originalText:
What is the use that now at this present I make of my soul? Thus
from time to time and upon all occasions thou must put this question to
thyself; what is now that part of mine which they call the rational
mistress part, employed about? Whose soul do I now properly possess? a
child's? or a youth's? a woman's? or a tyrant's? some brute, or some
wild beast's soul?
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: What am I doing with my soul right now? You must ask yourself this question often, at every moment: what is my mind focused on? Whose soul do I have? A child's? A young person's? A woman's? A tyrant's? Some animal's? Some wild beast's?

meditations_book-05.originalText: What those things are in themselves, which by the greatest part are esteemed good, thou mayest gather even from this. For if a man shall hear things mentioned as good, which are really good indeed, such as are prudence, temperance, justice, fortitude, after so much heard and conceived, he cannot endure to hear of any more, for the word good is properly spoken of them.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: You can see what things truly are by looking at what most people call "good." When someone hears about real goods — wisdom, self-control, justice, courage — and really understands them, they can't bear to hear anything else called "good." The word belongs to these things alone.

meditations_book-05.originalText: But as for those which by the vulgar are esteemed good, if he shall hear them mentioned as good, he doth hearken for more. He is well contented to hear, that what is spoken by the comedian, is but familiarly and popularly spoken, so that even the vulgar apprehend the difference. For why is it else, that this offends not and needs not to be excused, when virtues are styled good: but that which is spoken in commendation of wealth, pleasure, or honour, we entertain it only as merrily and pleasantly spoken? Proceed therefore, and inquire further, whether it may not be that those things also which being mentioned upon the stage were merrily, and with great applause of the multitude, scoffed at with this jest, that they that possessed them had not in all the world of their own, (such was their affluence and plenty) so much as a place where to avoid their excrements. Whether, I say, those ought not also in very deed to be much respected, and esteemed of, as the only things that are truly good.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: But when ordinary people hear things called 'good' that they think are good, they want to hear more. A person is happy to hear what comedians say on stage as just everyday talk that regular people understand. Why else would it be fine when comedians call virtues good without any excuse needed? But when they praise wealth, pleasure, or honor, we only take it as a joke? Keep thinking about this. Ask yourself if the things that get mocked on stage — where the crowd laughs at rich people who own so much they don't even have a private place to relieve themselves — ask if those things should really be valued as truly good.

meditations_book-05.originalText:
All that I consist of, is either form or matter. No corruption
can reduce either of these unto nothing: for neither did I of nothing
become a subsistent creature. Every part of mine then will by mutation
be disposed into a certain part of the whole world, and that in time
into another part; and so _in infinitum;_ by which kind of mutation, I
also became what I am, and so did they that begot me, and they before
them, and so upwards _in infinitum_. For so we may be allowed to speak,
though the age and government of the world, be to some certain periods
of time limited, and confined.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Everything I'm made of is either form or matter. Nothing can destroy either of these completely — I didn't come from nothing to begin with. Every part of me will change and become part of the world. Then it will change again into something else, and so on forever. This same endless change made me what I am now. It made my parents what they were, and their parents before them, going back forever. We can think this way even though the world itself might run in cycles with clear beginnings and ends.

meditations_book-05.originalText: Reason, and rational power, are faculties which content themselves with themselves, and their own proper operations. And as for their first inclination and motion, that they take from themselves. But their progress is right to the end and object, which is in their way, as it were, and lieth just before them: that is, which is feasible and possible, whether it be that which at the first they proposed to themselves, or no. For which reason also such actions are termed κατορθώσεις, to intimate the directness of the way, by which they are achieved. Nothing must be thought to belong to a man, which doth not belong unto him as he is a man. These, the event of purposes, are not things required in a man. The nature of man doth not profess any such things. The final ends and consummations of actions are nothing at all to a man's nature. The end therefore of a man, or the _summum bonum_ whereby that end is fulfilled, cannot consist in the consummation of actions purposed and intended.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Reason works by itself and is satisfied with its own proper actions. It starts moving on its own. But it moves straight toward whatever goal lies in front of it — whatever is actually possible to achieve. This might be different from what it first set out to do. That's why these actions are called "right actions" — because they follow the straight path to what can actually be done. Nothing belongs to a person unless it belongs to them as a human being. The outcomes of our plans are not what we require as humans. Human nature doesn't promise such things. The final results of our actions have nothing to do with our nature as people. So a person's purpose — the highest good that fulfills that purpose — cannot depend on completing the plans we set out to achieve.

meditations_book-05.originalText: Again, concerning these outward worldly things, were it so that any of them did properly belong unto man, then would it not belong unto man, to condemn them and to stand in opposition with them. Neither would he be praiseworthy that can live without them; or he good, (if these were good indeed) who of his own accord doth deprive himself of any of them. But we see contrariwise, that the more a man doth withdraw himself from these wherein external pomp and greatness doth consist, or any other like these; or the better he doth bear with the loss of these, the better he is accounted.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Think about these outside things — money, status, possessions. If they truly belonged to human nature, then it would be wrong to reject them or oppose them. A person who could live without them wouldn't be praised for it. And if these things were actually good, then someone who gave them up willingly wouldn't be called virtuous. But we see the opposite is true. The more someone pulls away from external wealth and status, or handles losing these things well, the more we respect them.

meditations_book-05.originalText: Such as thy thoughts and ordinary cogitations are, such will thy mind be in time. For the soul doth as it were receive its tincture from the fancies, and imaginations. Dye it therefore and thoroughly soak it with the assiduity of these cogitations. As for example. Wheresoever thou mayest live, there it is in thy power to live well and happy. But thou mayest live at the Court, there then also mayest thou live well and happy.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Whatever you think about regularly is what your mind becomes. The soul gets its color from your thoughts and imagination. So dye it completely with constant good thoughts. For example: wherever you live, you have the power to live well and be happy. You might live at court — well then, you can live well and be happy there too.

meditations_book-05.originalText: Again, that which everything is made for, he is also made unto that, and cannot but naturally incline unto it. That which anything doth naturally incline unto, therein is his end. Wherein the end of everything doth consist, therein also doth his good and benefit consist. Society therefore is the proper good of a rational creature. For that we are made for society, it hath long since been demonstrated. Or can any man make any question of this, that whatsoever is naturally worse and inferior, is ordinarily subordinated to that which is better? and that those things that are best, are made one for another? And those things that have souls, are better than those that have none? and of those that have, those best that have rational souls?
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Everything is made for a purpose, and naturally moves toward that purpose. Where something finds its purpose, there it finds its good. So society is the natural good for rational beings like us. We have long known that we are made for community. Can anyone doubt that lower things serve higher things? That the best things are made to work together? That things with souls are better than things without souls? And that among those with souls, the ones with rational souls are best?

meditations_book-05.originalText: To desire things impossible is the part of a mad man. But it is a thing impossible, that wicked man should not commit some such things. Neither doth anything happen to any man, which in the ordinary course of nature as natural unto him doth not happen. Again, the same things happen unto others also. And truly, if either he that is ignorant that such a thing hath happened unto him, or he that is ambitious to be commended for his magnanimity, can be patient, and is not grieved: is it not a grievous thing, that either ignorance, or a vain desire to please and to be commended, should be more powerful and effectual than true prudence?
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: To want impossible things is madness. But it's impossible for wicked people not to do wicked things. Nothing happens to you that doesn't naturally happen to people like you. The same things happen to others too. If someone who doesn't understand what happened to them can stay calm, or if someone seeking praise for being brave can bear it without complaint — isn't it sad that ignorance or vanity should be stronger than real wisdom?

meditations_book-05.originalText: As for the things themselves, they touch not the soul, neither can they have any access unto it: neither can they of themselves any ways either affect it, or move it. For she herself alone can affect and move herself, and according as the dogmata and opinions are, which she doth vouchsafe herself; so are those things which, as accessories, have any co-existence with her.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Things themselves cannot touch the soul. They have no way to reach it or affect it. The soul can only be moved by itself. Whatever beliefs and opinions the soul accepts — that's what shapes how it experiences the things around it.

meditations_book-05.originalText:
After one consideration, man is nearest unto us; as we are bound
to do them good, and to bear with them. But as he may oppose any of our
true proper actions, so man is unto me but as a thing indifferent: even
as the sun, or the wind, or some wild beast. By some of these it may be,
that some operation or other of mine, may be hindered; however, of my
mind and resolution itself, there can be no let or impediment, by reason
of that ordinary constant both exception (or reservation wherewith it
inclineth) and ready conversion of objects; from that which may not be,
to that which may be, which in the prosecution of its inclinations, as
occasion serves, it doth observe. For by these the mind doth turn and
convert any impediment whatsoever, to be her aim and purpose. So that
what before was the impediment, is now the principal object of her
working; and that which before was in her way, is now her readiest way.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: In one sense, other people are closest to us. We should help them and put up with them. But when someone gets in the way of what I need to do, that person becomes just another obstacle to me — like the sun, wind, or a wild animal. Some of these things might block what I'm trying to do. But they can't touch my mind or my will. My mind has a built-in ability to step back and shift focus — from what can't be done to what can be done. The mind turns any obstacle into its main target. What was blocking the way becomes the way forward.

meditations_book-05.originalText:
Honour that which is chiefest and most powerful in the world, and
that is it, which makes use of all things, and governs all things. So
also in thyself; honour that which is chiefest, and most powerful; and
is of one kind and nature with that which we now spake of. For it is the
very same, which being in thee, turneth all other things to its own use,
and by whom also thy life is governed.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Honor what is most important and powerful in the world — the thing that uses all things and governs all things. Do the same in yourself. Honor what is most important and powerful in you. It is the same kind of thing we just talked about. This same force in you turns everything else to its own use. It governs your life too.

meditations_book-05.originalText: That which doth not hurt the city itself; cannot hurt any citizen. This rule thou must remember to apply and make use of upon every conceit and apprehension of wrong. If the whole city be not hurt by this, neither am I certainly. And if the whole be not, why should I make it my private grievance? consider rather what it is wherein he is overseen that is thought to have done the wrong.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: What doesn't hurt the city itself can't hurt any citizen. Remember this rule whenever you think someone has wronged you. If the whole city isn't harmed by this, then neither am I. And if the whole isn't harmed, why should I take it personally? Instead, think about where the person who seems to have wronged you went astray.

meditations_book-05.originalText: Again, often meditate how swiftly all things that subsist, and all things that are done in the world, are carried away, and as it were conveyed out of sight: for both the substance themselves, we see as a flood, are in a continual flux; and all actions in a perpetual change; and the causes themselves, subject to a thousand alterations, neither is there anything almost, that may ever be said to be now settled and constant. Next unto this, and which follows upon it, consider both the infiniteness of the time already past, and the immense vastness of that which is to come, wherein all things are to be resolved and annihilated. Art not thou then a very fool, who for these things, art either puffed up with pride, or distracted with cares, or canst find in thy heart to make such moans as for a thing that would trouble thee for a very long time?
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish:
Think often about how quickly everything in the world gets swept away and disappears. The things themselves flow like a river. All actions are constantly changing. Even the causes behind things shift in a thousand ways. Almost nothing stays the same.

Next, consider the endless time that came before you and the vast time that will come after, when everything will dissolve and disappear. Aren't you foolish, then, to get puffed up with pride over these things? Or to worry yourself sick? Or to complain as if something could really trouble you for very long?

meditations_book-05.originalText: Consider the whole universe whereof thou art but a very little part, and the whole age of the world together, whereof but a short and very momentary portion is allotted unto thee, and all the fates and destinies together, of which how much is it that comes to thy part and share! Again: another doth trespass against me. Let him look to that. He is master of his own disposition, and of his own operation. I for my part am in the meantime in possession of as much, as the common nature would have me to possess: and that which mine own nature would have me do, I do.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Think about the whole universe — you are just a tiny part of it. Think about all of time — you get only a short moment. Think about all the events that happen — how little of it actually touches you! Now, someone wrongs me. That's his problem. He controls his own mind and actions. I am busy with what nature gives me to have. And what my own nature tells me to do, I do.

meditations_book-05.originalText:
Let not that chief commanding part of thy soul be ever subject to
any variation through any corporal either pain or pleasure, neither
suffer it to be mixed with these, but let it both circumscribe itself,
and confine those affections to their own proper parts and members.
But if at any time they do reflect and rebound upon the mind and
understanding (as in an united and compacted body it must needs;) then
must thou not go about to resist sense and feeling, it being natural.
However let not thy understanding to this natural sense and feeling,
which whether unto our flesh pleasant or painful, is unto us nothing
properly, add an opinion of either good or bad and all is well.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Don't let the ruling part of your mind be controlled by physical pain or pleasure. Keep it separate from these feelings. Let those feelings stay in the body where they belong. But sometimes in our connected body and mind, physical sensations will affect your thoughts. That's natural. When this happens, don't try to fight the feeling itself. Just don't let your mind add judgments about whether the sensation is good or bad. The pain or pleasure in your flesh means nothing to who you really are. If you can avoid judging it, you'll be fine.

meditations_book-05.originalText:
To live with the Gods. He liveth with the Gods, who at all times
affords unto them the spectacle of a soul, both contented and well
pleased with whatsoever is afforded, or allotted unto her; and
performing whatsoever is pleasing to that Spirit, whom (being part of
himself) Jove hath appointed to every man as his overseer and governor.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: To live with the Gods. A person lives with the Gods when they always show them a soul that is content and pleased with whatever happens to them. They do whatever pleases that divine spirit — part of themselves — that Zeus has given to each person as their guide and ruler.

meditations_book-05.originalText:
Be not angry neither with him whose breath, neither with him whose
arm holes, are offensive. What can he do? such is his breath naturally,
and such are his arm holes; and from such, such an effect, and such
a smell must of necessity proceed. 'O, but the man (sayest thou) hath
understanding in him, and might of himself know, that he by standing
near, cannot choose but offend.' And thou also (God bless thee!) hast
understanding. Let thy reasonable faculty, work upon his reasonable
faculty; show him his fault, admonish him. If he hearken unto thee, thou
hast cured him, and there will be no more occasion of anger.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Don't get angry with someone whose breath smells bad, or whose armpits stink. What can he do about it? That's just how his breath is naturally, and that's how his armpits are. From those things, that smell has to come. 'But,' you say, 'the man has a brain and could figure out that standing close to people will offend them.' Well, you have a brain too. Use your reason to work on his reason. Show him the problem. Give him advice. If he listens to you, you've helped him, and you won't need to be angry anymore.

meditations_book-05.originalText:
'Where there shall neither roarer be, nor harlot.' Why so? As
thou dost purpose to live, when thou hast retired thyself to some such
place, where neither roarer nor harlot is: so mayest thou here. And if
they will not suffer thee, then mayest thou leave thy life rather than
thy calling, but so as one that doth not think himself anyways wronged.
Only as one would say, Here is a smoke; I will out of it. And what a
great matter is this! Now till some such thing force me out, I will
continue free; neither shall any man hinder me to do what I will, and
my will shall ever be by the proper nature of a reasonable and sociable
creature, regulated and directed.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: You might dream of a place 'where there are no troublemakers or corrupt people.' Why dream of that? You plan to live virtuously when you retire to some perfect place where bad people don't exist. You can do the same thing right here. And if people won't let you live well, you can leave life itself rather than abandon your principles. But leave like someone who doesn't feel wronged. Just like someone saying, 'There's smoke here; I'll go outside.' What's the big deal? Until something forces me out, I'll stay free. No one will stop me from doing what I choose. And what I choose will always be guided by my nature as a thinking, social being.

meditations_book-05.originalText:
That rational essence by which the universe is governed, is for
community and society; and therefore hath it both made the things that
are worse, for the best, and hath allied and knit together those
which are best, as it were in an harmony. Seest thou not how it hath
sub-ordinated, and co-ordinated? and how it hath distributed unto
everything according to its worth? and those which have the pre-eminency
and superiority above all, hath it united together, into a mutual
consent and agreement.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: The rational force that governs the universe is built for community and connection. It has made the worse things serve the best. It has bound the best things together in harmony. Can't you see how it has arranged everything in order? How it has given each thing what it deserves? And the highest things of all — it has united them in agreement.

meditations_book-05.originalText: How hast thou carried thyself hitherto towards the Gods? towards thy parents? towards thy brethren? towards thy wife? towards thy children? towards thy masters? thy foster-fathers? thy friends? thy domestics? thy servants? Is it so with thee, that hitherto thou hast neither by word or deed wronged any of them?
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: How have you treated the gods so far? Your parents? Your brothers and sisters? Your wife? Your children? Your teachers? Those who raised you? Your friends? Your household? Your servants? Can you honestly say that you have never wronged any of them with your words or actions?

meditations_book-05.originalText: Remember withal through how many things thou hast already passed, and how many thou hast been able to endure; so that now the legend of thy life is full, and thy charge is accomplished. Again, how many truly good things have certainly by thee been discerned? how many pleasures, how many pains hast thou passed over with contempt? how many things eternally glorious hast thou despised? towards how many perverse unreasonable men hast thou carried thyself kindly, and discreetly?
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Remember all the things you have already been through and endured. Your life story is already full. Your duty is complete. Think of all the truly good things you have recognized. How many pleasures and pains have you looked past with indifference? How many supposedly glorious things have you seen through? How kindly and wisely have you treated difficult, unreasonable people?

meditations_book-05.originalText:
Why should imprudent unlearned souls trouble that which is
both learned, and prudent? And which is that that is so? she that
understandeth the beginning and the end, and hath the true knowledge of
that rational essence, that passeth through all things subsisting, and
through all ages being ever the same, disposing and dispensing as it
were this universe by certain periods of time.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Why should foolish, ignorant souls disturb what is both wise and learned? And what is this wise thing? It is the soul that understands the beginning and the end. It truly knows that rational essence that flows through all existing things and through all time, staying always the same. It arranges and governs the universe in cycles.

meditations_book-05.originalText: Within a very little while, thou wilt be either ashes, or a sceletum; and a name perchance; and perchance, not so much as a name. And what is that but an empty sound, and a rebounding echo? Those things which in this life are dearest unto us, and of most account, they are in themselves but vain, putrid, contemptible. The most weighty and serious, if rightly esteemed, but as puppies, biting one another: or untoward children, now laughing and then crying.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Very soon you will be either ashes or bones. Maybe you'll leave behind a name. Maybe not even that. And what is a name anyway? Just an empty sound that echoes and fades. The things we care about most in life — the things we think matter — are actually worthless, rotten, and pathetic. Even the most serious and important matters, if you really look at them, are like puppies fighting each other. Or like bratty children laughing one minute and crying the next.

meditations_book-05.originalText: As for faith, and modesty, and justice, and truth, they long since, as one of the poets hath it, have abandoned this spacious earth, and retired themselves unto heaven. What is it then that doth keep thee here, if things sensible be so mutable and unsettled? and the senses so obscure, and so fallible? and our souls nothing but an exhalation of blood? and to be in credit among such, be but vanity? What is it that thou dost stay for? an extinction, or a translation; either of them with a propitious and contented mind. But still that time come, what will content thee? what else, but to worship and praise the Gods; and to do good unto men. To bear with them, and to forbear to do them any wrong. And for all external things belonging either to this thy wretched body, or life, to remember that they are neither thine, nor in thy power.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Faith, modesty, justice, and truth have long since left this wide earth and gone to heaven, as one poet put it. So what keeps you here? Physical things change and shift constantly. Your senses are dim and unreliable. Your soul is just vapor from blood. Being respected by such people is empty. What are you waiting for? Death or transformation — either way, face it calmly. But until that time comes, what will satisfy you? Nothing except worshipping the gods and doing good for others. Put up with people. Don't harm them. Remember that everything outside you — your weak body, your life itself — none of it belongs to you or is under your control.

meditations_book-05.originalText:
Thou mayest always speed, if thou wilt but make choice of the
right way; if in the course both of thine opinions and actions, thou
wilt observe a true method. These two things be common to the souls, as
of God, so of men, and of every reasonable creature, first that in their
own proper work they cannot be hindered by anything: and secondly, that
their happiness doth consist in a disposition to, and in the practice of
righteousness; and that in these their desire is terminated.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: You can always make progress if you choose the right path. In both your thoughts and actions, follow a true method. Two things are common to all souls — God's, human, and every thinking being. First, nothing can stop them from doing their proper work. Second, their happiness comes from wanting to do what is right and actually doing it. This is where their desire ends.

meditations_book-05.originalText: If this neither be my wicked act, nor an act anyways depending from any wickedness of mine, and that by it the public is not hurt; what doth it concern me? And wherein can the public be hurt? For thou must not altogether be carried by conceit and common opinion: as for help thou must afford that unto them after thy best ability, and as occasion shall require, though they sustain damage, but in these middle or worldly things; but however do not thou conceive that they are truly hurt thereby: for that is not right.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: If this is not my wrongdoing, and does not come from any fault of mine, and the public is not harmed — why should it concern me? How could the public be hurt? Don't let yourself be swept away by assumptions and popular opinion. You should help others as best you can when the situation calls for it, even if they suffer losses in worldly matters. But don't imagine they are truly damaged by these things. That would be wrong.

meditations_book-05.originalText: But as that old foster-father in the comedy, being now to take his leave doth with a great deal of ceremony, require his foster-child's rhombus, or rattle-top, remembering nevertheless that it is but a rhombus; so here also do thou likewise. For indeed what is all this pleading and public bawling for at the courts? O man, hast thou forgotten what those things are! yea but they are things that others much care for, and highly esteem of. Wilt thou therefore be a fool too? Once I was; let that suffice.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Think of the old foster-father in the play. When he's leaving, he carefully asks for his foster-child's toy rattle back — but he remembers it's just a toy. Do the same thing here. What is all this arguing and shouting in the courts really about? Have you forgotten what these things actually are? Yes, but other people care deeply about them and think they're important. Will you be a fool too? I was once. Let that be enough.

meditations_book-05.originalText:
Let death surprise me when it will, and where it will, I may be
εὔμοιρος, or a happy man, nevertheless.

For he is a happy man, who in his lifetime dealeth unto himself a happy
lot and portion. A happy lot and portion is, good inclinations of the
soul, good desires, good actions.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish:
Let death surprise me when it will, and where it will. I can still be a happy man.

A happy man is one who gives himself a happy lot in life. A happy lot means good inclinations of the soul, good desires, and good actions.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
The matter itself, of which the universe doth consist, is of itself
very tractable and pliable. That rational essence that doth govern it,
hath in itself no cause to do evil. It hath no evil in itself; neither
can it do anything that is evil: neither can anything be hurt by it. And
all things are done and determined according to its will and prescript.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: The basic stuff that makes up the universe is easy to work with. The rational force that governs everything has no reason to do evil. It contains no evil. It cannot do evil things, and it cannot hurt anything. Everything happens according to its will and design.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
Be it all one unto thee, whether half frozen or well warm; whether
only slumbering, or after a full sleep; whether discommended or
commended thou do thy duty: or whether dying or doing somewhat else; for
that also 'to die,' must among the rest be reckoned as one of the duties
and actions of our lives.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: Let it be all the same to you whether you are half frozen or warm. Whether you are barely awake or fully rested. Whether people criticize you or praise you — do your duty. Whether you are dying or doing something else. Even dying must be counted as one of the duties and actions of our lives.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
Look in, let not either the proper quality, or the true worth of
anything pass thee, before thou hast fully apprehended it.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: Look inside yourself. Don't let the real nature or true value of anything slip by before you fully understand it.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
All substances come soon to their change, and either they shall
be resolved by way of exhalation (if so be that all things shall be
reunited into one substance), or as others maintain, they shall be
scattered and dispersed. As for that Rational Essence by which all
things are governed, as it best understandeth itself, both its own
disposition, and what it doth, and what matter it hath to do with and
accordingly doth all things; so we that do not, no wonder, if we wonder
at many things, the reasons whereof we cannot comprehend.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: All things change quickly. They either dissolve back into one substance, or they scatter and break apart. The Rational Essence that governs everything understands itself perfectly. It knows what it is, what it does, and what it works with. It acts accordingly. But we don't understand these things. So it's no wonder we're puzzled by so much that we can't grasp.

meditations_book-06.originalText: The best kind of revenge is, not to become like unto them.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: The best kind of revenge is not to become like them.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
Let this be thy only joy, and thy only comfort, from one sociable
kind action without intermission to pass unto another, God being ever in
thy mind.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: Let this be your only joy and comfort: to move from one kind act to another without stopping, always keeping God in mind.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
The rational commanding part, as it alone can stir up and turn
itself; so it maketh both itself to be, and everything that happeneth,
to appear unto itself, as it will itself.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: The rational part of your mind can control and direct itself. It makes itself what it is. It also shapes how everything that happens appears to you.

meditations_book-06.originalText: According to the nature of the universe all things particular are determined, not according to any other nature, either about compassing and containing; or within, dispersed and contained; or without, depending.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: Everything in the world is shaped by the nature of the universe itself. Not by some other force that surrounds it, or spreads through it, or hangs outside it.

meditations_book-06.originalText: Either this universe is a mere confused mass, and an intricate context of things, which shall in time be scattered and dispersed again: or it is an union consisting of order, and administered by Providence. If the first, why should I desire to continue any longer in this fortuit confusion and commixtion? or why should I take care for anything else, but that as soon as may be I may be earth again? And why should I trouble myself any more whilst I seek to please the Gods? Whatsoever I do, dispersion is my end, and will come upon me whether I will or no. But if the latter be, then am not I religious in vain; then will I be quiet and patient, and put my trust in Him, who is the Governor of all.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: Either this universe is just a confused mess of things that will eventually scatter and fall apart, or it has order and is guided by divine providence. If it's the first option, why would I want to stay longer in this random chaos? Why should I care about anything except returning to dust as soon as possible? Why should I bother trying to please the gods? Whatever I do, everything will scatter anyway, whether I want it to or not. But if the second option is true, then my devotion isn't pointless. Then I can be calm and patient, and trust in the one who governs everything.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
Whensoever by some present hard occurrences thou art constrained to
be in some sort troubled and vexed, return unto thyself as soon as may
be, and be not out of tune longer than thou must needs. For so shalt
thou be the better able to keep thy part another time, and to maintain
the harmony, if thou dost use thyself to this continually; once out,
presently to have recourse unto it, and to begin again.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: When hard times force you to feel troubled and upset, get back to yourself as quickly as you can. Don't stay out of tune longer than you have to. This way you'll be better able to play your part next time and keep the harmony. Make it a habit — whenever you slip, return to yourself right away and start again.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
If it were that thou hadst at one time both a stepmother, and
a natural mother living, thou wouldst honour and respect her also;
nevertheless to thine own natural mother would thy refuge, and recourse
be continually. So let the court and thy philosophy be unto thee. Have
recourse unto it often, and comfort thyself in her, by whom it is that
those other things are made tolerable unto thee, and thou also in those
things not intolerable unto others.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: If you had both a stepmother and your natural mother alive at the same time, you would honor and respect the stepmother too. But you would always go back to your natural mother for comfort and help. Let the court and philosophy be like this for you. Go to philosophy often for comfort. Through philosophy, you can bear the troubles of court life. And philosophy helps you be someone others can bear to be around.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
How marvellous useful it is for a man to represent unto himself
meats, and all such things that are for the mouth, under a right
apprehension and imagination! as for example: This is the carcass of a
fish; this of a bird; and this of a hog. And again more generally; This
phalernum, this excellent highly commended wine, is but the bare juice
of an ordinary grape. This purple robe, but sheep's hairs, dyed with
the blood of a shellfish. So for coitus, it is but the attrition of an
ordinary base entrail, and the excretion of a little vile snivel, with
a certain kind of convulsion: according to Hippocrates his opinion.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: How wonderfully useful it is to see food and drink as they really are! This is a dead fish. This is a dead bird. This is a dead pig. And more broadly: this fine wine that everyone praises is just grape juice. This purple robe is sheep's hair dyed with shellfish blood. As for sex, it's just rubbing body parts together and releasing fluids with some spasms — as Hippocrates described it.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
How
excellent useful are these lively fancies and representations of things,
thus penetrating and passing through the objects, to make their true
nature known and apparent! This must thou use all thy life long, and
upon all occasions: and then especially, when matters are apprehended
as of great worth and respect, thy art and care must be to uncover
them, and to behold their vileness, and to take away from them all those
serious circumstances and expressions, under which they made so grave
a show. For outward pomp and appearance is a great juggler; and then
especially art thou most in danger to be beguiled by it, when (to
a man's thinking) thou most seemest to be employed about matters of
moment.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: How useful these clear mental pictures are! They cut through the surface of things and show their true nature. Use this skill all your life, especially when something seems very important. Your job is to strip away the fancy packaging and see what's really underneath. Remove all the serious words and impressive circumstances that make things look so important. Outward show is a great deceiver. You're most likely to be fooled when you think you're dealing with something that really matters.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
See what Crates pronounceth concerning Xenocrates himself.

Those things which the common sort of people do admire, are most
of them such things as are very general, and may be comprehended under
things merely natural, or naturally affected and qualified: as stones,
wood, figs, vines, olives. Those that be admired by them that are more
moderate and restrained, are comprehended under things animated: as
flocks and herds. Those that are yet more gentle and curious, their
admiration is commonly confined to reasonable creatures only; not in
general as they are reasonable, but as they are capable of art, or of
some craft and subtile invention: or perchance barely to reasonable
creatures; as they that delight in the possession of many slaves. But
he that honours a reasonable soul in general, as it is reasonable and
naturally sociable, doth little regard anything else: and above all
things is careful to preserve his own, in the continual habit and
exercise both of reason and sociableness: and thereby doth co-operate
with him, of whose nature he doth also participate; God.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish:
See what Crates says about Xenocrates himself.

Most people admire very basic things. These are natural objects like stones, wood, figs, vines, and olives. People who are more thoughtful admire living things like flocks and herds. Those who are even more refined focus on rational creatures. But not because they can reason — because they have skills or clever abilities. Or maybe they just like owning many slaves. But the person who honors the rational soul simply because it can reason and naturally connect with others — he cares little for anything else. Above all, he works to keep his own soul in the constant practice of reason and fellowship. In this way, he works together with God, whose nature he shares.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
Some things hasten to be, and others to be no more. And even
whatsoever now is, some part thereof hath already perished. Perpetual
fluxes and alterations renew the world, as the perpetual course of time
doth make the age of the world (of itself infinite) to appear always
fresh and new. In such a flux and course of all things, what of these
things that hasten so fast away should any man regard, since among all
there is not any that a man may fasten and fix upon? as if a man would
settle his affection upon some ordinary sparrow living by him, who is no
sooner seen, than out of sight. For we must not think otherwise of our
lives, than as a mere exhalation of blood, or of an ordinary respiration
of air. For what in our common apprehension is, to breathe in the air
and to breathe it out again, which we do daily: so much is it and no
more, at once to breathe out all thy respirative faculty into that
common air from whence but lately (as being but from yesterday, and
to-day), thou didst first breathe it in, and with it, life.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: Some things rush into existence, others rush out of it. Even what exists right now is already partly gone. Everything flows and changes constantly. This renews the world, just as time's endless march makes the world always seem fresh and new. In this rushing flow of everything, why should anyone care about these fleeting things? You can't hold onto any of them. It's like falling in love with a sparrow that flies past your window — you see it for a moment, then it's gone. Think of your life the same way. It's just a puff of breath, an ordinary inhale and exhale. What we normally think of as breathing — taking air in and letting it out each day — that's all life is. One day you'll breathe out your last breath into the common air. The same air you first breathed in just yesterday, or today, along with life itself.

meditations_book-06.originalText: Not vegetative spiration, it is not surely (which plants have) that in this life should be so dear unto us; nor sensitive respiration, the proper life of beasts, both tame and wild; nor this our imaginative faculty; nor that we are subject to be led and carried up and down by the strength of our sensual appetites; or that we can gather, and live together; or that we can feed: for that in effect is no better, than that we can void the excrements of our food. What is it then that should be dear unto us? to hear a clattering noise? if not that, then neither to be applauded by the tongues of men. For the praises of many tongues, is in effect no better than the clattering of so many tongues. If then neither applause, what is there remaining that should be dear unto thee?
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: It's not the basic breathing that plants have that should matter to us in this life. It's not the animal breathing that beasts have, wild or tame. It's not our ability to imagine things. It's not being pulled around by our desires. It's not that we can gather together and live in groups. It's not that we can eat — that's really no better than being able to get rid of waste. So what should matter to us? Hearing noise and chatter? If not that, then not being praised by people either. The praise of many voices is really no better than the chattering of many tongues. So if praise doesn't matter, what is left that should be dear to you?

meditations_book-06.originalText: This I think: that in all thy motions and actions thou be moved, and restrained according to thine own true natural constitution and Construction only. And to this even ordinary arts and professions do lead us. For it is that which every art doth aim at, that whatsoever it is, that is by art effected and prepared, may be fit for that work that it is prepared for. This is the end that he that dresseth the vine, and he that takes upon him either to tame colts, or to train up dogs, doth aim at. What else doth the education of children, and all learned professions tend unto? Certainly then it is that, which should be dear unto us also. If in this particular it go well with thee, care not for the obtaining of other things. But is it so, that thou canst not but respect other things also?
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: Here's what I think: in everything you do, let your true nature guide and limit you. Even ordinary jobs and crafts point us toward this. Every art aims for the same thing — that whatever it creates should be fit for its purpose. This is what the vine-dresser aims for, and the person who breaks in colts or trains dogs. What else does educating children or learning any profession lead to? This should matter to us too. If you get this right, don't worry about getting other things. But can you really help caring about other things too?

meditations_book-06.originalText: Then canst not thou truly be free? then canst thou not have self-content: then wilt thou ever be subject to passions. For it is not possible, but that thou must be envious, and jealous, and suspicious of them whom thou knowest can bereave thee of such things; and again, a secret underminer of them, whom thou seest in present possession of that which is dear unto thee. To be short, he must of necessity be full of confusion within himself, and often accuse the Gods, whosoever stands in need of these things. But if thou shalt honour and respect thy mind only, that will make thee acceptable towards thyself, towards thy friends very tractable; and conformable and concordant with the Gods; that is, accepting with praises whatsoever they shall think good to appoint and allot unto thee.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: Then how can you truly be free? How can you be content? You will always be ruled by your emotions. You must feel envy and jealousy toward those who can take these things from you. You will secretly plot against those who have what you want. In short, anyone who needs these things will be confused inside and often blame the gods. But if you respect only your mind, that will make you happy with yourself. You will get along with your friends. You will be in harmony with the gods — accepting with gratitude whatever they choose to give you.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
Under, above, and about, are the motions of the elements; but
the motion of virtue, is none of those motions, but is somewhat more
excellent and divine. Whose way (to speed and prosper in it) must be
through a way, that is not easily comprehended.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: Below, above, and around us are the movements of the elements. But the movement of virtue is none of these movements. It is something more excellent and divine. Its path — to move forward and succeed in it — must be through a way that is not easily understood.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
Who can choose but wonder at them? They will not speak well of
them that are at the same time with them, and live with them; yet they
themselves are very ambitious, that they that shall follow, whom they
have never seen, nor shall ever see, should speak well of them. As if
a man should grieve that he hath not been commended by them, that lived
before him.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: Who can help but wonder at people? They won't speak well of those who live alongside them right now. Yet they desperately want people in the future — people they will never meet — to speak well of them. It's like grieving that people who lived before you never praised you.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
Do not ever conceive anything impossible to man, which by thee
cannot, or not without much difficulty be effected; but whatsoever in
general thou canst Conceive possible and proper unto any man, think that
very possible unto thee also.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: Don't think anything is impossible for you if other people can do it. If you see that something is possible and right for any person, believe that you can do it too.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
Suppose that at the palestra somebody hath all to-torn thee with
his nails, and hath broken thy head. Well, thou art wounded. Yet thou
dost not exclaim; thou art not offended with him. Thou dost not suspect
him for it afterwards, as one that watcheth to do thee a mischief. Yea
even then, though thou dost thy best to save thyself from him, yet not
from him as an enemy. It is not by way of any suspicious indignation,
but by way of gentle and friendly declination. Keep the same mind and
disposition in other parts of thy life also. For many things there be,
which we must conceit and apprehend, as though we had had to do with an
antagonist at the palestra. For as I said, it is very possible for us to
avoid and decline, though we neither suspect, nor hate.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: Imagine someone at the wrestling school scratches you badly with his nails and cuts your head. You're hurt. But you don't cry out. You don't get angry at him. You don't suspect him afterward of trying to harm you on purpose. Even then, you do your best to protect yourself from him — but not as if he were your enemy. You avoid him not out of angry suspicion, but with calm and friendly caution. Keep this same attitude in other parts of your life too. There are many situations we should handle as if we were dealing with an opponent at the wrestling school. As I said, we can avoid and protect ourselves without suspecting or hating.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
If anybody shall reprove me, and shall make it apparent unto me,
that in any either opinion or action of mine I do err, I will most
gladly retract. For it is the truth that I seek after, by which I am
sure that never any man was hurt; and as sure, that he is hurt that
continueth in any error, or ignorance whatsoever.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: If anyone corrects me and shows me that I'm wrong in my thinking or actions, I'll gladly change my mind. I'm looking for the truth. Truth never hurt anyone. But staying wrong or ignorant — that's what really hurts.

meditations_book-06.originalText: I for my part will do what belongs unto me; as for other things, whether things unsensible or things irrational; or if rational, yet deceived and ignorant of the true way, they shall not trouble or distract me. For as for those creatures which are not endued with reason and all other things and-matters of the world whatsoever I freely, and generously, as one endued with reason, of things that have none, make use of them. And as for men, towards them as naturally partakers of the same reason, my care is to carry myself sociably.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: I will do my part. As for other things — things without feeling, things without reason, or people who have reason but are deceived and lost — they will not trouble me or pull me off course. I use things without reason freely and generously, as someone with reason naturally would. And toward other people, since they share this same gift of reason, I try to act with friendship and care.

meditations_book-06.originalText: But whatsoever it is that thou art about, remember to call upon the Gods. And as for the time how long thou shalt live to do these things, let it be altogether indifferent unto thee, for even three such hours are sufficient.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: Whatever you're doing, remember to call on the gods for help. As for how long you'll live to do these things, don't worry about it. Even three hours can be enough.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
Alexander of Macedon, and he that dressed his mules, when once
dead both came to one. For either they were both resumed into those
original rational essences from whence all things in the world are
propagated; or both after one fashion were scattered into atoms.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: Alexander the Great and the man who groomed his mules both ended up the same when they died. Either they both returned to the universal reason that creates all things, or they both scattered into atoms the same way.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
Consider how many different things, whether they concern our
bodies, or our souls, in a moment of time come to pass in every one of
us, and so thou wilt not wonder if many more things or rather all things
that are done, can at one time subsist, and coexist in that both one and
general, which we call the world.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: Think about how many different things happen in our bodies and minds at the same moment. Then you won't be surprised that many more things — or really, all things — can exist at the same time in what we call the world.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
if any should put this question unto thee, how this word Antoninus
is written, wouldst thou not presently fix thine intention upon it, and
utter out in order every letter of it? And if any shall begin to gainsay
thee, and quarrel with thee about it; wilt thou quarrel with him again,
or rather go on meekly as thou hast begun, until thou hast numbered out
every letter? Here then likewise remember, that every duty that belongs
unto a man doth consist of some certain letters or numbers as it were,
to which without any noise or tumult keeping thyself thou must orderly
proceed to thy proposed end, forbearing to quarrel with him that would
quarrel and fall out with thee.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: If someone asked you how to spell the name Antoninus, you would focus and say each letter in order. And if someone argued with you about it, would you argue back? No — you would keep going calmly until you finished spelling it out. Remember this when doing your duties. Every task has steps, like letters in a word. Stay quiet and work through each step in order. Don't fight with people who want to pick fights with you.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
Is it not a cruel thing to forbid men to affect those things, which
they conceive to agree best with their own natures, and to tend most
to their own proper good and behoof? But thou after a sort deniest them
this liberty, as often as thou art angry with them for their sins. For
surely they are led unto those sins whatsoever they be, as to
their proper good and commodity. But it is not so (thou wilt object
perchance). Thou therefore teach them better, and make it appear unto
them: but be not thou angry with them.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: Isn't it cruel to stop people from pursuing what they think is best for their nature and their own good? But you deny them this freedom when you get angry at them for their mistakes. They are drawn to those mistakes because they think it will benefit them. "But that's not true," you might say. Then teach them better. Show them the truth. But don't be angry with them.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
Death is a cessation from the impression of the senses, the
tyranny of the passions, the errors of the mind, and the servitude of
the body.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: Death is an end to the input of the senses, the tyranny of emotions, the mistakes of the mind, and the slavery of the body.

meditations_book-06.originalText: If in this kind of life thy body be able to hold out, it is a shame that thy soul should faint first, and give over, take heed, lest of a philosopher thou become a mere Cæsar in time, and receive a new tincture from the court. For it may happen if thou dost not take heed.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: If your body can handle this kind of life, it's shameful for your soul to give up first. Be careful not to let the philosopher in you turn into just another Caesar over time. Don't let the court corrupt you. It can happen if you're not careful.

meditations_book-06.originalText: Keep thyself therefore, truly simple, good, sincere, grave, free from all ostentation, a lover of that which is just, religious, kind, tender-hearted, strong and vigorous to undergo anything that becomes thee. Endeavour to continue such, as philosophy (hadst thou wholly and constantly applied thyself unto it) would have made, and secured thee. Worship the Gods, procure the welfare of men, this life is short. Charitable actions, and a holy disposition, is the only fruit of this earthly life.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: Stay simple, good, honest, serious, and free from showing off. Love what is just. Be religious, kind, tender-hearted, and strong enough to handle whatever comes your way. Try to remain the person that philosophy would have made you — if you had truly committed to it. Honor the gods and help other people. This life is short. Kindness to others and a holy heart are the only things that matter in this earthly life.

meditations_book-06.originalText: Do all things as becometh the disciple of Antoninus Pius. Remember his resolute constancy in things that were done by him according to reason, his equability in all things, his sanctity; the cheerfulness of his countenance, his sweetness, and how free he was from all vainglory; how careful to come to the true and exact knowledge of matters in hand, and how he would by no means give over till he did fully, and plainly understand the whole state of the business; and how patiently, and without any contestation he would bear with them, that did unjustly condemn him: how he would never be over-hasty in anything, nor give ear to slanders and false accusations, but examine and observe with best diligence the several actions and dispositions of men.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: Do everything as a student of Antoninus Pius would. Remember how steady he was in all his decisions based on reason. Remember his balance in everything, his goodness, the cheerfulness in his face, his kindness. Remember how free he was from showing off. Remember how carefully he worked to truly understand every matter at hand. He would never give up until he fully grasped the whole situation. Remember how patiently he dealt with people who wrongly criticized him, without arguing back. He was never rushed in anything. He didn't listen to gossip or false charges. Instead, he carefully studied people's actions and characters.

meditations_book-06.originalText: Again, how he was no backbiter, nor easily frightened, nor suspicious, and in his language free from all affectation and curiosity: and how easily he would content himself with few things, as lodging, bedding, clothing, and ordinary nourishment, and attendance. How able to endure labour, how patient; able through his spare diet to continue from morning to evening without any necessity of withdrawing before his accustomed hours to the necessities of nature: his uniformity and constancy in matter of friendship. How he would bear with them that with all boldness and liberty opposed his opinions; and even rejoice if any man could better advise him: and lastly, how religious he was without superstition.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: He was not a gossip. He didn't scare easily or get suspicious. His speech was simple and natural — no show-off words or fancy talk. He was happy with basic things: a simple room, plain bed, ordinary clothes, simple food, and basic help. He could work hard and be patient. He ate so little that he could go from morning to evening without needing to step away for bathroom breaks before his usual times. He was steady and loyal as a friend. When people boldly disagreed with him, he listened well. He was even happy when someone gave him better advice. And he was deeply religious, but not superstitious.

meditations_book-06.originalText: All these things of him remember, that whensoever thy last hour shall come upon thee, it may find thee, as it did him, ready for it in the possession of a good conscience.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: Remember all these things about him, so that when your last hour comes, it will find you ready for it with a clear conscience, just as it found him.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
Stir up thy mind, and recall thy wits again from thy natural
dreams, and visions, and when thou art perfectly awoken, and canst
perceive that they were but dreams that troubled thee, as one newly
