We shouldn't think that nature has mixed the soul so completely with the body that the soul can't set its own boundaries and pursue its own purposes.

meditations_book-07.originalText:
For it is a thing very possible, that a man should be a very
divine man, and yet be altogether unknown. This thou must ever be
mindful of, as of this also, that a man's true happiness doth consist
in very few things. And that although thou dost despair, that thou shalt
ever be a good either logician, or naturalist, yet thou art never the
further off by it from being either liberal, or modest, or charitable,
or obedient unto God.
meditations_book-07.plainEnglish: It's very possible for someone to be truly good and yet be completely unknown. Always remember this. Also remember that real happiness comes from very few things. Even if you despair that you'll never be a good logician or scientist, that doesn't stop you from being generous, humble, kind, or obedient to God.

meditations_book-07.originalText: Free from all compulsion in all cheerfulness and alacrity thou mayst run out thy time, though men should exclaim against thee never so much, and the wild beasts should pull in sunder the poor members of thy pampered mass of flesh. For what in either of these or the like cases should hinder the mind to retain her own rest and tranquillity, consisting both in the right judgment of those things that happen unto her, and in the ready use of all present matters and occasions?
meditations_book-07.plainEnglish: You can live out your life freely, with joy and energy, even if people shout against you and wild beasts tear apart your soft body. What in any of these situations could stop your mind from staying calm and peaceful? Your peace comes from seeing things clearly and making good use of whatever happens to you.

meditations_book-07.originalText: So that her judgment may say, to that which is befallen her by way of cross: this thou art in very deed, and according to thy true nature: notwithstanding that in the judgment of opinion thou dust appear otherwise: and her discretion to the present object; thou art that, which I sought for. For whatsoever it be, that is now present, shall ever be embraced by me as a fit and seasonable object, both for my reasonable faculty, and for my sociable, or charitable inclination to work upon. And that which is principal in this matter, is that it may be referred either unto the praise of God, or to the good of men. For either unto God or man, whatsoever it is that doth happen in the world hath in the ordinary course of nature its proper reference; neither is there anything, that in regard of nature is either new, or reluctant and intractable, but all things both usual and easy.
meditations_book-07.plainEnglish: So that your judgment may say to whatever hardship comes your way: this is what you truly are, this is your real nature. Even though others might see it differently. And your reason should say to whatever is happening now: you are exactly what I was looking for. Whatever is present right now, I will always welcome it as the right material for my mind to work with and my social nature to act on. The main thing is that everything can be traced back either to praising God or helping people. Everything that happens in the world naturally points either toward God or toward helping others. Nothing is really new or impossible to handle. Everything is familiar and manageable.

meditations_book-07.originalText:
Then hath a man attained to the estate of perfection in his life and
conversation, when he so spends every day, as if it were his last day:
never hot and vehement in his affections, nor yet so cold and stupid as
one that had no sense; and free from all manner of dissimulation.
meditations_book-07.plainEnglish: A man reaches perfection in how he lives when he spends each day as if it were his last day. He is never too passionate or hot-headed, but also not cold and lifeless like someone who feels nothing. And he is completely honest, with no pretending.

meditations_book-07.originalText:
Can the Gods, who are immortal, for the continuance of so many ages
bear without indignation with such and so many sinners, as have ever
been, yea not only so, but also take such care for them, that they want
nothing; and dust thou so grievously take on, as one that could bear
with them no longer; thou that art but for a moment of time? yea thou
that art one of those sinners thyself? A very ridiculous thing it is,
that any man should dispense with vice and wickedness in himself, which
is in his power to restrain; and should go about to suppress it in
others, which is altogether impossible.
meditations_book-07.plainEnglish: The gods are immortal. For countless ages they have put up with all these sinners without getting angry. They even take care of these people and give them what they need. Yet you get so upset that you act like you can't stand them anymore — you who will only be here for a moment. You who are one of those sinners yourself. It's ridiculous. A person will excuse vice and wickedness in himself, which he actually has the power to stop. But then he tries to stop it in others, which is impossible.

meditations_book-07.originalText:
What object soever, our reasonable and sociable faculty doth meet
with, that affords nothing either for the satisfaction of reason, or for
the practice of charity, she worthily doth think unworthy of herself.
meditations_book-07.plainEnglish: Whatever our rational and social nature encounters that offers nothing for reason or for helping others, it rightly considers beneath itself.

meditations_book-07.originalText:
When thou hast done well, and another is benefited by thy action,
must thou like a very fool look for a third thing besides, as that
it may appear unto others also that thou hast done well, or that thou
mayest in time, receive one good turn for another? No man useth to be
weary of that which is beneficial unto him. But every action according
to nature, is beneficial. Be not weary then of doing that which is
beneficial unto thee, whilst it is so unto others.
meditations_book-07.plainEnglish: When you have done good and helped someone, don't be foolish and look for a third reward. Don't expect others to notice your good deed or wait for someone to return the favor. No one gets tired of what benefits them. And every natural action benefits you. So don't get tired of doing what benefits you, especially when it also benefits others.

meditations_book-07.originalText:
The nature of the universe did once certainly before it was
created, whatsoever it hath done since, deliberate and so resolve upon
the creation of the world. Now since that time, whatsoever it is, that
is and happens in the world, is either but a consequent of that one and
first deliberation: or if so be that this ruling rational part of the
world, takes any thought and care of things particular, they are surely
his reasonable and principal creatures, that are the proper object of
his particular care and providence. This often thought upon, will much
conduce to thy tranquillity.
meditations_book-07.plainEnglish: The universe once decided to create the world. Everything that happens now follows from that first choice. Or maybe the rational force that rules the world takes special care of thinking creatures like us. Either way, remembering this will bring you peace.

meditations_book-08.originalText: This also, among other things, may serve to keep thee from vainglory; if thou shalt consider, that thou art now altogether incapable of the commendation of one, who all his life long, or from his youth at least, hath lived a philosopher's life. For both unto others, and to thyself especially, it is well known, that thou hast done many things contrary to that perfection of life. Thou hast therefore been confounded in thy course, and henceforth it will be hard for thee to recover the title and credit of a philosopher. And to it also is thy calling and profession repugnant. If therefore thou dost truly understand, what it is that is of moment indeed; as for thy fame and credit, take no thought or care for that: let it suffice thee if all the rest of thy life, be it more or less, thou shalt live as thy nature requireth, or according to the true and natural end of thy making.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: This thought can also help keep you humble. You can never claim to be someone who has lived like a philosopher his whole life, or even from youth. Everyone knows — especially you — that you have done many things that fall short of that ideal. You have stumbled along the way. It will be hard now to earn the name of philosopher. Your position and duties work against it too. So if you truly understand what really matters, don't worry about your reputation. Let it be enough that you spend the rest of your life, however long or short, living as your nature requires — according to your true purpose.

meditations_book-08.originalText: Take pains therefore to know what it is that thy nature requireth, and let nothing else distract thee. Thou hast already had sufficient experience, that of those many things that hitherto thou hast erred and wandered about, thou couldst not find happiness in any of them. Not in syllogisms, and logical subtilties, not in wealth, not in honour and reputation, not in pleasure. In none of all these. Wherein then is it to be found? In the practice of those things, which the nature of man, as he is a man, doth require. How then shall he do those things? if his dogmata, or moral tenets and opinions (from which all motions and actions do proceed), be right and true. Which be those dogmata? Those that concern that which is good or evil, as that there is nothing truly good and beneficial unto man, but that which makes him just, temperate, courageous, liberal; and that there is nothing truly evil and hurtful unto man, but that which causeth the contrary effects.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: Work hard to understand what your nature needs, and don't let anything else pull you away. You have enough experience now. You have tried many things and wandered down many paths, but you couldn't find happiness in any of them. Not in clever arguments and logic puzzles. Not in wealth. Not in honor and fame. Not in pleasure. None of these worked. So where can happiness be found? In doing what human nature requires. But how do you do these things? Your core beliefs must be right and true. All your actions flow from your beliefs. What should those beliefs be? Beliefs about what is good and evil. Nothing is truly good for a person except what makes them just, self-controlled, brave, and generous. Nothing is truly evil except what has the opposite effects.

meditations_book-08.originalText:
Upon every action that thou art about, put this question to thyself;
How will this when it is done agree with me? Shall I have no occasion
to repent of it? Yet a very little while and I am dead and gone; and
all things are at end. What then do I care for more than this, that my
present action whatsoever it be, may be the proper action of one that
is reasonable; whose end is, the common good; who in all things is ruled
and governed by the same law of right and reason, by which God Himself
is.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: Before every action, ask yourself this question: How will this sit with me when it's done? Will I regret it? Very soon I'll be dead and gone, and everything will be over. What else matters beyond this — that whatever I'm doing right now is the proper action of a reasonable person? Someone whose goal is the common good. Someone who follows the same law of right and reason that governs God himself.

meditations_book-08.originalText:
Alexander, Caius, Pompeius; what are these to Diogenes, Heraclitus,
and Socrates? These penetrated into the true nature of things; into all
causes, and all subjects: and upon these did they exercise their power
and authority. But as for those, as the extent of their error was, so
far did their slavery extend.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: Alexander, Caesar, Pompey — what are they compared to Diogenes, Heraclitus, and Socrates? The philosophers saw into the true nature of things. They understood causes and subjects deeply. That's where they had real power and authority. But the conquerors? Their slavery went as far as their mistakes.

meditations_book-08.originalText:
What they have done, they will still do, although thou shouldst hang
thyself. First; let it not trouble thee. For all things both good and
evil: come to pass according to the nature and general condition of the
universe, and within a very little while, all things will be at an
end; no man will be remembered: as now of Africanus (for example) and
Augustus it is already come to pass. Then secondly; fix thy mind upon
the thing itself; look into it, and remembering thyself, that thou art
bound nevertheless to be a good man, and what it is that thy nature
requireth of thee as thou art a man, be not diverted from what thou art
about, and speak that which seemeth unto thee most just: only speak it
kindly, modestly, and without hypocrisy.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: What they have done, they will keep doing, even if you kill yourself over it. First, don't let it trouble you. All things, good and bad, happen according to the nature of the universe. And very soon, everything will be over. No one will be remembered — just look at Africanus and Augustus, already forgotten. Second, focus on the thing itself. Look at it clearly. Remember that you are bound to be a good person no matter what. Remember what your nature requires of you as a human being. Don't get distracted from your work. Speak what seems most just to you — but speak it kindly, humbly, and without pretense.

The universe is always busy moving things around. It takes what is here and moves it there. It changes things and then moves them somewhere else. So you don't need to fear anything new. Everything follows the same patterns. All things are handled with fairness.

meditations_book-08.originalText: Every particular nature hath content, when in its own proper course it speeds. A reasonable nature doth then speed, when first in matter of fancies and imaginations, it gives no consent to that which is either false uncertain. Secondly, when in all its motions and resolutions it takes its level at the common good only, and that it desireth nothing, and flieth from nothing, bet what is in its own power to compass or avoid. And lastly, when it willingly and gladly embraceth, whatsoever is dealt and appointed unto it by the common nature.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: Every nature finds contentment when it follows its proper path. A rational nature follows its path when it does three things. First, it doesn't accept false or uncertain thoughts. Second, in all its actions and decisions, it aims only at the common good. It wants nothing and avoids nothing except what is within its own power to get or avoid. Third, it willingly accepts whatever the universal nature assigns to it.

meditations_book-08.originalText: For it is part of it; even as the nature of any one leaf, is part of the common nature of all plants and trees. But that the nature of a leaf, is part of a nature both unreasonable and unsensible, and which in its proper end may be hindered; or, which is servile and slavish: whereas the nature of man is part of a common nature which cannot be hindered, and which is both reasonable and just. From whence also it is, that according to the worth of everything, she doth make such equal distribution of all things, as of duration, substance form, operation, and of events and accidents. But herein consider not whether thou shalt find this equality in everything absolutely and by itself; but whether in all the particulars of some one thing taken together, and compared with all the particulars of some other thing, and them together likewise.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: A leaf is part of the larger nature of all plants and trees. But a leaf's nature is part of something that lacks reason and feeling, something that can be stopped from reaching its purpose — something that serves without choice. Human nature, though, is part of a common nature that cannot be stopped. It is reasonable and just. Because of this, nature gives out everything fairly — time, substance, form, action, and events. But don't look for this fairness in each thing by itself. Look at all the parts of one thing together, then compare that whole to all the parts of another thing together.

meditations_book-08.originalText:
Thou hast no time nor opportunity to read. What then? Hast thou
not time and opportunity to exercise thyself, not to wrong thyself; to
strive against all carnal pleasures and pains, and to get the upper hand
of them; to contemn honour and vainglory; and not only, not to be angry
with them, whom towards thee thou doest find unsensible and unthankful;
but also to have a care of them still, and of their welfare?
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: You have no time to read. So what? Don't you have time to train yourself? Time to stop hurting yourself? Time to fight against bodily pleasures and pains, and master them? Time to look down on honor and fame? Time not just to avoid anger at people who seem blind and ungrateful toward you, but to actually care for them and their well-being?

meditations_book-08.originalText:
Forbear henceforth to complain of the trouble of a courtly life,
either in public before others, or in private by thyself.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: Stop complaining about the troubles of court life. Don't do it in public around others, and don't do it in private to yourself either.

meditations_book-08.originalText:
Repentance is an inward and self-reprehension for the neglect or
omission of somewhat that was profitable. Now whatsoever is good, is
also profitable, and it is the part of an honest virtuous man to set by
it, and to make reckoning of it accordingly. But never did any honest
virtuous man repent of the neglect or omission of any carnal pleasure:
no carnal pleasure then is either good or profitable.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: Repentance is feeling bad about yourself for neglecting or skipping something that would have helped you. Whatever is good is also helpful. An honest, virtuous person values good things and treats them as important. But no honest, virtuous person ever regrets missing out on bodily pleasures. So bodily pleasures are neither good nor helpful.

meditations_book-08.originalText:
This, what is it in itself, and by itself, according to its proper
constitution? What is the substance of it? What is the matter, or proper
use? What is the form or efficient cause? What is it for in this world,
and how long will it abide? Thus must thou examine all things, that
present themselves unto thee.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: When something comes before you, ask yourself: What is this thing really? What is it made of? What is it supposed to do? Why does it exist in this world, and how long will it last? This is how you must examine everything that comes your way.

meditations_book-08.originalText:
When thou art hard to be stirred up and awaked out of thy sleep,
admonish thyself and call to mind, that, to perform actions tending to
the common good is that which thine own proper constitution, and
that which the nature of man do require. But to sleep, is common to
unreasonable creatures also. And what more proper and natural, yea what
more kind and pleasing, than that which is according to nature?
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: When you find it hard to get out of bed, remind yourself of this: doing things that help others is what your nature requires. It's what being human means. But sleeping? Even animals do that. What could be more natural and satisfying than living according to your true nature?

meditations_book-08.originalText:
As every fancy and imagination presents itself unto thee, consider
(if it be possible) the true nature, and the proper qualities of it, and
reason with thyself about it.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: When any thought or image comes to mind, look at it clearly (if you can). See what it really is and what qualities it has. Think it through.

meditations_book-08.originalText: At thy first encounter with any one, say presently to thyself: This man, what are his opinions concerning that which is good or evil? as concerning pain, pleasure, and the causes of both; concerning honour, and dishonour, concerning life and death? thus and thus. Now if it be no wonder that a man should have such and such opinions, how can it be a wonder that he should do such and such things? I will remember then, that he cannot but do as he doth, holding those opinions that he doth.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: When you first meet someone, ask yourself right away: What does this person think is good or bad? What do they think about pain and pleasure? What about honor and shame, life and death? Once you know their views, it makes sense that they act the way they do. If their opinions don't surprise you, then their actions shouldn't surprise you either. Remember — they can't help but act according to what they believe.

meditations_book-08.originalText: Remember, that as it is a shame for any man to wonder that a fig tree should bear figs, so also to wonder that the world should bear anything, whatsoever it is which in the ordinary course of nature it may bear. To a physician also and to a pilot it is a shame either for the one to wonder, that such and such a one should have an ague; or for the other, that the winds should prove Contrary.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: Remember, it would be foolish to wonder that a fig tree bears figs. In the same way, it's foolish to wonder that the world produces whatever it naturally produces. A doctor shouldn't be surprised when someone gets a fever. A ship captain shouldn't be surprised when the winds turn against him.

meditations_book-08.originalText:
Remember, that to change thy mind upon occasion, and to follow him
that is able to rectify thee, is equally ingenuous, as to find out at
the first, what is right and just, without help. For of thee nothing is
required, ti, is beyond the extent of thine own deliberation and jun.
merit, and of thine own understanding.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: Remember that changing your mind when the situation calls for it, and following someone who can set you right, is just as honest as figuring out what's right and just on your own from the start. Nothing is required of you that goes beyond your own thinking, judgment, and understanding.

meditations_book-08.originalText:
If it were thine act and in thine own power, wouldest thou do
it? If it were not, whom dost tin accuse? the atoms, or the Gods? For to
do either, the part of a mad man. Thou must therefore blame nobody, but
if it be in thy power, redress what is amiss; if it be not, to what end
is it to complain? For nothing should be done but to some certain end.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: If it were your action and in your control, would you do it? If it's not your doing, who are you blaming? The atoms, or the gods? Either way, that's crazy. Don't blame anyone. If it's in your power, fix what's wrong. If it's not, what's the point of complaining? Everything should be done for a reason.

meditations_book-08.originalText:
Whatsoever dieth and falleth, however and wheresoever it die
and fall, it cannot fall out of the world, here it have its abode
and change, here also shall it have its dissolution into its proper
elements. The same are the world's elements, and the elements of which
thou dost consist. And they when they are changed, they murmur not; why
shouldest thou?
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: Whatever dies and falls, no matter how or where it happens, it cannot fall out of the world. Here it lived and changed, and here it will break down into its basic parts. These are the same elements that make up the world, and the same elements that make up you. When they change, they don't complain. Why should you?

meditations_book-08.originalText:
Whatsoever is, was made for something: as a horse, a vine. Why
wonderest thou? The sun itself will say of itself, I was made for
something; and so hath every god its proper function. What then were
then made for? to disport and delight thyself? See how even common sense
and reason cannot brook it.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: Everything was made for a purpose. A horse has a purpose. A vine has a purpose. Why are you surprised by this? Even the sun would say, "I was made for something." Every god has its own job to do. So what were you made for? To play around and have fun? See how even basic common sense can't accept that.

meditations_book-08.originalText:
Nature hath its end as well in the end and final consummation of
anything that is, as in the begin-nine and continuation of it.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: Nature has its purpose in the ending and final completion of anything, just as much as in the beginning and continuation of it.

meditations_book-08.originalText: As one that tosseth up a ball. And what is a ball the better, if the motion of it be upwards; or the worse if it be downwards; or if it chance to fall upon the ground? So for the bubble; if it continue, what it the better? and if it dissolve, what is it the worse And so is it of a candle too. And so must thou reason with thyself, both in matter of fame, and in matter of death.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: Think of someone tossing a ball up in the air. Is the ball any better when it goes up? Any worse when it comes down or hits the ground? The same goes for a soap bubble. Is it better when it lasts? Worse when it pops? A candle is the same way. You should think about fame and death like this too.

meditations_book-08.originalText: For as for the body itself, (the subject of death) wouldest thou know the vileness of it? Turn it about that thou mayest behold it the worst sides upwards as well, as in its more ordinary pleasant shape; how doth it look, when it is old and withered? when sick and pained? when in the act of lust, and fornication?
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: As for the body itself—what death takes away—do you want to see how worthless it is? Look at it from all angles, not just when it appears pleasant. How does it look when it's old and shriveled? When it's sick and in pain? When it's driven by lust and desire?

meditations_book-08.originalText: And as for fame. This life is short. Both he that praiseth, and he that is praised; he that remembers, and he that is remembered, will soon be dust and ashes. Besides, it is but in one corner of this part of the world that thou art praised; and yet in this corner, thou hast not the joint praises of all men; no nor scarce of any one constantly. And yet the whole earth itself, what is it but as one point, in regard of the whole world?
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: And as for fame. This life is short. The person who praises and the person being praised will both soon be dust and ashes. So will the one who remembers and the one being remembered. Besides, you are only praised in one small corner of the world. And even in that corner, you don't have everyone's praise. You don't even have one person's praise all the time. And yet the whole earth itself — what is it but one tiny point compared to the entire universe?

meditations_book-08.originalText:
That which must be the subject of thy consideration, is either the
matter itself, or the dogma, or the operation, or the true sense and
signification.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: Whatever you need to think about falls into one of four categories: the thing itself, the belief about it, what it does, or what it really means.

meditations_book-08.originalText:
Most justly have these things happened unto thee: why dost not
thou amend? O but thou hadst rather become good to-morrow, than to be
so to-day.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: These things happened to you for good reason. So why don't you change? But you would rather become good tomorrow than today.

meditations_book-08.originalText:
Shall I do it? I will; so the end of my action be to do good unto
men. Doth anything by way of cross or adversity happen unto me? I accept
it, with reference unto the Gods, and their providence; the fountain of
all things, from which whatsoever comes to pass, doth hang and depend.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: Should I do it? I will, as long as my action helps people. Does something difficult or painful happen to me? I accept it, knowing it comes from the gods and their plan — the source of all things, from which everything that happens flows.

meditations_book-08.originalText:
By one action judge of the rest: this bathing which usually takes
up so much of our time, what is it? Oil, sweat, filth; or the sordes of
the body: an excrementitious viscosity, the excrements of oil and other
ointments used about the body, and mixed with the sordes of the body:
all base and loathsome. And such almost is every part of our life;
and every worldly object.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: Judge everything else by this one example: bathing, which takes up so much of our time — what is it really? Oil, sweat, dirt. The grime of the body. A sticky mess of waste — leftover oils and lotions mixed with body filth. All of it disgusting and vile. This is what almost every part of our life is like. Every worldly thing is the same.

meditations_book-08.originalText: Lucilla buried Verus; then was Lucilla herself buried by others. So Secunda Maximus, then Secunda herself. So Epitynchanus, Diotimus; then Epitynchanus himself. So Antoninus Pius, Faustina his wife; then Antoninus himself. This is the course of the world. First Celer, Adrianus; then Adrianus himself. And those austere ones; those that foretold other men's deaths; those that were so proud and stately, where are they now? Those austere ones I mean, such as were Charax, and Demetrius the Platonic, and Eudaemon, and others like unto those. They were all but for one day; all dead and gone long since. Some of them no sooner dead, than forgotten. Others soon turned into fables. Of others, even that which was fabulous, is now long since forgotten.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: Lucilla buried Verus, then others buried Lucilla. So Secunda buried Maximus, then Secunda herself was buried. So Epitynchanus buried Diotimus, then Epitynchanus himself. So Antoninus Pius buried his wife Faustina, then Antoninus himself was buried. This is how the world works. First Celer buried Adrianus, then Adrianus himself was buried. And what about those stern philosophers? Those who predicted other men's deaths? Those who were so proud and grand—where are they now? I mean those stern ones like Charax, Demetrius the Platonic, Eudaemon, and others like them. They lasted only a day. All dead and gone long ago. Some were forgotten as soon as they died. Others became legends. But even the legends are now forgotten.

meditations_book-08.originalText: This thereafter thou must remember, that whatsoever thou art compounded of, shall soon be dispersed, and that thy life and breath, or thy soul, shall either be no more or shall ranslated (sp.), and appointed to some certain place and station.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: Remember this: whatever you are made of will soon scatter apart. Your life and breath, or your soul, will either be gone completely or moved to some other place.

meditations_book-08.originalText:
The true joy of a man, is to do that which properly belongs unto a
man. That which is most proper unto a man, is, first, to be kindly
affected towards them that are of the same kind and nature as he is
himself to contemn all sensual motions and appetites, to discern rightly
all plausible fancies and imaginations, to contemplate the nature of the
universe; both it, and things that are done in it. In which kind of
contemplation three several relations are to be observed The first, to
the apparent secondary cause. The Second to the first original cause,
God, from whom originally proceeds whatsoever doth happen in the world.
The third and last, to them that we live and converse with: what use may
be made of it, to their use and benefit.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: True joy comes from doing what humans are meant to do. What belongs to us most is this: first, to feel kindness toward other people like ourselves. Then to resist physical urges and desires. To see through false ideas and fantasies. To think about the nature of the universe — both the universe itself and what happens in it. When you think about these things, notice three connections. First, the immediate cause of events. Second, the original cause — God, from whom everything in the world comes. Third, the people around you — how this knowledge can help them.

meditations_book-08.originalText:
If pain be an evil, either it is in regard of the body; (and that
cannot be, because the body of itself is altogether insensible:) or in
regard of the soul But it is in the power of the soul, to preserve her
own peace and tranquillity, and not to suppose that pain is evil. For
all judgment and deliberation; all prosecution, or aversation is from
within, whither the sense of evil (except it be let in by opinion)
cannot penetrate.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: If pain is an evil, it must affect either the body or the soul. It can't be the body, because the body itself has no awareness. So it must be the soul. But the soul has the power to keep its own peace and calm. It doesn't have to think that pain is evil. All judgment and choice, all desire and rejection, comes from within. The sense of evil cannot get in there unless we let it in through our opinions.

meditations_book-08.originalText:
Wipe off all idle fancies, and say unto thyself incessantly; Now
if I will, it is in my power to keep out of this my soul all wickedness,
all lust, and concupiscences, all trouble and confusion. But on the
contrary to behold and consider all things according to their true
nature, and to carry myself towards everything according to its true
worth. Remember then this thy power that nature hath given thee.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: Stop all pointless thoughts, and keep telling yourself: Right now, if I choose, I have the power to keep all wickedness out of my soul. All lust and desires, all trouble and confusion. Instead, I can see things as they really are and treat everything according to its true value. Remember this power that nature has given you.

meditations_book-08.originalText:
Whether thou speak in the Senate or whether thou speak to any
particular, let thy speech In always grave and modest. But thou must
not openly and vulgarly observe that sound and exact form of speaking,
concerning that which is truly good and truly civil; the vanity of
the world, and of worldly men: which otherwise truth and reason doth
prescribe.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: Whether you speak in the Senate or to anyone else, keep your speech serious and humble. But don't make a show of using the proper, exact way of speaking about what is truly good and truly noble. Don't parade around talking about the emptiness of the world and worldly people — even though truth and reason tell us these things are right.

meditations_book-08.originalText:
Augustus his court; his wife, his daughter, his nephews, his
sons-in-law his sister, Agrippa, his kinsmen, his domestics, his
friends; Areus, Mæcenas, his slayers of beasts for sacrifice and
divination: there thou hast the death of a whole court together. Proceed
now on to the rest that have been since that of Augustus. Hath death
dwelt with them otherwise, though so many and so stately whilst they
lived, than it doth use to deal with any one particular man? Consider
now the death of a whole kindred and family, as of that of the Pompeys,
as that also that useth to be written upon some monuments, HE WAS THE
LAST OF HIS OWN KINDRED. O what care did his predecessors take, that
they might leave a successor, yet behold at last one or other must of
necessity be THE LAST. Here again therefore consider the death of a
whole kindred.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: Think of Augustus and his court: his wife, daughter, nephews, sons-in-law, sister, Agrippa, his relatives, servants, friends, Areus, Maecenas, his fortune-tellers and priests. There you have the death of an entire court. Now move on to all the others who have died since Augustus. Did death treat them any differently? They were so many, so grand while they lived. But death dealt with them just as it deals with any ordinary person. Consider the death of whole families, like the Pompeys. Think of those monuments that read "He was the last of his family." How much care his ancestors took to leave an heir behind! Yet in the end, someone must always be the last. Here again, think about the death of entire bloodlines.

meditations_book-08.originalText:
Contract thy whole life to the measure and proportion of one single
action. And if in every particular action thou dost perform what is
fitting to the utmost of thy power, let it suffice thee. And who can
hinder thee, but that thou mayest perform what is fitting? But there may
be some outward let and impediment. Not any, that can hinder thee, but
that whatsoever thou dost, thou may do it, justly, temperately, and
with the praise of God. Yea, but there may be somewhat, whereby some
operation or other of thine may be hindered. And then, with that very
thing that doth hinder, thou mayest he well pleased, and so by this
gentle and equanimious conversion of thy mind unto that which may be,
instead of that which at first thou didst intend, in the room of that
former action there succeedeth another, which agrees as well with this
contraction of thy life, that we now speak of.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: Focus your whole life on the measure of one single action. If you do what is right to the best of your ability in each particular action, let that be enough. Who can stop you from doing what is right? But there might be some outside obstacle. Nothing can stop you from acting justly, with self-control, and in praise of God, whatever you do. Yes, but something might block some particular effort of yours. Then you can be pleased with that very thing that blocks you. By gently and calmly turning your mind to what is possible instead of what you first intended, another action takes the place of the former one. This new action fits just as well with this focused way of living.

meditations_book-08.originalText:
Receive temporal blessings without ostentation, when they are sent
and thou shalt be able to part with them with all readiness and facility
when they are taken from thee again.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: Accept good fortune without showing off when it comes. Then you'll be able to let it go easily when it's taken away.

meditations_book-08.originalText:
If ever thou sawest either a hand, or a foot, or a head lying by
itself, in some place or other, as cut off from the rest of the body,
such must thou conceive him to make himself, as much as in him lieth,
that either is offended with anything that is happened, (whatsoever it
be) and as it were divides himself from it: or that commits anything
against the natural law of mutual correspondence, and society among men:
or, he that, commits any act of uncharitableness. Whosoever thou art,
thou art such, thou art cast forth I know not whither out of the general
unity, which is according to nature. Thou went born indeed a part, but
now thou hast cut thyself off.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: If you ever saw a hand, foot, or head lying somewhere by itself, cut off from the body — that's what a person becomes when they get upset about what happens to them and separate themselves from it. Or when they act against the natural law that connects all people. Or when they act without kindness. If you are like this, you have cut yourself off from the natural unity of things. You were born as part of something larger, but now you have severed yourself from it.

meditations_book-08.originalText:
However, herein is matter of joy and
exultation, that thou mayst be united again. God hath not granted
it unto any other part, that once separated and cut off, it might be
reunited, and come together again. But, behold, that GOODNESS how great
and immense it is! which hath so much esteemed MAN. As at first he
was so made, that he needed not, except he would himself, have divided
himself from the whole; so once divided and cut off, IT hath so provided
and ordered it, that if he would himself, he might return, and grow
together again, and be admitted into its former rank and place of a
part, as he was before.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: But here is something to celebrate: you can be united again. God has not granted this to any other part — once separated and cut off, it cannot rejoin the whole. But look at this great GOODNESS! See how much it values humanity. At first, man was made so that he never had to separate himself from the whole unless he chose to. And once separated and cut off, IT has arranged things so that if he chooses, he can return and grow together again. He can be welcomed back to his former place as part of the whole.

meditations_book-08.originalText:
As almost all her other faculties and properties the nature of
the universe hath imparted unto every reasonable creature, so this in
particular we have received from her, that as whatsoever doth oppose
itself unto her, and doth withstand her in her purposes and intentions,
she doth, though against its will and intention, bring it about to
herself, to serve herself of it in the execution of her own destinated
ends; and so by this though not intended co-operation of it with herself
makes it part of herself whether it will or no. So may every reasonable
creature, what crosses and impediments soever it meets with in the
course of this mortal life, it may use them as fit and proper objects,
to the furtherance of whatsoever it intended and absolutely proposed
unto itself as its natural end and happiness.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: Nature has given us many gifts. Here's one in particular: whatever opposes nature or stands in her way, she turns to her own use. Even against its will, she makes it serve her purposes. Through this unwilling cooperation, she makes it part of herself whether it wants to be or not. We can do the same thing. Whatever obstacles or setbacks we face in life, we can use them to help us reach our goals and find happiness.

meditations_book-08.originalText:
Let not the general representation unto thyself of the
wretchedness of this our mortal life, trouble thee. Let not thy mind
wander up and down, and heap together in her thoughts the many troubles
and grievous calamities which thou art as subject unto as any other. But
as everything in particular doth happen, put this question unto thyself,
and say: What is it that in this present matter, seems unto thee so
intolerable? For thou wilt be ashamed to confess it. Then upon this
presently call to mind, that neither that which is future, nor that
which is past can hurt thee; but that only which is present. (And that
also is much lessened, if thou dost lightly circumscribe it:) and then
check thy mind if for so little a while, (a mere instant), it cannot
hold out with patience.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: Don't let the general idea of how miserable life is get to you. Don't let your mind wander around piling up all the troubles and disasters you might face. Instead, when something specific happens, ask yourself: What exactly about this situation seems so unbearable? You'll be embarrassed to admit it. Then remember that neither the future nor the past can hurt you — only what's happening right now. And even that becomes much smaller if you look at it closely. Then ask your mind: if this is really so brief — just a moment — can't it hold out with a little patience?

meditations_book-08.originalText:
What? are either Panthea or Pergamus abiding to this day by their
masters' tombs? or either Chabrias or Diotimus by that of Adrianus? O
foolery! For what if they did, would their masters be sensible of It? or
if sensible, would they be glad of it? or if glad, were these immortal?
Was not it appointed unto them also (both men and women,) to become
old in time, and then to die? And these once dead, what would become of
these former? And when all is done, what is all this for, but for a mere
bag of blood and corruption?
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: What? Are Panthea or Pergamus still keeping watch by their masters' tombs? Or are Chabrias or Diotimus still at Adrianus's grave? What nonsense! Even if they were, would their dead masters know? And if they knew, would they care? And if they cared, would that make these servants live forever? They too are destined to grow old and die. Once they're gone, what happens to their devotion? In the end, what is all this loyalty for? Just a bag of blood and decay.

meditations_book-08.originalText:
If thou beest quick-sighted, be so in matter of judgment, and
best discretion, saith he.

In the whole constitution of man, I see not any virtue contrary
to justice, whereby it may be resisted and opposed. But one whereby
pleasure and voluptuousness may be resisted and opposed, I see:
continence.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish:
If you have sharp eyes, use them for good judgment and wisdom.

Looking at human nature, I don't see any virtue that opposes justice. But I do see one that can resist pleasure and indulgence: self-control.

meditations_book-08.originalText:
If thou canst but withdraw conceit and opinion concerning that
which may seem hurtful and offensive, thou thyself art as safe, as safe
may be. Thou thyself? and who is that? Thy reason. 'Yea, but I am not
reason.' Well, be it so. However, let not thy reason or understanding
admit of grief, and if there be anything in thee that is grieved, let
that, (whatsoever it be,) conceive its own grief, if it can.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: If you can just drop your opinions about what seems harmful and upsetting, you yourself are as safe as you can be. You yourself? Who is that? Your reason. 'Yes, but I am not just reason.' Fine. Even so, don't let your reason feel grief. And if there is anything in you that does grieve, let that part deal with its own grief, if it can.

meditations_book-08.originalText:
That which is a hindrance of the senses, is an evil to the
sensitive nature. That which is a hindrance of the appetitive and
prosecutive faculty, is an evil to the sensitive nature. As of the
sensitive, so of the vegetative constitution, whatsoever is a hindrance
unto it, is also in that respect an evil unto the same. And so likewise,
whatsoever is a hindrance unto the mind and understanding, must needs
be the proper evil of the reasonable nature. Now apply all those things
unto thyself. Do either pain or pleasure seize on thee? Let the senses
look to that. Hast thou met with Some obstacle or other in thy purpose
and intention? If thou didst propose without due reservation and
exception now hath thy reasonable part received a blow indeed But if in
general thou didst propose unto thyself what soever might be, thou art
not thereby either hurt, nor properly hindered. For in those things that
properly belong unto the mind, she cannot be hindered by any man. It
is not fire, nor iron; nor the power of a tyrant nor the power of a
slandering tongue; nor anything else that can penetrate into her.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: What harms the senses is bad for our sensing nature. What blocks our desires and actions is bad for our feeling nature. What harms our growth is bad for our living nature. And what blocks the mind is bad for our thinking nature. Now think about yourself. Do pain or pleasure grab you? Let your senses handle that. Have you hit some obstacle in your plans? If you planned without thinking it through, then yes, your reasoning has taken a hit. But if you planned in general terms—whatever might happen—then you're not really hurt or blocked. The mind itself can't be hindered by anyone. Fire can't reach it. Neither can weapons, tyrants, or lies. Nothing can break through to it.

meditations_book-08.originalText: If once round and solid, there is no fear that ever it will change.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: If something is once round and solid, there is no fear it will ever change.

meditations_book-08.originalText:
Why should I grieve myself; who never did willingly grieve any
other! One thing rejoices one and another thing another. As for me, this
is my joy, if my understanding be right and sound, as neither averse
from any man, nor refusing any of those things which as a man I am
subject unto; if I can look upon all things in the world meekly and
kindly; accept all things and carry myself towards everything according
to to true worth of the thing itself.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: Why should I trouble myself? I never willingly troubled anyone else. Different things bring joy to different people. This brings me joy: when my thinking is clear and sound, when I don't turn away from anyone, when I don't refuse the things that come to me as a human being. When I can look at everything in the world with gentleness and kindness. When I accept all things and treat everything according to its true worth.

meditations_book-08.originalText:
This time that is now present, bestow thou upon thyself. They that
rather hunt for fame after death, do not consider, that those men that
shall be hereafter, will be even such, as these whom now they can so
hardly bear with. And besides they also will be mortal men. But to
consider the thing in itself, if so many with so many voices, shall make
such and such a sound, or shall have such and such an opinion concerning
thee, what is it to thee?
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: Give this present time to yourself. People who chase fame after death don't realize something. The future people they want to impress will be just like the people they can barely stand today. And those future people will also die. But think about it clearly. If many people make noise about you or have opinions about you, what does that matter to you?

meditations_book-08.originalText:
Take me and throw me where thou wilt: I am indifferent. For there
also I shall have that spirit which is within me propitious; that is
well pleased and fully contented both in that constant disposition, and
with those particular actions, which to its own proper constitution are
suitable and agreeable.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: Take me and throw me wherever you want: I don't care. Even there I will have my inner spirit working for me. It stays content with its steady character and with the actions that fit its true nature.

meditations_book-08.originalText:
Is this then a thing of that worth, that for it my soul should
suffer, and become worse than it was? as either basely dejected, or
disordinately affected, or confounded within itself, or terrified? What
can there be, that thou shouldest so much esteem?
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: Is this really worth it? Should I let my soul suffer and become worse than it was? Should I let myself sink into despair, get thrown off balance, become confused, or live in fear? What could possibly be so important?

meditations_book-08.originalText: Nothing can happen unto thee, which is not incidental unto thee, as thou art a man. As nothing can happen either to an ox, a vine, or to a stone, which is not incidental unto them; unto every one in his own kind. If therefore nothing can happen unto anything, which is not both usual and natural; why art thou displeased? Sure the common nature of all would not bring anything upon any, that were intolerable.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: Nothing can happen to you that isn't part of being human. Just like nothing happens to an ox, a vine, or a stone that isn't natural to what they are. Everything follows its own nature. So if nothing can happen that isn't usual and natural, why are you upset? The nature that governs everything would never bring something that's truly unbearable.

meditations_book-08.originalText: If therefore it be a thing external that causes thy grief, know, that it is not that properly that doth cause it, but thine own conceit and opinion concerning the thing: which thou mayest rid thyself of, when thou wilt. But if it be somewhat that is amiss in thine own disposition, that doth grieve thee, mayest thou not rectify thy moral tenets and opinions. But if it grieve thee, that thou doest not perform that which seemeth unto thee right and just, why doest not thou choose rather to perform it than to grieve? But somewhat that is stronger than thyself doth hinder thee. Let it not grieve thee then, if it be not thy fault that the thing is not performed. 'Yea but it is a thing of that nature, as that thy life is not worth the while, except it may be performed.' If it be so, upon condition that thou be kindly and lovingly disposed towards all men, thou mayest be gone. For even then, as much as at any time, art thou in a very good estate of performance, when thou doest die in charity with those, that are an obstacle unto thy performance.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: If something outside you causes your grief, know that it's not really the thing itself that hurts you. It's your own thoughts and opinions about it. You can change those whenever you want. But if something wrong in your own character is what grieves you, can't you fix your beliefs and attitudes? And if you're upset that you're not doing what seems right and just to you, why not just do it instead of being upset? But something stronger than you is stopping you. Then don't let it grieve you, since it's not your fault the thing isn't getting done. 'Yes, but life isn't worth living if I can't do this.' If that's true, then as long as you stay kind and loving toward everyone, you can leave this life. Even then, you're doing as well as you ever could — dying with goodwill toward the very people who blocked you.

meditations_book-08.originalText:
Remember that thy mind is of that nature as that it becometh
altogether unconquerable, when once recollected in herself, she seeks no
other content than this, that she cannot be forced: yea though it so
fall out, that it be even against reason itself, that it cloth bandy.
How much less when by the help of reason she is able to judge of things
with discretion? And therefore let thy chief fort and place of defence
be, a mind free from passions. A stronger place, (whereunto to make his
refuge, and so to become impregnable) and better fortified than this,
hath no man. He that seeth not this is unlearned. He that seeth it, and
betaketh not himself to this place of refuge, is unhappy.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: Remember that your mind has this nature: when it pulls itself together and looks inward, it becomes completely unconquerable. It needs nothing else but this - that it cannot be forced. This is true even when the mind stubbornly resists what reason tells it. How much more true when reason helps it judge things clearly? So make this your strongest defense: a mind free from strong emotions. No one has a stronger refuge than this, or a better fortress to retreat to and become unbreakable. Anyone who doesn't see this is ignorant. Anyone who sees it but doesn't use this refuge is foolish.

meditations_book-08.originalText:
Keep thyself to the first bare and naked apprehensions of things,
as they present themselves unto thee, and add not unto them. It is
reported unto thee, that such a one speaketh ill of thee. Well; that he
speaketh ill of thee, so much is reported. But that thou art hurt
thereby, is not reported: that is the addition of opinion, which thou
must exclude. I see that my child is sick. That he is sick, I see, but
that he is in danger of his life also, I see it not. Thus thou must use
to keep thyself to the first motions and apprehensions of things, as
they present themselves outwardly; and add not unto them from within
thyself through mere conceit and opinion. Or rather add unto them: hut
as one that understandeth the true nature of all things that happen in
the world.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: Stick to your first, simple impressions of things as they happen to you. Don't add to them. Someone tells you that a person spoke badly about you. Fine — they spoke badly about you. That's what happened. But you're not hurt by it unless you add that idea yourself. That's your opinion, which you should leave out. I see that my child is sick. Yes, he's sick — I can see that. But I don't see that his life is in danger. That's me adding something extra. This is how you should handle things. Stay with the first, basic facts as they appear on the outside. Don't add to them from your own thoughts and opinions. Or if you do add to them, do it like someone who understands the true nature of everything that happens in the world.

meditations_book-08.originalText: Is the cucumber bitter? set it away. Brambles are in the way? avoid them. Let this suffice. Add not presently speaking unto thyself, What serve these things for in the world? For, this, one that is acquainted with the mysteries of nature, will laugh at thee for it; as a carpenter would or a shoemaker, if meeting in either of their shops with some shavings, or small remnants of their work, thou shouldest blame them for it.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: Is the cucumber bitter? Put it aside. Are there brambles in the way? Go around them. That's enough. Don't start asking yourself, "What purpose do these things serve in the world?" Someone who understands how nature works will laugh at you for this. It's like going into a carpenter's shop or a shoemaker's shop and complaining about the wood shavings or scraps you find there.

meditations_book-08.originalText: And yet those men, it is not for want of a place where to throw them that they keep them in their shops for a while: but the nature of the universe hath no such out-place; but herein doth consist the wonder of her art and skill, that she having once circumscribed herself within some certain bounds and limits, whatsoever is within her that seems either corrupted, or old, or unprofitable, she can change it into herself, and of these very things can make new things; so that she needeth not to seek elsewhere out of herself either for a new supply of matter and substance, or for a place where to throw out whatsoever is irrecoverably putrid and corrupt. Thus she, as for place, so for matter and art, is herself sufficient unto herself.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: People keep old goods in their shops not because they lack a place to throw them away, but because they might still sell them. But the universe has no such dump or storage room. Here's what's amazing about nature's skill: she sets her own boundaries, then takes everything within them that seems rotten, old, or useless and transforms it back into herself. She makes new things from these old materials. She doesn't need to look outside herself for fresh supplies or for somewhere to dump what's truly spoiled. She is completely self-sufficient in space, materials, and craft.

meditations_book-08.originalText:
Not to be slack and negligent; or loose, and wanton in thy
actions; nor contentious, and troublesome in thy conversation; nor to
rove and wander in thy fancies and imaginations. Not basely to contract
thy soul; nor boisterously to sally out with it, or furiously to launch
out as it were, nor ever to want employment.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: Don't be lazy or careless in what you do. Don't be loose or wild in your actions. Don't be argumentative or difficult when you talk with people. Don't let your mind wander into useless fantasies. Don't shrink your soul down to nothing. Don't let it burst out wildly or launch into fury. And never be without meaningful work to do.

meditations_book-08.originalText:
'They kill me, they cut my flesh; they persecute my person with
curses.' What then? May not thy mind for all this continue pure,
prudent, temperate, just? As a fountain of sweet and clear water, though
she be cursed by some stander by, yet do her springs nevertheless still
run as sweet and clear as before; yea though either dirt or dung be
thrown in, yet is it no sooner thrown, than dispersed, and she cleared.
She cannot be dyed or infected by it. What then must I do, that I
may have within myself an overflowing fountain, and not a well? Beget
thyself by continual pains and endeavours to true liberty with charity,
and true simplicity and modesty.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: They might kill me, cut my flesh, or curse me. So what? Can't my mind stay pure, wise, balanced, and just through all of this? Think of a spring with sweet, clear water. Even if someone curses it, the water keeps flowing just as sweet and clear. Even if dirt or dung gets thrown in, it gets washed away quickly and the spring runs clear again. The spring can't be stained or infected. So how can I have this kind of overflowing fountain inside me, not just a stagnant well? I must work constantly to build true freedom with kindness, true simplicity, and humility.

meditations_book-08.originalText:
He that knoweth not what the world is, knoweth not where he himself
is. And he that knoweth not what the world was made for, cannot possibly
know either what are the qualities, or what is the nature of the world.
Now he that in either of these is to seek, for what he himself was made
is ignorant also. What then dost thou think of that man, who proposeth
unto himself, as a matter of great moment, the noise and applause
of men, who both where they are, and what they are themselves, are
altogether ignorant? Dost thou desire to be commended of that man, who
thrice in one hour perchance, doth himself curse himself? Dost thou
desire to please him, who pleaseth not himself? or dost thou think that
he pleaseth himself, who doth use to repent himself almost of everything
that he doth?
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: Someone who doesn't know what the world is doesn't know where he stands. Someone who doesn't know what the world was made for can't know its qualities or nature either. Anyone ignorant of these things is also ignorant of what he himself was made for. What do you think of someone who cares deeply about the noise and applause of people who don't know where they are or what they are? Do you want praise from someone who curses himself three times in an hour? Do you want to please someone who can't please himself? Do you think someone pleases himself when he regrets almost everything he does?

meditations_book-08.originalText:
Not only now henceforth to have a common breath, or to hold
correspondency of breath, with that air, that compasseth us about; but
to have a common mind, or to hold correspondency of mind also with that
rational substance, which compasseth all things. For, that also is of
itself, and of its own nature (if a man can but draw it in as he should)
everywhere diffused; and passeth through all things, no less than the
air doth, if a man can but suck it in.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: Not only to breathe the same air that surrounds us, but to share in the same mind — to connect with the rational force that flows through all things. This force spreads everywhere, just like air does. It passes through everything, if you know how to take it in.

meditations_book-08.originalText: Wickedness in general doth not hurt the world. Particular wickedness doth not hurt any other: only unto him it is hurtful, whosoever he be that offends, unto whom in great favour and mercy it is granted, that whensoever he himself shall but first desire it, he may be presently delivered of it.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: Evil in general does not harm the world. Someone's particular evil does not hurt anyone else. It only hurts the person who does wrong. And even then, that person has been given a great gift — whenever he truly wants to be free of his wickedness, he can be rid of it immediately.

meditations_book-08.originalText: Unto my free-will my neighbour's free-will, whoever he be, (as his life, or his bode), is altogether indifferent. For though we are all made one for another, yet have our minds and understandings each of them their own proper and limited jurisdiction. For else another man's wickedness might be my evil which God would not have, that it might not be in another man's power to make me unhappy: which nothing now can do but mine own wickedness.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: My neighbor's choices are none of my business, just like his life or body are none of my business. We were made to help each other, but our minds are separate. Each person has their own thoughts and judgments. If this weren't true, another person's bad behavior could harm me. But God didn't design it that way. No one else has the power to make me unhappy. Only my own bad choices can do that.

meditations_book-08.originalText:
The sun seemeth to be shed abroad. And indeed it is diffused but
not effused. For that diffusion of it is a τάσις or an extension. For
therefore are the beams of it called ἀκτῖνες from the word ἐκτείνεσθαι
to be stretched out and extended. Now what a sunbeam is, thou mayest
know if thou observe the light of the sun, when through some narrow
hole it pierceth into some room that is dark. For it is always in a
direct line. And as by any solid body, that it meets with in the way
that is not penetrable by air, it is divided and abrupted, and yet
neither slides off, or falls down, but stayeth there nevertheless: such
must the diffusion in the mind be; not an effusion, but an extension.
What obstacles and impediments soever she meeteth within her way, she
must not violently, and by way of an impetuous onset light upon them;
neither must she fall down; but she must stand, and give light unto
that which doth admit of it. For as for that which doth not, it is its
own fault and loss, if it bereave itself of her light.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: The sun seems to pour out everywhere. And it does spread out, but it doesn't spill out. Its spreading is more like stretching or extending. The sun's rays are called rays because they stretch out and extend. You can see what a sunbeam is if you watch sunlight coming through a small hole into a dark room. It always travels in a straight line. When it hits something solid that air can't pass through, the light gets cut off and stopped. But it doesn't slide away or fall down. It stays right there. This is how the mind should spread out too — not spilling over, but extending steadily. Whatever obstacles and barriers the mind meets, it shouldn't crash into them violently or with force. It shouldn't collapse either. It should stay put and give light to whatever can receive it. As for what can't receive it, that's its own fault and loss if it shuts out the light.

meditations_book-08.originalText:
He that feareth death, either feareth that he shall have no sense at
all, or that his senses will not be the same. Whereas, he should rather
comfort himself, that either no sense at all, and so no sense of evil;
or if any sense, then another life, and so no death properly.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: Someone who fears death either fears having no awareness at all, or fears that their awareness will be different. But they should comfort themselves with this: either there's no awareness at all, and so no sense of suffering; or if there is awareness, then it's another life, and so not really death.

meditations_book-08.originalText:
All men are made one for another: either then teach them better, or
bear with them.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: All people are made to help each other. So either teach them to do better, or put up with them.

meditations_book-08.originalText:
The motion of the mind is not as the motion of a dart. For
the mind when it is wary and cautelous, and by way of diligent
circumspection turneth herself many ways, may then as well be said to
go straight on to the object, as when it useth no such circumspection.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: The mind doesn't move like an arrow flies. When the mind is careful and cautious, turning many different ways to examine something closely, it still reaches its target just as well as when it moves without such care.

meditations_book-08.originalText:
To pierce and penetrate into the estate of every one's
understanding that thou hast to do with: as also to make the estate of
thine own open, and penetrable to any other.
meditations_book-08.plainEnglish: Look deeply into how other people think when you deal with them. And let them see clearly into your own mind too.

meditations_book-09.originalText: He that is unjust, is also impious. For the nature of the universe, having made all reasonable creatures one for another, to the end that they should do one another good; more or less according to the several persons and occasions but in nowise hurt one another: it is manifest that he that doth transgress against this her will, is guilty of impiety towards the most ancient and venerable of all the deities. For the nature of the universe, is the nature the common parent of all, and therefore piously to be observed of all things that are, and that which now is, to whatsoever first was, and gave it its being, hath relation of blood and kindred. She is also called truth and is the first cause of all truths.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: Someone who acts unjustly is also acting against the gods. The nature of the universe made all thinking beings to help each other — some more, some less, depending on the person and situation — but never to harm each other. Anyone who goes against this natural law commits a sin against the oldest and most sacred of all divine powers. The nature of the universe is like a common parent to everything. So we should respect it with reverence. Everything that exists now is related by blood to whatever came first and gave it life. This nature is also called truth, and it's the source of all truths.

meditations_book-09.originalText: He therefore that willingly and wittingly doth lie, is impious in that he doth receive, and so commit injustice: but he that against his will, in that he disagreeth from the nature of the universe, and in that striving with the nature of the world he doth in his particular, violate the general order of the world. For he doth no better than strive and war against it, who contrary to his own nature applieth himself to that which is contrary to truth. For nature had before furnished him with instincts and opportunities sufficient for the attainment of it; which he having hitherto neglected, is not now able to discern that which is false from that which is true.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: Someone who lies on purpose is impious because he deceives others and commits injustice. But someone who lies without meaning to still goes against the nature of the universe. He fights against the natural order of the world. He is like someone who wars against his own nature by chasing what is false. Nature gave him the instincts and chances he needed to find truth. But he ignored them for so long that now he cannot tell what is false from what is true.

meditations_book-09.originalText: He also that pursues after pleasures, as that which is truly good and flies from pains, as that which is truly evil: is impious. For such a one must of necessity oftentimes accuse that common nature, as distributing many things both unto the evil, and unto the good, not according to the deserts of either: as unto the bad oftentimes pleasures, and the causes of pleasures; so unto the good, pains, and the occasions of pains. Again, he that feareth pains and crosses in this world, feareth some of those things which some time or other must needs happen in the world. And that we have already showed to be impious. And he that pursueth after pleasures, will not spare, to compass his desires, to do that which is unjust, and that is manifestly impious. Now those things which unto nature are equally indifferent (for she had not created both, both pain and pleasure, if both had not been unto her equally indifferent): they that will live according to nature, must in those things (as being of the same mind and disposition that she is) be as equally indifferent.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: Someone who chases pleasure as if it were truly good, and runs from pain as if it were truly evil, is acting against the gods. Such a person will often blame nature for giving many things to bad people and good people alike — not based on what they deserve. Bad people often get pleasures and what causes pleasure. Good people often get pain and what causes pain. Also, someone who fears pain and trouble in this world fears things that must happen sometimes. We already showed this goes against the gods. Someone who chases pleasures will do wrong things to get what they want. This clearly goes against the gods. Now, nature treats pain and pleasure as equally unimportant. She would not have created both if they were not equally unimportant to her. Those who want to live according to nature must be just as indifferent to these things as she is.

meditations_book-09.originalText: Whosoever therefore in either matter of pleasure and pain; death and life; honour and dishonour, (which things nature in the administration of the world, indifferently doth make use of), is not as indifferent, it is apparent that he is impious. When I say that common nature doth indifferently make use of them, my meaning is, that they happen indifferently in the ordinary course of things, which by a necessary consequence, whether as principal or accessory, come to pass in the world, according to that first and ancient deliberation of Providence, by which she from some certain beginning, did resolve upon the creation of such a world, conceiving then in her womb as it were some certain rational generative seeds and faculties of things future, whether subjects, changes, successions; both such and such, and just so many.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: If someone cannot stay neutral about pleasure and pain, life and death, honor and disgrace, then they are working against nature. Nature uses all these things without preference in running the world. By this I mean these things happen naturally in the normal course of events. They follow necessarily from Providence's original plan. From the very beginning, Providence decided to create this kind of world. It planted the seeds for everything that would come — all the subjects, changes, and cycles we see, exactly as they are and in just these numbers.

meditations_book-09.originalText:
It were indeed more happy and comfortable, for a man to depart out
of this world, having lived all his life long clear from all falsehood,
dissimulation, voluptuousness, and pride. But if this cannot be, yet it
is some comfort for a man joyfully to depart as weary, and out of love
with those; rather than to desire to live, and to continue long in those
wicked courses. Hath not yet experience taught thee to fly from the
plague? For a far greater plague is the corruption of the mind, than any
certain change and distemper of the common air can be. This is a plague
of creatures, as they are living creatures; but that of men as they are
men or reasonable.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: It would be better to leave this world having lived your whole life free from lies, fakeness, pleasure-seeking, and pride. But if that's not possible, at least it's some comfort to die gladly when you're tired of these things and sick of them. This is better than wanting to keep living and stay caught up in bad habits. Haven't you learned yet to run from the plague? The corruption of the mind is a far worse plague than any disease that changes the air. That kind of plague affects creatures simply because they're alive. But this plague affects people as thinking beings.

meditations_book-09.originalText: Thou must not in matter of death carry thyself scornfully, but as one that is well pleased with it, as being one of those things that nature hath appointed. For what thou dost conceive of these, of a boy to become a young man, to wax old, to grow, to ripen, to get teeth, or a beard, or grey hairs to beget, to bear, or to be delivered; or what other action soever it be, that is natural unto man according to the several seasons of his life; such a thing is it also to be dissolved. It is therefore the part of a wise man, in matter of death, not in any wise to carry himself either violently, or proudly but patiently to wait for it, as one of nature's operations: that with the same mind as now thou dost expect when that which yet is but an embryo in thy wife's belly shall come forth, thou mayst expect also when thy soul shall fall off from that outward coat or skin: wherein as a child in the belly it lieth involved and shut up.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish:
Don't be scornful about death, but welcome it as one of the things nature has planned. Think about all the natural changes you accept — a boy becoming a young man, growing old, getting teeth or a beard or gray hair, having children. Death is just like these changes. It's another natural process that happens at its proper time.

A wise person doesn't approach death with violence or pride, but waits for it patiently. It's just another one of nature's operations. You wait eagerly for the child in your wife's belly to be born. In the same way, you can wait for your soul to shed its outer coat — the body that wraps it up like a child in the womb.

meditations_book-09.originalText: But thou desirest a more popular, and though not so direct and philosophical, yet a very powerful and penetrative recipe against the fear of death, nothing can make they more willing to part with thy life, than if thou shalt consider, both what the subjects themselves are that thou shalt part with, and what manner of disposition thou shalt no more have to do with. True it is, that, offended with them thou must not be by no means, but take care of them, and meekly bear with them However, this thou mayst remember, that whensoever it happens that thou depart, it shall not be from men that held the same opinions that thou dost. For that indeed, (if it were so) is the only thing that might make thee averse from death, and willing to continue here, if it were thy hap to live with men that had obtained the same belief that thou hast. But now, what a toil it is for thee to live with men of different opinions, thou seest: so that thou hast rather occasion to say, Hasten, I thee pray, O Death; lest I also in time forget myself.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: You want a more popular remedy against the fear of death — one that is not as philosophical but still powerful and convincing. Nothing will make you more willing to leave this life than considering what you are actually leaving behind. Think about the people themselves and the kinds of attitudes you will no longer have to deal with. You should not be angry with them. You should care for them and bear with them patiently. But remember this — when you die, you will not be leaving behind people who share your beliefs. If that were the case, it might be the one thing that would make you reluctant to die and want to stay here longer.
