But as it stands, you can see what a struggle it is to live among people with such different views. So you have more reason to say, 'Come quickly, Death, before I too forget who I am.'

meditations_book-09.originalText:
He that sinneth, sinneth unto himself. He that is unjust, hurts
himself, in that he makes himself worse than he was before. Not he only
that committeth, but he also that omitteth something, is oftentimes
unjust.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: When someone does wrong, they hurt themselves. When someone is unjust, they damage themselves by becoming worse than they were before. It's not just what you do that can be wrong — what you fail to do can also be unjust.

meditations_book-09.originalText:
If my present apprehension of the object be right, and my present
action charitable, and this, towards whatsoever doth proceed from God,
be my present disposition, to be well pleased with it, it sufficeth.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: If I see things clearly, and my actions are kind, and I accept whatever comes from God with a good attitude, that's enough.

meditations_book-09.originalText:
To wipe away fancy, to use deliberation, to quench concupiscence, to
keep the mind free to herself.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: To clear away false impressions, to think carefully, to quiet desire, to keep the mind its own master.

meditations_book-09.originalText:
Of all unreasonable creatures, there is but one unreasonable soul;
and of all that are reasonable, but one reasonable soul, divided betwixt
them all. As of all earthly things there is but one earth, and but one
light that we see by; and but one air that we breathe in, as many as
either breathe or see. Now whatsoever partakes of some common thing,
naturally affects and inclines unto that whereof it is part, being of
one kind and nature with it. Whatsoever is earthly, presseth downwards
to the common earth. Whatsoever is liquid, would flow together. And
whatsoever is airy, would be together likewise. So that without some
obstacle, and some kind of violence, they cannot well be kept asunder.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: All unreasonable creatures share one unreasonable soul. All reasonable creatures share one reasonable soul, divided among them all. Just as there is one earth for all earthly things, and one light we all see by, and one air we all breathe. Whatever shares something common naturally moves toward what it belongs to, being the same kind. Whatever is earthly falls down to the earth. Whatever is liquid flows together. Whatever is airy wants to join together too. Without some barrier or force, they cannot easily be kept apart.

meditations_book-09.originalText:
Whatsoever is fiery, doth not only by reason of the elementary fire tend
upwards; but here also is so ready to join, and to burn together, that
whatsoever doth want sufficient moisture to make resistance, is easily
set on fire. Whatsoever therefore is partaker of that reasonable common
nature, naturally doth as much and more long after his own kind. For by
how much in its own nature it excels all other things, by so much more
is it desirous to be joined and united unto that, which is of its own
nature. As for unreasonable creatures then, they had not long been, but
presently begun among them swarms, and flocks, and broods of young ones,
and a kind of mutual love and affection.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: Fire naturally rises up and burns. It's ready to join with other fire and burn together. Anything that lacks moisture catches fire easily. In the same way, anything that shares in our common rational nature longs even more to connect with its own kind. The more excellent something is by nature, the more it wants to join with others like itself. Even unreasonable creatures quickly form swarms, flocks, and groups of young ones. They show a kind of mutual love and care.

meditations_book-09.originalText:
For though but unreasonable,
yet a kind of soul these had, and therefore was that natural desire of
union more strong and intense in them, as in creatures of a more
excellent nature, than either in plants, or stones, or trees. But among
reasonable creatures, begun commonwealths, friendships, families, public
meetings, and even in their wars, conventions, and truces. Now among
them that were yet of a more excellent nature, as the stars and planets,
though by their nature far distant one from another, yet even among them
began some mutual correspondency and unity. So proper is it to
excellency in a high degree to affect unity, as that even in things so
far distant, it could operate unto a mutual sympathy.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: Even unreasonable creatures had a kind of soul. So their natural desire for union was strong and intense — stronger than in plants, stones, or trees. Among reasonable creatures came communities, friendships, families, and public gatherings. Even in wars there were agreements and truces. Among creatures of even higher nature — like stars and planets — there is mutual harmony and unity, despite the vast distances between them. Excellence naturally seeks unity. It is so powerful that it creates sympathy even between things that are far apart.

meditations_book-09.originalText:
But now behold,
what is now come to pass. Those creatures that are reasonable, are now
the only creatures that have forgotten their natural affection and
inclination of one towards another. Among them alone of all other things
that are of one kind, there is not to be found a general disposition to
flow together. But though they fly from nature, yet are they stopt in
their course, and apprehended. Do they what they can, nature doth
prevail. And so shalt thou confess, if thou dost observe it. For sooner
mayst thou find a thing earthly, where no earthly thing is, than find a
man that naturally can live by himself alone.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: But look at what has happened now. Rational creatures — humans — are the only ones who have forgotten their natural love for each other. Of all living things, only we have lost the instinct to come together. We try to run from our nature, but we can't escape it. We are caught despite our efforts. Nature wins in the end. You will see this if you pay attention. You are more likely to find something earthly where nothing earthly exists than to find a person who can truly live alone.

meditations_book-09.originalText:
Man, God, the world, every one in their kind, bear some fruits.
All things have their proper time to bear. Though by custom, the word
itself is in a manner become proper unto the vine, and the like, yet is
it so nevertheless, as we have said. As for reason, that beareth both
common fruit for the use of others; and peculiar, which itself doth
enjoy. Reason is of a diffusive nature, what itself is in itself, it
begets in others, and so doth multiply.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: Everything bears fruit in its own way — people, God, the world. All things have their proper time to produce something. We usually think of fruit as something that comes from vines and trees. But it's true for everything. Reason produces two kinds of fruit. It creates common fruit that benefits others. And it creates special fruit that it enjoys itself. Reason spreads naturally. Whatever it is in itself, it creates in others. This is how it multiplies.

meditations_book-09.originalText:
Either teach them better if it be in thy power; or if it be not,
remember that for this use, to bear with them patiently, was mildness
and goodness granted unto thee. The Gods themselves are good unto such;
yea and in some things, (as in matter of health, of wealth, of honour,)
are content often to further their endeavours: so good and gracious are
they. And mightest thou not be so too? or, tell me, what doth hinder
thee?
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: Either teach them better if you can. If you can't, remember that patience was given to you for exactly this purpose — to deal with them calmly. The gods themselves are good to such people. They even help them sometimes with health, wealth, and honor. That's how generous the gods are. Why can't you be the same way? What's stopping you?

meditations_book-09.originalText:
Labour not as one to whom it is appointed to be wretched, nor as one
that either would be pitied, or admired; but let this be thine only care
and desire; so always and in all things to prosecute or to forbear, as
the law of charity, or mutual society doth require.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: Don't work like someone who expects to be miserable. Don't work for pity or praise. Care about only this: in everything you do or don't do, follow what love and community require.

meditations_book-09.originalText:
This day I did come out of all my trouble. Nay I have cast out all
my trouble; it should rather be for that which troubled thee, whatsoever
it was, was not without anywhere that thou shouldest come out of it, but
within in thine own opinions, from whence it must be cast out, before
thou canst truly and constantly be at ease.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: Today I came out of all my trouble. Actually, I cast out all my trouble. That's more accurate. Whatever was troubling you wasn't something outside that you needed to escape from. It was inside, in your own thoughts. That's where it has to be thrown out before you can truly have peace.

meditations_book-09.originalText:
All those things, for matter of experience are usual and ordinary;
for their continuance but for a day; and for their matter, most base and
filthy. As they were in the days of those whom we have buried, so are
they now also, and no otherwise.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: All these things we experience are common and ordinary. They last only a day. And most of them are base and dirty. They were the same in the days of those we have buried. They are the same now, and no different.

meditations_book-09.originalText:
The things themselves that affect us, they stand without doors,
neither knowing anything themselves nor able to utter anything unto
others concerning themselves. What then is it, that passeth verdict on
them? The understanding.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: The things that affect us stand outside our doors. They know nothing about themselves and can't tell us anything about themselves. So what is it that judges them? Our understanding.

meditations_book-09.originalText:
As virtue and wickedness consist not in passion, but in action; so
neither doth the true good or evil of a reasonable charitable man
consist in passion, but in operation and action.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: Virtue and evil are not about what you feel, but what you do. In the same way, what makes a good person truly good or bad is not their emotions, but their actions.

meditations_book-09.originalText:
To the stone that is cast up, when it comes down it is no hurt unto
it; as neither benefit, when it doth ascend.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: A stone thrown up isn't harmed when it falls back down. And it gains nothing when it goes up either.

meditations_book-09.originalText:
Sift their minds and understandings, and behold what men they be,
whom thou dost stand in fear of what they shall judge of thee, what they
themselves judge of themselves.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: Look closely at their minds and thoughts. See what kind of people they really are — these people whose judgment you fear. See what they think of themselves.

meditations_book-09.originalText:
All things that are in the world, are always in the estate
of alteration. Thou also art in a perpetual change, yea and under
corruption too, in some part: and so is the whole world.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: Everything in the world is always changing. You are always changing too, and part of you is always breaking down. So is the whole world.

meditations_book-09.originalText:
it is not thine, but another man's sin. Why should it trouble
thee? Let him look to it, whose sin it is.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: It is not your sin, but another person's sin. Why should it trouble you? Let them deal with it — it's their sin.

meditations_book-09.originalText: Of an operation and of a purpose there is an ending, or of an action and of a purpose we say commonly, that it is at an end: from opinion also there is an absolute cessation, which is as it were the death of it. In all this there is no hurt.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: Every action has an ending. Every purpose reaches completion. We say they are finished. Even our opinions come to an end — they die off. In all of this, there is no harm.

meditations_book-09.originalText: Apply this now to a man's age, as first, a child; then a youth, then a young man, then an old man; every change from one age to another is a kind of death And all this while here no matter of grief yet. Pass now unto that life first, that which thou livedst under thy grandfather, then under thy mother, then under thy father. And thus when through the whole course of thy life hitherto thou hast found and observed many alterations, many changes, many kinds of endings and cessations, put this question to thyself What matter of grief or sorrow dost thou find in any of these? Or what doest thou suffer through any of these? If in none of these, then neither in the ending and consummation of thy whole life, which is also but a cessation and change.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: Think about a man's life: first a child, then a youth, then a young man, then an old man. Each change from one age to another is a kind of death. And yet none of this causes grief. Now think about your own life — first under your grandfather, then under your mother, then under your father. When you look back at your whole life so far, you see many changes, many endings, many things that stopped. Ask yourself: what grief or sorrow do you find in any of these changes? What harm did they cause you? If none of them hurt you, then neither will the final ending of your whole life, which is also just another change.

meditations_book-09.originalText:
As occasion shall require, either to thine own understanding, or to
that of the universe, or to his, whom thou hast now to do with, let thy
refuge be with all speed. To thine own, that it resolve upon nothing
against justice. To that of the universe, that thou mayest remember,
part of whom thou art. Of his, that thou mayest consider whether in the
estate of ignorance, or of knowledge. And then also must thou call to
mind, that he is thy kinsman.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: When you need help, turn quickly to one of three sources of understanding. Turn to your own mind, so it chooses nothing unjust. Turn to the universe's mind, so you remember you are part of something larger. Turn to the other person's mind, so you can see whether they act from ignorance or knowledge. And remember — that person is your family.

meditations_book-09.originalText:
As thou thyself, whoever thou art, were made for the perfection and
consummation, being a member of it, of a common society; so must every
action of thine tend to the perfection and consummation of a life that
is truly sociable. What action soever of thine therefore that either
immediately or afar off, hath not reference to the common good, that is
an exorbitant and disorderly action; yea it is seditious; as one among
the people who from such and such a consent and unity, should factiously
divide and separate himself.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: You were made to be part of human society and to help it flourish. So every action you take should help create a truly social life. Any action that doesn't serve the common good — whether directly or indirectly — is out of line and disruptive. It's like rebellion. It's like someone breaking away from the unity that holds people together.

meditations_book-09.originalText:
Children's anger, mere babels; wretched souls bearing up dead
bodies, that they may not have their fall so soon: even as it is in that
common dirge song.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: Children's anger is just noise and babble. We are wretched souls carrying around dead bodies, trying to keep them from falling apart too quickly. Just like in that funeral song everyone knows.

meditations_book-09.originalText:
Go to the quality of the cause from which the effect doth
proceed. Behold it by itself bare and naked, separated from all that is
material. Then consider the utmost bounds of time that that cause, thus
and thus qualified, can subsist and abide.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: Look at the real cause behind what happens. See it for what it truly is, stripped of all the extras. Then think about how long that cause can actually last.

meditations_book-09.originalText:
Infinite are the troubles and miseries, that thou hast already
been put to, by reason of this only, because that for all happiness
it did not suffice thee, or, that thou didst not account it sufficient
happiness, that thy understanding did operate according to its natural
constitution.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: You have brought endless troubles and miseries on yourself for one reason alone. It wasn't enough for you to be happy that your mind was working as it should. You didn't count that as sufficient happiness.

meditations_book-09.originalText:
When any shall either impeach thee with false accusations, or
hatefully reproach thee, or shall use any such carriage towards thee,
get thee presently to their minds and understandings, and look in them,
and behold what manner of men they be. Thou shalt see, that there is no
such occasion why it should trouble thee, what such as they are think of
thee. Yet must thou love them still, for by nature they are thy friends.
And the Gods themselves, in those things that they seek from them as
matters of great moment, are well content, all manner of ways, as by
dreams and oracles, to help them as well as others.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: When someone accuses you falsely or speaks hatefully to you, look into their minds and hearts. See what kind of people they really are. You will find there is no reason to be troubled by what such people think of you. But you must still love them, because by nature they are your friends. Even the gods are willing to help these people in important matters, using dreams and signs, just as they help everyone else.

meditations_book-09.originalText:
Up and down, from one age to another, go the ordinary things of
the world; being still the same. And either of everything in particular
before it come to pass, the mind of the universe doth consider with
itself and deliberate: and if so, then submit for shame unto the
determination of such an excellent understanding: or once for all it did
resolve upon all things in general; and since that whatsoever happens,
happens by a necessary consequence, and all things indivisibly in a
manner and inseparably hold one of another. In sum, either there is a
God, and then all is well; or if all things go by chance and fortune,
yet mayest thou use thine own providence in those things that concern
thee properly; and then art thou well.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: The same ordinary things keep happening throughout history. Either the universe thinks through each event before it happens — and if that's true, then accept what such perfect wisdom decides. Or the universe decided everything all at once long ago, and whatever happens now follows from that. All things are connected and flow from each other. In short, either there is a God and everything is fine, or if things happen by chance, you can still use your own good judgment for the things that are up to you. Either way, you'll be fine.

meditations_book-09.originalText:
Within a while the earth shall cover us all, and then she herself
shall have her change. And then the course will be, from one period of
eternity unto another, and so a perpetual eternity. Now can any man
that shall consider with himself in his mind the several rollings or
successions of so many changes and alterations, and the swiftness of all
these rulings; can he otherwise but contemn in his heart and despise
all worldly things? The cause of the universe is as it were a strong
torrent, it carrieth all away.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: Soon the earth will cover us all. Then even the earth itself will change. And the cycle will go on from one eternal period to another, forever and ever. Think about all these endless changes rolling over each other, one after another. Think about how fast everything shifts and moves. How can you not feel contempt for all the things people chase in this world? The force behind the universe is like a powerful river. It sweeps everything away.

meditations_book-09.originalText: And these your professed politicians, the only true practical philosophers of the world, (as they think of themselves) so full of affected gravity, or such professed lovers of virtue and honesty, what wretches be they in very deed; how vile and contemptible in themselves? O man! what ado doest thou keep? Do what thy nature doth now require. Resolve upon it, if thou mayest: and take no thought, whether anybody shall know it or no.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: And these so-called politicians, who think they are the world's only true practical philosophers — so full of fake seriousness, or claiming to love virtue and honesty — what wretches they really are! How vile and contemptible! Oh man, what a fuss you make! Do what your nature requires right now. Just decide, if you can. And don't worry about whether anyone will know.

meditations_book-09.originalText: Yea, but sayest thou, I must not expect a Plato's commonwealth. If they profit though never so little, I must be content; and think much even of that little progress. Doth then any of them forsake their former false opinions that I should think they profit? For without a change of opinions, alas! what is all that ostentation, but mere wretchedness of slavish minds, that groan privately, and yet would make a show of obedience to reason, and truth? Go too now and tell me of Alexander and Philippus, and Demetrius Phalereus. Whether they understood what the common nature requireth, and could rule themselves or no, they know best themselves. But if they kept a life, and swaggered; I (God be thanked) am not bound to imitate them. The effect of true philosophy is, unaffected simplicity and modesty. Persuade me not to ostentation and vainglory.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: You say I shouldn't expect a perfect society like Plato described. If people improve even a little, I should be happy with that small progress. But do any of them actually give up their old wrong ideas? Without changing their beliefs, what good is all their showing off? It's just the misery of slave-like minds. They complain in private but pretend to follow reason and truth. Go ahead and tell me about Alexander and Philip and Demetrius. Whether they understood what nature requires and could control themselves — they know best. But if they lived for show and bragged, I'm not required to copy them. Real philosophy leads to simple honesty and humility. Don't try to convince me to show off and seek empty praise.

meditations_book-09.originalText: From some high place as it were to look down, and to behold here flocks, and there sacrifices, without number; and all kind of navigation; some in a rough and stormy sea, and some in a calm: the general differences, or different estates of things, some, that are now first upon being; the several and mutual relations of those things that are together; and some other things that are at their last.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: Imagine looking down from some high place. You see flocks of animals here, sacrifices there, countless ships sailing. Some sail through rough storms, others in calm waters. You see the general differences in all things. Some things are just beginning to exist. You see how things relate to each other. And you see other things that are ending.

meditations_book-09.originalText: Their lives also, who were long ago, and theirs who shall be hereafter, and the present estate and life of those many nations of barbarians that are now in the world, thou must likewise consider in thy mind. And how many there be, who never so much as heard of thy name, how many that will soon forget it; how many who but even now did commend thee, within a very little while perchance will speak ill of thee. So that neither fame, nor honour, nor anything else that this world doth afford, is worth the while.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: Think about the lives of people who lived long ago, and those who will live in the future, and the current lives of all the foreign nations around the world today. Consider how many people have never even heard your name, how many will soon forget it, and how many who praise you now might speak badly of you very soon. So fame, honor, and anything else this world offers is not worth pursuing.

meditations_book-09.originalText: The sum then of all; whatsoever doth happen unto thee, whereof God is the cause, to accept it contentedly: whatsoever thou doest, whereof thou thyself art the cause, to do it justly: which will be, if both in thy resolution and in thy action thou have no further end, than to do good unto others, as being that, which by thy natural constitution, as a man, thou art bound unto.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: Here's the summary of it all: Whatever happens to you that comes from God, accept it willingly. Whatever you do that comes from your own choice, do it justly. This means having no other goal in your decisions and actions than to help others. This is what you are naturally bound to do as a human being.

meditations_book-09.originalText:
Many of those things that trouble and straiten thee, it is in thy
power to cut off, as wholly depending from mere conceit and opinion; and
then thou shalt have room enough.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: Many of the things that trouble and limit you are in your power to cut off. They depend entirely on your own thoughts and opinions. Then you will have room enough.

meditations_book-09.originalText:
To comprehend the whole world together in thy mind, and the whole
course of this present age to represent it unto thyself, and to fix thy
thoughts upon the sudden change of every particular object. How short
the time is from the generation of anything, unto the dissolution of
the same; but how immense and infinite both that which was before the
generation, and that which after the generation of it shall be. All
things that thou seest, will soon be perished, and they that see their
corruptions, will soon vanish away themselves. He that dieth a hundred
years old, and he that dieth young, shall come all to one.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: Try to picture the whole world in your mind, and the whole span of this age we live in. Focus on how quickly everything changes. How short the time is between when something comes into being and when it falls apart. But how vast and endless the time before it existed, and the time after it's gone. Everything you see will soon be destroyed. And those who watch things decay will soon vanish themselves. Someone who dies at a hundred and someone who dies young both end up in the same place.

meditations_book-09.originalText:
What are their minds and understandings; and what the things that
they apply themselves unto: what do they love, and what do they hate
for? Fancy to thyself the estate of their souls openly to be seen. When
they think they hurt them shrewdly, whom they speak ill of; and when
they think they do them a very good turn, whom they commend and extol: O
how full are they then of conceit, and opinion!
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: What are their minds like? What do they think about? What do they spend their time on? What do they love and hate? Imagine you could see their souls laid bare. When they think they're really hurting someone by speaking badly of them, and when they think they're doing someone a great favor by praising them — how full of themselves they are!

meditations_book-09.originalText:
Loss and corruption, is in very deed nothing else but change and
alteration; and that is it, which the nature of the universe doth most
delight in, by which, and according to which, whatsoever is done, is
well done. For that was the estate of worldly things from the beginning,
and so shall it ever be. Or wouldest thou rather say, that all things
in the world have gone ill from the beginning for so many ages, and
shall ever go ill? And then among so many deities, could no divine power
be found all this while, that could rectify the things of the world? Or
is the world, to incessant woes and miseries, for ever condemned?
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: Loss and decay are really just change. And change is what the universe loves most. Everything that happens through change is good. This is how things have always been, and how they will always be. Would you rather say that everything in the world has gone wrong from the beginning? That for all these ages, everything has been bad and always will be? If that were true, then among all the gods, wouldn't at least one have the power to fix things? Or do you think the world is doomed to endless suffering forever?

meditations_book-09.originalText:
How base and putrid, every common matter is! Water, dust, and
from the mixture of these bones, and all that loathsome stuff that our
bodies do consist of: so subject to be infected, and corrupted. And
again those other things that are so much prized and admired, as marble
stones, what are they, but as it were the kernels of the earth? gold and
silver, what are they, but as the more gross faeces of the earth? Thy
most royal apparel, for matter, it is but as it were the hair of a silly
sheep, and for colour, the very blood of a shell-fish; of this nature
are all other things. Thy life itself, is some such thing too; a mere
exhalation of blood: and it also, apt to be changed into some other
common thing.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: How cheap and rotten everything ordinary is! Water, dust, and from mixing these together — bones and all the disgusting stuff our bodies are made of. So easily infected and ruined. And those other things people prize so much, like marble stones — what are they but the seeds of dirt? Gold and silver are just the earth's waste. Your finest royal clothes are nothing but sheep hair. Their color comes from the blood of shellfish. Everything else is like this too. Your life itself is the same kind of thing — just blood turned to vapor. And it can easily change into something else just as common.

meditations_book-09.originalText:
Will this querulousness, this murmuring, this complaining and
dissembling never be at an end? What then is it, that troubleth thee?
Doth any new thing happen unto thee? What doest thou so wonder at? At
the cause, or the matter? Behold either by itself, is either of that
weight and moment indeed? And besides these, there is not anything. But
thy duty towards the Gods also, it is time thou shouldst acquit thyself
of it with more goodness and simplicity.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: Will this complaining and grumbling and pretending never end? What is actually bothering you? Is anything really new happening? What are you so surprised about? The cause or the thing itself? Look at either one alone. Is it really that important? Besides these, there is nothing else. But your duty to the gods — it's time you handled that with more honesty and straightforwardness.

meditations_book-09.originalText:
It is all one to see these things for a hundred of years together
or but for three years.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: It makes no difference whether you see these things for a hundred years or just three years.

meditations_book-09.originalText:
If he have sinned, his is the harm, not mine. But perchance he
hath not.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: If he has done wrong, the harm is his, not mine. But maybe he hasn't done wrong at all.

meditations_book-09.originalText:
Either all things by the providence of reason happen unto every
particular, as a part of one general body; and then it is against reason
that a part should complain of anything that happens for the good of the
whole; or if, according to Epicurus, atoms be the cause of all things
and that life be nothing else but an accidentary confusion of things,
and death nothing else, but a mere dispersion and so of all other
things: what doest thou trouble thyself for?
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: Either everything happens by divine reason, and we are all parts of one great whole — and then it makes no sense for a part to complain about what helps the whole. Or maybe Epicurus was right that atoms cause everything, that life is just a random mixing of particles, and death is just those particles breaking apart. If that's true, why are you worrying about anything?

meditations_book-09.originalText:
Sayest thou unto that rational part, Thou art dead; corruption
hath taken hold on thee? Doth it then also void excrements? Doth it like
either oxen, or sheep, graze or feed; that it also should be mortal, as
well as the body?
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: Do you say to your rational mind, 'You are dead; corruption has taken hold of you'? Does it void waste like an animal? Does it graze and feed like oxen or sheep, so that it too should die along with the body?

meditations_book-09.originalText: Either the Gods can do nothing for us at all, or they can still and allay all the distractions and distempers of thy mind. If they can do nothing, why doest thou pray? If they can, why wouldst not thou rather pray, that they will grant unto thee, that thou mayst neither fear, nor lust after any of those worldly things which cause these distractions and distempers of it? Why not rather, that thou mayst not at either their absence or presence, be grieved and discontented: than either that thou mayst obtain them, or that thou mayst avoid them? For certainly it must needs be, that if the Gods can help us in anything, they may in this kind also.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: Either the gods can't help us at all, or they can calm all the chaos and troubles in your mind. If they can't help, why pray? If they can help, why not pray for something better? Ask them to free you from fear and craving for worldly things that cause this mental chaos. Ask that you won't be upset whether you have these things or not. This is better than praying to get what you want or avoid what you fear. If the gods can help us with anything, surely they can help us with this.

meditations_book-09.originalText: But thou wilt say perchance, 'In those things the Gods have given me my liberty: and it is in mine own power to do what I will.' But if thou mayst use this liberty, rather to set thy mind at true liberty, than wilfully with baseness and servility of mind to affect those things, which either to compass or to avoid is not in thy power, wert not thou better? And as for the Gods, who hath told thee, that they may not help us up even in those things that they have put in our own power? whether it be so or no, thou shalt soon perceive, if thou wilt but try thyself and pray.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: But you might say, 'In those things the gods have given me freedom. I have the power to do what I want.' But if you have this freedom, wouldn't it be better to use it to free your mind truly? Don't waste it chasing things you can't control or running from what you can't avoid. That's just mental slavery. And who told you the gods won't help us even with the things they put in our power? You don't know if that's true or not. Try it yourself. Pray and see what happens.

meditations_book-09.originalText: One prayeth that he may compass his desire, to lie with such or such a one, pray thou that thou mayst not lust to lie with her. Another how he may be rid of such a one; pray thou that thou mayst so patiently bear with him, as that thou have no such need to be rid of him. Another, that he may not lose his child. Pray thou that thou mayst not fear to lose him. To this end and purpose, let all thy prayer be, and see what will be the event.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: One person prays to sleep with someone they desire. You should pray that you won't lust after her. Another prays to get rid of someone who bothers him. You should pray for patience to bear with that person, so you won't need to get rid of him. Another prays not to lose his child. You should pray not to fear losing yours. Turn all your prayers toward this purpose, and see what happens.

meditations_book-09.originalText:
'In my sickness' (saith Epicurus of himself:) 'my discourses were
not concerning the nature of my disease, neither was that, to them that
came to visit me, the subject of my talk; but in the consideration and
contemplation of that, which was of especial weight and moment, was all
my time bestowed and spent, and among others in this very thing, how my
mind, by a natural and unavoidable sympathy partaking in some sort with
the present indisposition of my body, might nevertheless keep herself
free from trouble, and in present possession of her own proper
happiness.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: Epicurus said: 'When I was sick, I didn't spend my time talking about my illness. When people came to see me, that wasn't what we discussed either. Instead, I focused on what really mattered. I thought about how my mind could stay free from worry, even though it naturally shares in the body's suffering. I wanted to keep my inner peace and happiness, despite what was happening to my body.'

meditations_book-09.originalText:
Neither did I leave the ordering of my body to the physicians
altogether to do with me what they would, as though I expected any
great matter from them, or as though I thought it a matter of such great
consequence, by their means to recover my health: for my present estate,
methought, liked me very well, and gave me good content.' Whether
therefore in sickness (if thou chance to sicken) or in what other kind
of extremity soever, endeavour thou also to be in thy mind so affected,
as he doth report of himself: not to depart from thy philosophy for
anything that can befall thee, nor to give ear to the discourses of
silly people, and mere naturalists.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: I didn't leave my body completely in the hands of doctors to do whatever they wanted. I didn't expect miracles from them or think it was desperately important to get my health back through them. My present condition seemed fine to me and gave me peace. So whether you get sick or face any other kind of trouble, try to have the same attitude he describes: don't abandon your philosophy for anything that happens to you, and don't listen to foolish people or those who only see the physical world.

meditations_book-09.originalText:
It is common to all trades and professions to mind and intend that
only, which now they are about, and the instrument whereby they work.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: All trades and professions have this in common: they focus only on what they're doing right now, and on the tools they use to do it.

meditations_book-09.originalText: When at any time thou art offended with any one's impudency, put presently this question to thyself: 'What? Is it then possible, that there should not be any impudent men in the world! Certainly it is not possible.' Desire not then that which is impossible. For this one, (thou must think) whosoever he be, is one of those impudent ones, that the world cannot be without. So of the subtile and crafty, so of the perfidious, so of every one that offendeth, must thou ever be ready to reason with thyself. For whilst in general thou dost thus reason with thyself, that the kind of them must needs be in the world, thou wilt be the better able to use meekness towards every particular. This also thou shalt find of very good use, upon every such occasion, presently to consider with thyself, what proper virtue nature hath furnished man with, against such a vice, or to encounter with a disposition vicious in this kind. As for example, against the unthankful, it hath given goodness and meekness, as an antidote, and so against another vicious in another kind some other peculiar faculty.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: When someone's rudeness offends you, ask yourself this question right away: 'Is it possible for there to be no rude people in the world?' Of course not. So don't wish for something impossible. This person, whoever they are, is one of those rude people the world can't do without. The same goes for sneaky people, liars, and everyone else who bothers you. You must always be ready to think this way. When you remind yourself that these types of people must exist in the world, you'll find it easier to be gentle with each particular person. You'll also find this helpful: whenever this happens, think about what virtue nature gave us to deal with that specific vice. For example, against ungrateful people, nature gave us kindness and gentleness as a remedy. And against other vices, it gave us other special abilities.

meditations_book-09.originalText: And generally, is it not in thy power to instruct him better, that is in an error? For whosoever sinneth, doth in that decline from his purposed end, and is certainly deceived, And again, what art thou the worse for his sin? For thou shalt not find that any one of these, against whom thou art incensed, hath in very deed done anything whereby thy mind (the only true subject of thy hurt and evil) can be made worse than it was. And what a matter of either grief or wonder is this, if he that is unlearned, do the deeds of one that is unlearned? Should not thou rather blame thyself, who, when upon very good grounds of reason, thou mightst have thought it very probable, that such a thing would by such a one be committed, didst not only not foresee it, but moreover dost wonder at it, that such a thing should be.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: And in general, can't you teach someone who is making a mistake? Anyone who does wrong is missing their real goal and is clearly confused. And how does their mistake hurt you? You won't find that any of these people you're angry with has actually done anything to damage your mind — which is the only thing that can truly harm you. Why should it surprise or upset you when someone who doesn't know better acts like someone who doesn't know better? You should blame yourself instead. You had good reason to expect this person would do exactly this kind of thing. Yet not only did you fail to see it coming — you're actually surprised it happened.

meditations_book-09.originalText: But then especially, when thou dost find fault with either an unthankful, or a false man, must thou reflect upon thyself. For without all question, thou thyself art much in fault, if either of one that were of such a disposition, thou didst expect that he should be true unto thee: or when unto any thou didst a good turn, thou didst not there bound thy thoughts, as one that had obtained his end; nor didst not think that from the action itself thou hadst received a full reward of the good that thou hadst done. For what wouldst thou have more? Unto him that is a man, thou hast done a good turn: doth not that suffice thee?
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: But especially when you find fault with someone who is ungrateful or dishonest, you must look at yourself. You are clearly at fault too. If you expected someone with that character to be loyal to you, that was your mistake. Or when you did someone a favor, you should have stopped there — satisfied that you had done what you meant to do. You should have thought that the action itself was your full reward. What more do you want? You did a good thing for another human being. Isn't that enough?

meditations_book-09.originalText: What thy nature required, that hast thou done. Must thou be rewarded for it? As if either the eye for that it seeth, or the feet that they go, should require satisfaction. For as these being by nature appointed for such an use, can challenge no more, than that they may work according to their natural constitution: so man being born to do good unto others whensoever he doth a real good unto any by helping them out of error; or though but in middle things, as in matter of wealth, life, preferment, and the like, doth help to further their desires he doth that for which he was made, and therefore can require no more.
meditations_book-09.plainEnglish: You did what your nature required. Should you expect a reward for it? Does the eye demand payment for seeing, or do the feet ask for thanks for walking? These parts were made for their purpose. They can ask for nothing more than to work as they were designed. So too with humans. We were born to help others. When you help someone escape error, or even with ordinary things like money, health, or career advancement, you are doing what you were made for. You can ask for nothing more.

meditations_book-10.originalText: O my soul, the time I trust will be, when thou shalt be good, simple, single, more open and visible, than that body by which it is enclosed. Thou wilt one day be sensible of their happiness, whose end is love, and their affections dead to all worldly things. Thou shalt one day be full, and in want of no external thing: not seeking pleasure from anything, either living or insensible, that this world can afford; neither wanting time for the continuation of thy pleasure, nor place and opportunity, nor the favour either of the weather or of men.
meditations_book-10.plainEnglish: O my soul, I trust the time will come when you will be good, simple, and pure. You will be more clear and open than this body that holds you. One day you will understand the happiness of those who live for love alone. Their hearts are dead to all worldly things. One day you will be complete and need nothing from outside yourself. You won't seek pleasure from anything in this world, whether living or lifeless. You won't need more time to enjoy things, or special places, or good weather, or the approval of other people.

meditations_book-10.originalText: When thou shalt have content in thy present estate, and all things present shall add to thy content: when thou shalt persuade thyself, that thou hast all things; all for thy good, and all by the providence of the Gods: and of things future also shalt be as confident, that all will do well, as tending to the maintenance and preservation in some sort, of his perfect welfare and happiness, who is perfection of life, of goodness, and beauty; who begets all things, and containeth all things in himself, and in himself doth recollect all things from all places that are dissolved, that of them he may beget others again like unto them.
meditations_book-10.plainEnglish: When you find peace with your current situation, and everything around you adds to that peace — when you convince yourself that you have everything you need, all of it good, all of it guided by the gods — then you will also feel confident about the future. You will trust that everything will work out well, because it all serves to maintain the perfect happiness of the divine force that is pure life, goodness, and beauty. This force creates all things and holds all things within itself. It gathers up everything that falls apart and uses it to create new things just like them.

meditations_book-10.originalText: Such one day shall be thy disposition, that thou shalt be able, both in regard of the Gods, and in regard of men, so to fit and order thy conversation, as neither to complain of them at any time, for anything that they do; nor to do anything thyself, for which thou mayest justly be condemned.
meditations_book-10.plainEnglish: One day you will reach a state of mind where you can handle both the gods and other people properly. You won't complain about what they do to you. And you won't do anything that deserves blame.

meditations_book-10.originalText:
As one who is altogether governed by nature, let it be thy care to
observe what it is that thy nature in general doth require. That
done, if thou find not that thy nature, as thou art a living sensible
creature, will be the worse for it, thou mayest proceed. Next then thou
must examine, what thy nature as thou art a living sensible creature,
doth require. And that, whatsoever it be, thou mayest admit of and do
it, if thy nature as thou art a reasonable living creature, will not be
the worse for it. Now whatsoever is reasonable, is also sociable, Keep
thyself to these rules, and trouble not thyself about idle things.
meditations_book-10.plainEnglish: Since you are completely guided by nature, pay attention to what your nature generally needs. Once you do that, check if your nature as a living, feeling creature will be harmed by it. If not, you can go ahead. Next, examine what your nature as a living, feeling creature requires. Whatever that is, you can accept it and do it, as long as your nature as a reasoning creature won't be harmed. Whatever is reasonable is also social. Stick to these rules and don't worry about pointless things.

meditations_book-10.originalText:
Whatsoever doth happen unto thee, thou art naturally by thy natural
constitution either able, or not able to bear. If thou beest able, be
not offended, but bear it according to thy natural constitution, or as
nature hath enabled thee. If thou beest not able, be not offended. For
it will soon make an end of thee, and itself, (whatsoever it be) at the
same time end with thee. But remember, that whatsoever by the strength
of opinion, grounded upon a certain apprehension of both true profit and
duty, thou canst conceive tolerable; that thou art able to bear that by
thy natural constitution.
meditations_book-10.plainEnglish: Whatever happens to you, you are naturally either able to bear it or not. If you can bear it, don't be upset. Just bear it as nature made you able to do. If you can't bear it, don't be upset either. It will soon kill you, and then it will end along with you. But remember this: whatever you can make tolerable through the strength of your beliefs—based on what is truly good and right—that you can bear by your natural makeup.

meditations_book-10.originalText:
Him that offends, to teach with love and meek ness, and to show him
his error. But if thou canst not, then to blame thyself; or rather not
thyself neither, if thy will and endeavours have not been wanting.
meditations_book-10.plainEnglish: When someone does wrong, teach them with love and gentleness. Show them their mistake. But if you can't reach them, then blame yourself. Or better yet, don't blame yourself either, if you really tried your best.

meditations_book-10.originalText:
Whatsoever it be that happens unto thee, it is that which from all
time was appointed unto thee. For by the same coherence of causes, by
which thy substance from all eternity was appointed to be, was also
whatsoever should happen unto it, destinated and appointed.
meditations_book-10.plainEnglish: Whatever happens to you was meant to happen from the beginning of time. The same forces that shaped your existence also decided everything that would happen to you.

meditations_book-10.originalText: Either with Epicurus, we must fondly imagine the atoms to be the cause of all things, or we must needs grant a nature. Let this then be thy first ground, that thou art part of that universe, which is governed by nature. Then secondly, that to those parts that are of the same kind and nature as thou art, thou hast relation of kindred.
meditations_book-10.plainEnglish: Either we believe with Epicurus that random atoms cause everything, or we must accept that nature governs the world. Start with this: you are part of a universe ruled by nature. Second, you are connected to all other parts that share your same nature.

meditations_book-10.originalText: For of these, if I shall always be mindful, first as I am a part, I shall never be displeased with anything, that falls to my particular share of the common chances of the world. For nothing that is behoveful unto the whole, can be truly hurtful to that which is part of it. For this being the common privilege of all natures, that they contain nothing in themselves that is hurtful unto them; it cannot be that the nature of the universe (whose privilege beyond other particular natures, is, that she cannot against her will by any higher external cause be constrained,) should beget anything and cherish it in her bosom that should tend to her own hurt and prejudice.
meditations_book-10.plainEnglish: If I keep these things in mind, first that I am a part of the whole, I will never be upset with whatever happens to me in life. Nothing that serves the whole can truly harm any part of it. All natural things have this trait: they contain nothing that hurts themselves. The universe has this same trait, but even stronger. No outside force can make it act against its will. So it cannot create or nurture anything that would damage itself.

meditations_book-10.originalText: As then I bear in mind that I am a part of such an universe, I shall not be displeased with anything that happens. And as I have relation of kindred to those parts that are of the same kind and nature that I am, so I shall be careful to do nothing that is prejudicial to the community, but in all my deliberations shall they that are of my kind ever be; and the common good, that, which all my intentions and resolutions shall drive unto, as that which is contrary unto it, I shall by all means endeavour to prevent and avoid. These things once so fixed and concluded, as thou wouldst think him a happy citizen, whose constant study and practice were for the good and benefit of his fellow citizens, and the carriage of the city such towards him, that he were well pleased with it; so must it needs be with thee, that thou shalt live a happy life.
meditations_book-10.plainEnglish: When I remember that I am part of this whole universe, I won't be upset by anything that happens. And since I'm connected to other parts that are like me, I'll be careful not to harm the community. In everything I decide, I'll think of others like me. The common good — that's what all my plans and choices should aim for. Whatever goes against it, I'll try to prevent and avoid. Once these things are settled, think about this: you would call a citizen happy if he constantly worked for his fellow citizens' good, and if the city treated him so well that he was pleased with it. In the same way, you must live a happy life.

meditations_book-10.originalText: All parts of the world, (all things I mean that are contained within the whole world), must of necessity at some time or other come to corruption. Alteration I should say, to speak truly and properly; but that I may be the better understood, I am content at this time to use that more common word. Now say I, if so be that this be both hurtful unto them, and yet unavoidable, would not, thinkest thou, the whole itself be in a sweet case, all the parts of it being subject to alteration, yea and by their making itself fitted for corruption, as consisting of things different and contrary?
meditations_book-10.plainEnglish: All parts of the world must eventually change and decay. I should say 'change' to be precise, but I'll use the common word 'corruption' so you understand. Now, if this is both harmful to things and unavoidable, wouldn't the whole world be in trouble? All its parts are subject to change, and the world itself is built for decay since it's made of different and opposing elements.

meditations_book-10.originalText: And did nature then either of herself thus project and purpose the affliction and misery of her parts, and therefore of purpose so made them, not only that haply they might, but of necessity that they should fall into evil; or did not she know what she did, when she made them? For either of these two to say, is equally absurd. But to let pass nature in general, and to reason of things particular according to their own particular natures; how absurd and ridiculous is it, first to say that all parts of the whole are, by their proper natural constitution, subject to alteration; and then when any such thing doth happen, as when one doth fall sick and dieth, to take on and wonder as though some strange thing had happened?
meditations_book-10.plainEnglish: Did nature plan for her parts to suffer and be miserable? Did she make them knowing they would have to fall into evil? Or did she not know what she was doing when she made them? Either idea is absurd. But forget about nature in general. Think about individual things and their own natures. How ridiculous is it to first say that all parts of the whole are naturally subject to change, and then when something like this happens — when someone gets sick and dies — to get upset and act surprised as if something strange had occurred?

meditations_book-10.originalText: Though this besides might move not so grievously to take on when any such thing doth happen, that whatsoever is dissolved, it is dissolved into those things, whereof it was compounded. For every dissolution is either a mere dispersion, of the elements into those elements again whereof everything did consist, or a change, of that which is more solid into earth; and of that which is pure and subtile or spiritual, into air. So that by this means nothing is lost, but all resumed again into those rational generative seeds of the universe; and this universe, either after a certain period of time to lie consumed by fire, or by continual changes to be renewed, and so for ever to endure.
meditations_book-10.plainEnglish: Here's another thought that might make it less painful when such things happen: whatever breaks down returns to the parts it was made from. Every breakdown is either a simple scattering of elements back into their original forms, or a change where solid matter becomes earth and pure, light matter becomes air. This way nothing is truly lost. Everything goes back into the creative seeds of the universe. And this universe will either burn up after a certain time, or keep renewing itself through constant changes, and last forever.

meditations_book-10.originalText: Now that solid and spiritual that we speak of, thou must not conceive it to be that very same, which at first was, when thou wert born. For alas! all this that now thou art in either kind, either for matter of substance, or of life, hath but two or three days ago partly from meats eaten, and partly from air breathed in, received all its influx, being the same then in no other respect, than a running river, maintained by the perpetual influx and new supply of waters, is the same. That therefore which thou hast since received, not that which came from thy mother, is that which comes to change and corruption. But suppose that that for the general substance, and more solid part of it, should still cleave unto thee never so close, yet what is that to the proper qualities and affections of it, by which persons are distinguished, which certainly are quite different?
meditations_book-10.plainEnglish: Don't think that your body and soul are the same as when you were born. Everything that makes you who you are now — both your physical body and your life force — came to you just a few days ago. Some from the food you ate, some from the air you breathed. You are like a flowing river. The river stays the same only because new water keeps flowing into it. What you have gained since birth, not what came from your mother, is what will change and decay. Even if the solid parts of your body could somehow stick with you forever, what would that matter? The real qualities that make you who you are — those are completely different now.

meditations_book-10.originalText: Now that thou hast taken these names upon thee of good, modest, true; of ἔμφρων, σύμφρων, ὑπέρφρων; take heed lest at any times by doing anything that is contrary, thou be but improperly so called, and lose thy right to these appellations. Or if thou do, return unto them again with all possible speed. And remember, that the word ἔμφρων notes unto thee an intent and intelligent consideration of every object that presents itself unto thee, without distraction. And the word σύμφρων, a ready and contented acceptation of whatsoever by the appointment of the common nature, happens unto thee. And the word ὑπέρφρων, a super-extension, or a transcendent, and outreaching disposition of thy mind, whereby it passeth by all bodily pains and pleasures, honour and credit, death and whatsoever is of the same nature, as matters of absolute indifferency, and in no wise to be stood upon by a wise man.
meditations_book-10.plainEnglish: You have taken on these names: good, modest, true. You call yourself thoughtful, accepting, and above petty concerns. Be careful not to lose the right to these names by acting against them. If you slip up, get back to them as quickly as you can. Remember what these words mean. Being thoughtful means you consider each situation clearly, without getting distracted. Being accepting means you welcome whatever happens to you through the natural order of things. Being above petty concerns means your mind rises above physical pain and pleasure, fame and shame, death and similar things. These are all matters that don't really matter. A wise person doesn't get worked up over them.

meditations_book-10.originalText: These then if inviolably thou shalt observe, and shalt not be ambitious to be so called by others, both thou thyself shalt become a new man, and thou shalt begin a new life. For to continue such as hitherto thou hast been, to undergo those distractions and distempers as thou must needs for such a life as hitherto thou hast lived, is the part of one that is very foolish, and is overfond of his life. Whom a man might compare to one of those half-eaten wretches, matched in the amphitheatre with wild beasts; who as full as they are all the body over with wounds and blood, desire for a great favour, that they may be reserved till the next day, then also, and in the same estate to be exposed to the same nails and teeth as before.
meditations_book-10.plainEnglish: If you follow these principles without fail, and don't worry about what others call you, you will become a new person and start a new life. To keep living as you have been, putting up with the same chaos and troubles that come with your old way of life — that would be foolish. It's like being too attached to a life that's destroying you. You'd be like those half-dead fighters in the arena, torn up by wild animals, covered in wounds and blood, who beg to be saved so they can come back tomorrow and face the same claws and teeth all over again.

meditations_book-10.originalText: Away therefore, ship thyself; and from the troubles and distractions of thy former life convey thyself as it were unto these few names; and if thou canst abide in them, or be constant in the practice and possession of them, continue there as glad and joyful as one that were translated unto some such place of bliss and happiness as that which by Hesiod and Plato is called the Islands of the Blessed, by others called the Elysian Fields. And whensoever thou findest thyself; that thou art in danger of a relapse, and that thou art not able to master and overcome those difficulties and temptations that present themselves in thy present station: get thee into any private corner, where thou mayst be better able. Or if that will not serve forsake even thy life rather. But so that it be not in passion but in a plain voluntary modest way: this being the only commendable action of thy whole life that thus thou art departed, or this having been the main work and business of thy whole life, that thou mightest thus depart.
meditations_book-10.plainEnglish: So leave all that behind. Take yourself away from the troubles and chaos of your old life. Move toward these few simple principles. If you can stay with them and practice them steadily, remain there. Be as happy as someone who has reached the blessed islands that Hesiod and Plato wrote about—the place others call the Elysian Fields. Whenever you find yourself slipping back, when you cannot handle the difficulties and temptations of where you are now, go somewhere private where you can do better. If even that does not work, then leave life itself. But do it calmly, not in anger or passion—do it as a quiet, deliberate choice. Let this be the one thing you can be proud of in your whole life: that you left this way. Or let this be your life's main work: preparing to leave this way.

meditations_book-10.originalText: Now for the better remembrance of those names that we have spoken of, thou shalt find it a very good help, to remember the Gods as often as may be: and that, the thing which they require at our hands of as many of us, as are by nature reasonable creation is not that with fair words, and outward show of piety and devotion we should flatter them, but that we should become like unto them: and that as all other natural creatures, the fig tree for example; the dog the bee: both do, all of them, and apply themselves unto that which by their natural constitution, is proper unto them; so man likewise should do that, which by his nature, as he is a man, belongs unto him.
meditations_book-10.plainEnglish: To better remember what we've talked about, it helps to think of the gods often. What they want from us — as rational beings — is not empty words or fake displays of devotion. They want us to become like them. Just as other natural creatures do what they're meant to do — the fig tree bears fruit, the dog is loyal, the bee makes honey — we should do what belongs to our nature as human beings.

meditations_book-10.originalText: Toys and fooleries at home, wars abroad: sometimes terror, sometimes torpor, or stupid sloth: this is thy daily slavery. By little and little, if thou doest not better look to it, those sacred dogmata will be blotted out of thy mind.
meditations_book-10.plainEnglish: Trivial distractions at home, wars abroad. Sometimes fear, sometimes numbness, or dull laziness. This is your daily slavery. Little by little, if you don't pay attention, those sacred principles will fade from your mind.

meditations_book-10.originalText: How many things be there, which when as a mere naturalist, thou hast barely considered of according to their nature, thou doest let pass without any further use? Whereas thou shouldst in all things so join action and contemplation, that thou mightest both at the same time attend all present occasions, to perform everything duly and carefully and yet so intend the contemplative part too, that no part of that delight and pleasure, which the contemplative knowledge of everything according to its true nature doth of itself afford, might be lost.
meditations_book-10.plainEnglish: How many things do you observe as a student of nature, understanding their true form, but then let pass without putting that knowledge to use? You should combine action and thought in everything. This way you can handle what needs doing with care and attention, while still enjoying the pleasure that comes from truly understanding how things work.

meditations_book-10.originalText: Or, that the true and contemnplative knowledge of everything according to its own nature, might of itself, (action being subject to many lets and impediments) afford unto thee sufficient pleasure and happiness. Not apparent indeed, but not concealed. And when shalt thou attain to the happiness of true simplicity, and unaffected gravity? When shalt thou rejoice in the certain knowledge of every particular object according to its true nature: as what the matter and substance of it is; what use it is for in the world: how long it can subsist: what things it doth consist of: who they be that are capable of it, and who they that can give it, and take it away?
meditations_book-10.plainEnglish: Or maybe the true understanding of everything — seeing things as they really are — could give you enough pleasure and happiness by itself, even when action is blocked by obstacles. This happiness isn't obvious to others, but it's not hidden either. When will you reach the joy of true simplicity and natural dignity? When will you delight in really knowing each thing for what it is: what it's made of, what purpose it serves, how long it lasts, what parts make it up, who can have it, and who can give it or take it away?

meditations_book-10.originalText:
As the spider, when it hath caught the fly that it hunted after, is
not little proud, nor meanly conceited of herself: as he likewise that
hath caught an hare, or hath taken a fish with his net: as another for
the taking of a boar, and another of a bear: so may they be proud,
and applaud themselves for their valiant acts against the Sarmatai, or
northern nations lately defeated. For these also, these famous soldiers
and warlike men, if thou dost look into their minds and opinions, what
do they for the most part but hunt after prey?
meditations_book-10.plainEnglish: A spider catches a fly and feels proud of itself. A hunter catches a rabbit or snares a fish and feels the same way. Another hunter kills a boar or a bear and celebrates. In the same way, soldiers feel proud when they defeat enemies like the Sarmatians or other northern tribes. These famous warriors think they're doing something noble. But if you look at what's really in their minds, what are they doing? They're just hunting for prey like any other predator.

meditations_book-10.originalText:
To find out, and set to thyself some certain way and method of
contemplation, whereby thou mayest clearly discern and represent unto
thyself, the mutual change of all things, the one into the other. Bear
it in thy mind evermore, and see that thou be throughly well exercised
in this particular. For there is not anything more effectual to beget
true magnanimity.
meditations_book-10.plainEnglish: Find a clear way to think about how all things change into each other. Keep this always in mind and practice it well. Nothing else will build true greatness of spirit as effectively.

meditations_book-10.originalText:
He hath got loose from the bonds of his body, and perceiving that
within a very little while he must of necessity bid the world farewell,
and leave all these things behind him, he wholly applied himself, as to
righteousness in all his actions, so to the common nature in all things
that should happen unto him. And contenting himself with these two
things, to do all things justly, and whatsoever God doth send to like
well of it: what others shall either say or think of him, or shall do
against him, he doth not so much as trouble his thoughts with it. To go
on straight, whither right and reason directed him, and by so doing to
follow God, was the only thing that he did mind, that, his only business
and occupation.
meditations_book-10.plainEnglish: He broke free from his body's hold on him. He saw that soon he would have to say goodbye to the world and leave everything behind. So he focused completely on two things: doing what was right in everything he did, and accepting whatever nature brought his way. He was content with just these two goals — to act justly and to welcome whatever God sent him. What other people might say or think about him, or do against him — he didn't even bother thinking about it. His only concern was to keep moving forward where right and reason led him. By doing this, he was following God. That was his only focus, his only work.

meditations_book-10.originalText: What use is there of suspicion at all? or, why should thoughts of mistrust, and suspicion concerning that which is future, trouble thy mind at all?
meditations_book-10.plainEnglish: What's the point of suspicion at all? Why should doubts and mistrust about the future trouble your mind?

meditations_book-10.originalText: What now is to be done, if thou mayest search and inquiry into that, what needs thou care for more? And if thou art well able to perceive it alone, let no man divert thee from it. But if alone thou doest not so well perceive it, suspend thine action, and take advice from the best. And if there be anything else that doth hinder thee, go on with prudence and discretion, according to the present occasion and opportunity, still proposing that unto thyself, which thou doest conceive most right and just. For to hit that aright, and to speed in the prosecution of it, must needs be happiness, since it is that only which we can truly and properly be said to miss of, or miscarry in.
meditations_book-10.plainEnglish: What needs to be done? If you can figure this out on your own, why worry about anything else? And if you can see it clearly by yourself, don't let anyone talk you out of it. But if you can't see it clearly alone, stop and ask for advice from the best people you know. If something else is blocking you, move forward carefully and wisely. Work with what the situation gives you. Always keep in mind what you think is most right and just. To hit this target and succeed at it must be happiness. It's the only thing we can truly fail at or mess up.

meditations_book-10.originalText:
What is that that is slow, and yet quick? merry, and yet grave? He
that in all things doth follow reason for his guide.
meditations_book-10.plainEnglish: What is slow yet quick? Light yet serious? Someone who follows reason as their guide in all things.

meditations_book-10.originalText: In the morning as soon as thou art awaked, when thy judgment, before either thy affections, or external objects have wrought upon it, is yet most free and impartial: put this question to thyself, whether if that which is right and just be done, the doing of it by thyself, or by others when thou art not able thyself; be a thing material or no. For sure it is not.
meditations_book-10.plainEnglish: In the morning when you first wake up, your mind is still clear. Your emotions haven't kicked in yet. Outside things haven't influenced you. This is when you should ask yourself: Does it matter if the right thing gets done by you or by someone else when you can't do it yourself? It doesn't matter at all.

meditations_book-10.originalText: And as for these that keep such a life, and stand so much upon the praises, or dispraises of other men, hast thou forgotten what manner of men they be? that such and such upon their beds, and such at their board: what their ordinary actions are: what they pursue after, and what they fly from: what thefts and rapines they commit, if not with their hands and feet, yet with that more precious part of theirs, their minds: which (would it but admit of them) might enjoy faith, modesty, truth, justice, a good spirit.
meditations_book-10.plainEnglish: And what about these people who live for praise and fear criticism? Have you forgotten what they're really like? How they act in bed and at the dinner table? What they do every day? What they chase after and what they run from? What they steal and grab — maybe not with their hands, but with their minds, which is far worse. Their minds could hold faith, humility, truth, justice, and goodness. But they won't let them in.

meditations_book-10.originalText:
Give what thou wilt, and take away what thou wilt, saith he that is
well taught and truly modest, to Him that gives, and takes away. And it
is not out of a stout and peremptory resolution, that he saith it, but
in mere love, and humble submission.
meditations_book-10.plainEnglish: "Give what you want, and take away what you want," says the person who is well taught and truly humble, speaking to God who gives and takes away. He doesn't say this from stubborn defiance, but from pure love and humble acceptance.

meditations_book-10.originalText:
So live as indifferent to the world and all worldly objects, as
one who liveth by himself alone upon some desert hill. For whether here,
or there, if the whole world be but as one town, it matters not much for
the place. Let them behold and see a man, that is a man indeed, living
according to the true nature of man. If they cannot bear with me, let
them kill me. For better were it to die, than so to live as they would
have thee.
meditations_book-10.plainEnglish: Live detached from the world and worldly things, like someone living alone on a mountain. Whether here or there, if the whole world is just one town, the place doesn't matter much. Let them see a real man, living according to human nature. If they can't stand me, let them kill me. It's better to die than to live the way they want you to.

meditations_book-10.originalText:
Make it not any longer a matter of dispute or discourse, what are
the signs and proprieties of a good man, but really and actually to be
such.
meditations_book-10.plainEnglish: Stop arguing about what makes a good person. Just be one.

meditations_book-10.originalText:
Ever to represent unto thyself; and to set before thee, both the
general age and time of the world, and the whole substance of it. And
how all things particular in respect of these are for their substance,
as one of the least seeds that is: and for their duration, as the
turning of the pestle in the mortar once about. Then to fix thy mind
upon every particular object of the world, and to conceive it, (as it
is indeed,) as already being in the state of dissolution, and of change;
tending to some kind of either putrefaction or dispersion; or whatsoever
else it is, that is the death as it were of everything in his own kind.
meditations_book-10.plainEnglish: Always picture this to yourself: think about the vast age of the world and all that exists in it. See how each particular thing is like the tiniest seed compared to the whole. And how brief each thing lasts — like one turn of a pestle in a mortar. Then focus on any single thing in the world. See it as it really is: already breaking down and changing. Everything tends toward some kind of decay or scattering. This is the death that comes to all things in their own way.

meditations_book-10.originalText:
Consider them through all actions and occupations, of their lives:
as when they eat, and when they sleep: when they are in the act of
necessary exoneration, and when in the act of lust. Again, when they
either are in their greatest exultation; and in the middle of all
their pomp and glory; or being angry and displeased, in great state and
majesty, as from an higher place, they chide and rebuke. How base and
slavish, but a little while ago, they were fain to be, that they might
come to this; and within a very little while what will be their estate,
when death hath once seized upon them.
meditations_book-10.plainEnglish: Picture people going through all their daily activities and jobs. See them when they eat and when they sleep. When they relieve themselves and when they have sex. See them at their highest moments — full of pride and glory. Or when they're angry and upset, acting important and superior, scolding others from their high position. How low and servile they had to be just a little while ago to reach this point. And in a very short time, what will their condition be once death takes them?

meditations_book-10.originalText:
That is best for every one, that the common nature of all doth send
unto every one, and then is it best, when she doth send it.
meditations_book-10.plainEnglish: What's best for each person is what the common nature of all things sends to them. And it's best when nature sends it.

meditations_book-10.originalText:
